    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.1 Fundamentals

    How to Run a System Design Interview

    system design frameworkrequirementsfunctional requirementsnon-functional requirementsback-of-the-envelopecapacity estimationQPSAPI designdata modelhigh-level designdeep divebottlenecktrade-offslatency numbersCAP
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ · Redis Pub/Sub vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka · Celery with Redis as Broker · The 4-Step Framework (Alex Xu, with a News Feed Example) · SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases
    On this page
    1. 1. Requirements: ask before drawing
    2. 2. Estimates: rough, fast, out loud
    3. 3. API
    4. 4. Data model
    5. 5. High-level design
    6. 6. Deep dives: where you get the most credit
    7. 7. Wrap-up
    8. Communication habits

    What: a fixed path to follow in every system design interview (45–60 min), so you never freeze or jump into boxes too early. The interviewer grades how you think: clarifying, prioritizing, justifying trade-offs. A "perfect architecture" isn't the goal.

    Time budget (45 min; scale it for 60):

    # Step Time Output on the board
    1 Requirements 5–8 min functional list, non-functional list, out-of-scope
    2 Estimates 3–5 min QPS (avg/peak), read:write ratio, storage, bandwidth
    3 API 3–5 min 3–5 main endpoints/events
    4 Data model 3–5 min entities, keys, DB choice
    5 High-level design 10 min boxes and arrows for the main flows
    6 Deep dives 10–15 min 2–3 bottlenecks solved in detail
    7 Wrap-up 2–3 min trade-offs, failures, monitoring, what's next
    ↑ top

    1. Requirements: ask before drawing

    Functional (what it does): list the 3–5 core features and agree on them. Explicitly park the rest: "I'll leave search and admin out of scope unless you want them."

    Non-functional (how well): go through this checklist out loud:

    • Scale: how many users / DAU, requests per second, data size, growth?
    • Read vs write heavy? (This decides caching and replicas.)
    • Latency: what has to be fast (e.g. p99 < 200 ms for the feed)?
    • Consistency vs availability: is stale data OK (a feed, a like count) or not (payments, inventory)?
    • Durability: can we ever lose data?
    • Special: real-time? ordering? global/multi-region? security/privacy?

    Questions to always ask: "Who are the users and how many?", "What's the most important flow?", "Is it read-heavy or write-heavy?", "Is eventual consistency acceptable here?"

    ↑ top

    2. Estimates: rough, fast, out loud

    Round aggressively; the goal is the order of magnitude, which drives decisions.

    • 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s, so 1M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS, and 100M/day ≈ 1,200 QPS.
    • Peak ≈ 2–3× average.
    • Storage = new items/day × item size × retention. Example: 10M posts/day × 1 KB × 365 days × 5 years ≈ 18 TB.
    • Bandwidth = QPS × response size.
    • Size units: 1 KB text row, ~100 KB–1 MB image, ~MBs/s video.

    Latency numbers to know (rough):

    Operation Time
    Memory read ~100 ns
    SSD random read ~100 µs
    Round trip within a datacenter ~0.5 ms
    HDD seek ~10 ms
    Round trip across continents ~150 ms

    Rough single-node capacity: a Redis node handles ~100k simple ops/s; a well-indexed Postgres/MySQL node handles thousands to ~10k simple queries/s; a Kafka broker handles hundreds of MB/s. Then say what that implies: "1,200 write QPS fits one primary DB; 50k read QPS needs cache + replicas."

    ↑ top

    3. API

    Write only the core calls, with their key params and responses:

    POST /orders            {user_id, items}       → {order_id, status}
GET  /orders/{id}                              → order
GET  /feed?user_id=&cursor=&limit=20           → {items, next_cursor}

    Mention pagination (cursor), idempotency keys for writes that must not repeat (payments), auth, and rate limiting. For async flows, name the events (order_created) instead of endpoints.

    ↑ top

    4. Data model

    • List the entities and their main fields, plus primary keys and access patterns ("fetch orders by user, newest first" → index (user_id, created_at)).
    • Pick the DB from the access patterns:
    • SQL for relations, transactions and consistency (orders, payments).
    • Key-value or wide-column for huge, simple lookups.
    • Document DB for flexible schemas.
    • A search engine for full-text.
    • Object storage (S3) for files.
    • Say the partition / shard key if the scale requires it, and why (even distribution, queries hit one shard).
    ↑ top

    5. High-level design

    Draw the main request flow end to end, simplest version first:

    client → CDN → load balancer → stateless app servers → cache → DB
                                         └→ queue → workers (async jobs)
                                         └→ object storage (files)

    Walk through 1–2 core use cases on the diagram ("when a user posts…"). Keep app servers stateless so they scale horizontally.

    ↑ top

    6. Deep dives: where you get the most credit

    Pick the 2–3 hardest parts (or ask: "which part would you like me to go deeper on?"). The usual toolkit:

    Problem Tools
    Read-heavy / slow reads cache (Redis) with cache-aside + TTL, read replicas, CDN, denormalization
    Write-heavy sharding, a write queue/buffer, batching, an LSM-based store (Cassandra)
    Big data / hot keys sharding + consistent hashing, splitting hot keys, rate limiting
    Slow or long work async via queue + workers (RabbitMQ / Kafka)
    Real-time push WebSockets/SSE + Redis Pub/Sub fan-out across servers
    Reliability replication, retries with backoff, idempotency, DLQs, circuit breakers
    Consistency transactions, the outbox pattern, sagas, optimistic locking (version column)
    Feeds / timelines fan-out on write vs on read (hybrid for celebrities)
    Unique IDs UUID, Snowflake-style IDs (time-ordered)

    For each deep dive, cover: the problem (with a number) → options → your choice → its trade-off.

    ↑ top

    7. Wrap-up

    • Bottlenecks and single points of failure: what breaks first at 10× load?
    • Failure handling: what happens if the cache, the DB primary, or a worker dies?
    • Monitoring: QPS, p99 latency, error rate, queue/consumer lag, alerts.
    • What you'd do next with more time.
    ↑ top

    Communication habits

    • Think out loud and check in often: "Does this match what you had in mind?"
    • Trade-off sentence for every choice: "I'll use X because Y; the cost is Z, and that's acceptable because…"
    • If the interviewer pushes on something, follow them: it's a hint about what they want to see.
    • Name what you're not doing and why. Silence reads as not knowing.
    • Keep the board clean: requirements and numbers on one side, the diagram in the middle.

    Practice: write each problem up in system-design/<problem>.md using the same steps (template in system-design/README.md), then add a "My mistakes / what I missed" section.

    ⚠ Common traps
    • Drawing boxes in minute 1 without requirements.
    • Over-engineering: Kafka, microservices and sharding for 10 QPS.
    • Naming tech without justification ("use Cassandra" without saying why).
    • Skipping numbers, then making scaling choices that don't follow from anything.
    • Going deep on one component and running out of time before the end-to-end flow exists.

    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.1 Fundamentals

    Kafka vs RabbitMQ

    KafkaRabbitMQcompeting consumersdirect exchangetopic exchangefanout exchangeTTLpriority queuerequest/replyRPCcorrelation_idreply_tomessage brokermessage queueevent streamingpub/subpartitionconsumer groupoffsetexchangerouting keyackdead letter queueDLQreplayorderingbackpressureexactly-onceKRaftquorum queueRabbitMQ streamsat-most-onceat-least-onceidempotent producerproducer IDsequence numberKafka transactionstransactional.idread_committedEOS
    See also Redis Pub/Sub vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka · Celery with Redis as Broker · How to Run a System Design Interview · V1·10 Notification System · V1·14 YouTube · V2·3 Google Maps · V2·4 Distributed Message Queue · V2·5 Metrics Monitoring and Alerting · V2·6 Ad Click Event Aggregation · V2·11 Payment System · SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    What: both move messages between services asynchronously, but they're different models.

    • RabbitMQ is a message broker (smart broker, dumb consumer). It routes each message to queues. A consumer takes a message, acks it, and the message is deleted.
    • Kafka is a distributed append-only log (dumb broker, smart consumer). Messages are written to partitions and kept for a retention period. Each consumer tracks its own offset (position) and can re-read.
    ℹ Why it matters

    "which queue would you use and why?" comes up in almost every system design round. The answer should follow from requirements (replay? ordering? throughput? routing?), not habit.

    Mental model:

    RabbitMQ:  producer → exchange ──(routing key / bindings)──► queue → consumer (ack → deleted)
Kafka:     producer → topic [partition 0 | partition 1 | ...] ← consumer group (each reads its offset)

    Comparison:

    RabbitMQ Kafka
    Model queue: work is distributed and then gone log: events are stored and re-readable
    After consume deleted on ack kept until retention (time/size) or compaction
    Replay no (classic queues); yes with RabbitMQ Streams yes: reset the offset and re-read history
    Routing rich: exchanges (direct, topic, fanout, headers) simple: topic + partition key; consumers filter
    Ordering per queue, but lost with multiple competing consumers or requeues per partition (same key → same partition → ordered)
    Scaling consumers add consumers to a queue (competing consumers) parallelism = number of partitions; one partition → one consumer in a group
    Throughput ~tens of thousands of msgs/s per queue ~millions of msgs/s; scales out by adding partitions and brokers
    Delivery push, with prefetch limiting in-flight messages pull, so consumers control their pace (natural backpressure)
    Per-message features ack/nack, requeue, TTL, priority queues, dead-letter exchanges, delayed messages (plugin) none per message; retries/DLQ are built by the app (retry topics)
    Many independent readers of the same data needs a fanout exchange plus one queue per reader free: each consumer group reads the same log independently
    Exactly-once at-least-once + idempotent consumers exactly-once within Kafka (idempotent producer + transactions); external effects still need idempotency
    Ops single node is simple; quorum queues for HA heavier: brokers, partitions, replication, rebalancing (KRaft replaced ZooKeeper in Kafka 4.0)

    Pick RabbitMQ when:

    • It's a task/job queue: send email, resize image, process payment. Each job is handled once by one worker.
    • You need complex routing (route by type, region, priority).
    • You need per-message control: retries with requeue, TTL, priority, delayed jobs, dead-lettering.
    • The volume is moderate and you want low latency and simple ops.
    • Request/reply (RPC-style) messaging.

    Pick Kafka when:

    • It's an event stream / source of truth: user activity, clicks, logs, metrics, CDC (database change capture).
    • Several consumers need the same events: analytics, search indexing, notifications, each at its own pace.
    • You need replay: reprocess history after a bug, or rebuild a new service's state from the beginning.
    • The throughput is high and you need ordering per key (all events of user_id=42 in order).
    • Stream processing (Kafka Streams, Flink) and event sourcing.

    Why RabbitMQ fits those cases (in depth):

    1. Task/job queue: each job goes to one worker. With many workers on one queue (competing consumers), RabbitMQ hands each message to exactly one. The worker acks when it's done, and the message is deleted. If the worker crashes before acking, the message is redelivered to another worker. Scale by adding workers. Kafka here: parallelism is capped by partitions (3 partitions → at most 3 workers), and one slow job (a 10-minute encode) blocks everything behind it in that partition.

    2. Complex routing. Producers publish to an exchange, and bindings decide which queues get a copy:

      Exchange Rule Example
      direct exact key pdf → pdf_queue
      topic wildcards order.eu.* → EU team, order.*.refund → refunds, order.# → audit
      fanout every bound queue user_signed_up → email + analytics + CRM
      headers header match region=eu AND priority=high

      The producer doesn't know who receives it. Kafka here: consumers read the whole topic and filter themselves, or you add more topics.

    3. Per-message control. Each message is managed individually:

      • nack/requeue to retry
      • TTL: drop it if it isn't processed in 30s (e.g. an OTP)
      • priority queues: VIP orders first
      • delayed delivery: a plugin, or TTL + DLX
      • dead-lettering: after N failures, or on TTL expiry, the message goes to a DLQ to inspect later

      Kafka here: nothing per message, so you build retry and DLQ topics yourself.

    4. Moderate volume, low latency, simple ops. Thousands to tens of thousands of msgs/s covers most business apps. RabbitMQ pushes each message to a waiting consumer (Kafka consumers poll in batches). One node or a small cluster with quorum queues is easy to run; Kafka needs partitions, replication, retention, rebalancing and lag monitoring.

    5. Request/reply (RPC). The request carries reply_to (the queue to answer on) and correlation_id (to match the reply to its request). RabbitMQ supports this natively, including the built-in "direct reply-to". With Kafka you'd build it yourself on topics.

    RabbitMQ = a smart post office: it routes each letter to the right mailbox, one person handles it, it's retried or set aside on failure, then thrown away. Kafka = a recorded journal: everything is written in order and kept, and anyone can read it from any point, any number of times.

    Kafka delivery semantics, mechanically (a common follow-up question): there are two independent failure points — producer→broker, and broker→consumer. Each can be tuned separately.

    How the producer behaves How the consumer behaves Result
    At-most-once fire and forget, or don't retry on a failed ack commit the offset before processing a message can be lost (dropped on a network blip, or skipped if the consumer crashes after commit but before finishing), never duplicated
    At-least-once (Kafka's default) acks=all + retries process first, commit offset after never silently lost, but a retried send or a crash-before-commit can duplicate a message → consumers must be idempotent (dedupe by message id, upsert by key)
    Exactly-once (EOS) idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true): each producer gets a PID and tags every message with a per-partition sequence number; the broker drops a retry with an already-seen sequence number reads with isolation.level=read_committed a producer's retries never duplicate, within one producer session and one partition

    Exactly-once across the full read-process-write loop needs a second mechanism on top: transactions (transactional.id set, beginTransaction() / commitTransaction()). This lets an app write to several output partitions and commit its input offset as one atomic unit — if it crashes mid-way, the whole transaction rolls back and looks like it never ran, so the replay is clean. This is how Kafka Streams gets exactly-once by default.

    The caveat worth saying out loud: Kafka's EOS is exactly-once inside Kafka (topic → topic). The moment the pipeline writes to something external — a database, an HTTP call, an email — Kafka can't make that write transactional. You still need an idempotent write on the external side (upsert keyed by message id, or an outbox) to get an exactly-once effect end to end.

    Interview answer template:

    "If this is a work queue where each task is processed once and I need retries and routing, I'd use RabbitMQ. If it's a stream of events that several services consume independently, or that I may need to replay, with high throughput and per-key ordering, I'd use Kafka. Either way, consumers are idempotent because delivery is at-least-once."

    ✓ Key points
    • Kafka ordering is only per partition. Choose the partition key (e.g. order_id) so related events land together.
    • Kafka parallelism is capped by the partition count: having more consumers than partitions leaves some idle.
    • A slow Kafka consumer doesn't hurt others: it just lags (monitor consumer lag). In RabbitMQ, slow consumers mean queues grow in broker memory/disk.
    • Both are at-least-once by default, so make consumers idempotent (dedupe by message id, upserts).
    • Poison messages: in RabbitMQ, use a dead-letter exchange. In Kafka, use a retry topic and then a DLQ topic, so one bad message doesn't block the partition.
    • The two are converging. RabbitMQ Streams add a replayable log, and Kafka is adding queue-style share groups (KIP-932). The default trade-off above still holds.
    ⚠ Common trap

    "Kafka is just a faster RabbitMQ." No: it's a different model (a log vs a queue). Picking Kafka for a simple job queue gives you no per-message retry/priority/TTL and more ops work. Picking RabbitMQ for event streaming loses replay and multi-consumer fan-out.

    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.1 Fundamentals

    The 4-Step Framework (Alex Xu, with a News Feed Example)

    system design frameworkAlex Xudesign scopehigh-level designbuy-indeep divewrap upuse casenews feedfanouttime allocation
    See also How to Run a System Design Interview · V1·11 News Feed System
    On this page
    1. Step 1 — Understand the problem and establish design scope
    2. Step 2 — Propose a high-level design and get buy-in
    3. Step 3 — Design deep dive
    4. Step 4 — Wrap up
    5. Dos and Don'ts

    What: the framework from System Design Interview (Alex Xu), chapter 3. It has 4 steps. It is the same idea as the 7-step path in coarser steps: there, steps 1–2 are Xu's step 1, steps 3–5 are his step 2, step 6 is his step 3, and step 7 is his step 4. Each step below has a short version and a worked news feed example.

    What the interviewer grades: collaboration, working under pressure, resolving ambiguity, and asking good questions. The final design matters less than how you got there. Red flags: over-engineering, narrow-mindedness, stubbornness.

    # Step Time (45 min)
    1 Understand the problem and establish design scope 3–10 min
    2 Propose a high-level design and get buy-in 10–15 min
    3 Design deep dive 10–25 min
    4 Wrap up 3–5 min
    ↑ top

    Step 1 — Understand the problem and establish design scope

    • Don't answer fast (the book's "Jimmy" story). Quick answers earn no points. Answering without understanding the requirements is a red flag.
    • Ask about the exact requirements:
    • What features are we building?
    • How many users are there?
    • How fast will it grow? What scale do we expect in 3 months, 6 months and a year?
    • What is the tech stack? Which existing services can we reuse?
    • If the interviewer says "you decide", write your assumptions on the board. You will need them later.
    News feed example

    The candidate asks, and the interviewer answers:

    Question Answer
    Mobile app, web app, or both? Both
    Most important features? Make a post, and see friends' news feed
    Feed order: reverse chronological or ranked? Reverse chronological (keep it simple)
    How many friends can a user have? 5,000
    Traffic? 10M DAU
    Text only, or media too? Images and videos too

    Scope you write down: post + view feed, newest first, ≤ 5,000 friends, 10M DAU, media allowed. Every later choice should trace back to one of these lines.

    ↑ top

    Step 2 — Propose a high-level design and get buy-in

    • Sketch an initial blueprint and ask for feedback. Treat the interviewer as a teammate.
    • Draw box diagrams: clients (mobile/web), APIs, web servers, data stores, cache, CDN, message queue.
    • Do back-of-the-envelope math to check the blueprint fits the scale. Think out loud, and ask whether the math is needed first.
    • Walk through 1–2 concrete use cases: follow one real request through the boxes. This frames the design and exposes edge cases.
    • API endpoints and DB schema: include them only if the problem is small enough. Yes for a poker game backend; too low-level for "design Google search". Ask the interviewer.
    News feed example

    Split the design into two flows:

    Feed publishing (Figure 3-1): the user writes a post. It is saved to cache/DB and pushed into friends' feeds.

    client ──POST /v1/me/feed?content=Hello──► load balancer ► web servers
   web servers ─► Post Service ─► post cache ─► post DB
               ─► Fanout Service ─► news feed cache
               ─► Notification Service

    News feed building (Figure 3-2): the feed is the friends' posts, newest first.

    client ──GET /v1/me/feed──► load balancer ► web servers ► News Feed Service ► news feed cache

    Use-case walkthrough:

    1. Alice posts "Hello": the Post Service stores it, the Fanout Service adds it to every friend's feed cache, and the Notification Service tells the friends.
    2. Bob opens his feed: the News Feed Service reads Bob's precomputed feed from the cache.

    Edge cases this walkthrough exposes:

    • Alice has 5,000 friends, so one post means 5,000 cache writes. Do them synchronously or async? → queue + workers (step 3).
    • The feed cache holds IDs, so where do the names and post text come from? → hydration from user/post caches (step 3).
    • Videos should not go through the web servers. → CDN.
    • Alice deletes the post, or Bob unfriends her. → store only IDs in feeds and filter at read time (skip deleted posts and non-friends). Cleanup in the background is optional.
    ↑ top

    Step 3 — Design deep dive

    By now you should have: agreed goals and scope, a high-level blueprint, feedback on it, and an idea of which areas to focus on.

    • Prioritize components with the interviewer. Every interview differs: some want high level only. Senior roles often focus on performance, bottlenecks and resource estimates. Most want one or two components in detail.
    • URL shortener → the hash function that turns a long URL into a short one.
    • Chat system → lowering latency, and online/offline status.
    • Time management: don't get lost in details that show no design skill. For example, Facebook's EdgeRank ranking algorithm takes time and proves nothing about scaling.
    News feed example

    Deep-dive the two most important use cases. Full details are in Xu's chapter 11.

    1. Feed publishing (Figure 3-3)

    • Web servers also do authentication and rate limiting (to stop spam posts).

    • The Fanout Service: 1. gets the friend IDs from a graph DB; 2. gets the friends' data from the user cache (backed by the user DB); 3. puts a fanout job on a message queue; 4. fanout workers consume the queue; 5. the workers write into the news feed cache.

    • Why the queue: the post request returns fast, and the 5,000 writes happen async and can scale with more workers.

    2. News feed retrieval (Figure 3-4)

    1. The client sends GET /v1/me/feed.
    2. The load balancer routes it to the web servers (auth + rate limiting).
    3. The web servers call the News Feed Service.
    4. It reads the post IDs from the news feed cache.
    5. It hydrates them: user data from the user cache/DB and post content from the post cache/DB.
    6. It returns the full feed as JSON. Images and videos come from the CDN.
    ↑ top

    Step 4 — Wrap up

    • Bottlenecks and improvements. Never say the design is perfect; there is always something to improve. Use this to show critical thinking.
    • Recap the design, especially if you discussed several options.
    • Error cases: server failure, network loss.
    • Operations: monitoring metrics and error logs, and how to roll the system out.
    • The next scale curve: what changes from 1M to 10M users?
    • Refinements you would add with more time.
    News feed example

    A 3–5 minute wrap-up might sound like this:

    • Bottleneck: fanout for users with huge follower counts. Use a hybrid: push to normal friends' feeds on write, and pull celebrities' posts at read time.
    • Recap: "Two flows: publishing goes through a queue and fanout workers into feed caches; retrieval reads post IDs from the cache and hydrates them from the user and post caches. Media is on the CDN."
    • Errors: if the cache dies, rebuild the feed from the DB. If a worker crashes, the job stays in the queue and is retried.
    • Ops: watch queue lag, p99 feed latency, cache hit rate and error rate. Roll out behind gradual deploys.
    • Next 10×: shard the caches and DBs by user ID, add more fanout workers, and add read replicas.
    ↑ top

    Dos and Don'ts

    Do Don't
    Ask for clarification; don't trust your own assumptions Be unprepared for the typical questions
    Understand the requirements; there is no single right answer Jump into a solution before clarifying the requirements
    Think out loud and tell the interviewer what you're thinking Go deep on one component before the high-level design exists
    Suggest multiple approaches Stay stuck silently; ask for hints
    After the blueprint is agreed, detail the most critical components first Think in silence
    Bounce ideas off the interviewer as a teammate; never give up Assume you're done when the design is drawn. You're done when the interviewer says so; ask for feedback early and often
    ⚠ Common trap

    drawing the "final" architecture in minute 2. Scope first, then get buy-in, then go deep.

    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.1 Fundamentals

    Redis Pub/Sub vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka

    RedisRedis Pub/SubPUBLISHSUBSCRIBEPSUBSCRIBEfire-and-forgetat-most-onceRedis StreamsXADDXREADGROUPXACKXAUTOCLAIMRedis List queueBRPOPBLMOVEWebSocket fan-outcache invalidation
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ · Celery with Redis as Broker · How to Run a System Design Interview · V1·12 Chat System · V2·2 Nearby Friends · Web & Networking Fundamentals

    What: PUBLISH channel msg pushes the message to every client subscribed right now, then Redis forgets it.

    publisher ──PUBLISH chat:room1 "hi"──► Redis ──► every subscriber connected *right now*
    • No storage: if a subscriber is offline, reconnecting, or not subscribed yet, it never gets the message.
    • No ack / retry: if a subscriber crashes while handling the message, it's gone. This is at-most-once delivery.
    • Broadcast only: every subscriber gets every message; there's no "one job → one worker".
    • Slow subscriber: its output buffer fills up and Redis disconnects it, so those messages are lost.
    • Very fast (in-memory, sub-ms) and trivial to use: SUBSCRIBE, PSUBSCRIBE news.*.

    Comparison:

    Redis Pub/Sub RabbitMQ Kafka
    Model live broadcast queue (routed, deleted on ack) log (retained)
    Stored? no until acked until retention expires
    Offline consumer misses messages gets them when back reads from its offset when back
    Delivery at-most-once at-least-once at-least-once (exactly-once within Kafka)
    Ack / retry / DLQ none yes app-built
    One job → one worker no yes yes (per partition, in a group)
    Replay no no (except Streams) yes
    Latency lowest low low (batching)
    Ops trivial if you already run Redis moderate heavy

    Use Redis Pub/Sub when a lost message doesn't matter, because it's only useful right now or the real data is stored elsewhere:

    • WebSocket fan-out across app servers: users of one chat room are connected to different instances. Each instance subscribes to chat:room1, so one publish reaches all of them. The message itself is saved in the DB.
    • Live UI signals: typing indicators, online status, live prices or scores, where a newer value replaces the old one.
    • Cache invalidation broadcast: "key X changed, drop it". If an instance misses one, the TTL covers it.
    • Config reload signals.

    Never use it for orders, payments, emails or anything that must happen: use RabbitMQ (jobs) or Kafka (events).

    Durable options inside Redis:

    How Gives you Limits
    Streams XADD / XREADGROUP / XACK append-only log with IDs (replay), consumer groups (one entry → one consumer), a pending list + XAUTOCLAIM to take over a dead consumer's entries memory-bound (trim with MAXLEN); scales far less than Kafka
    List queue LPUSH + BRPOP (or BLMOVE for a safer "move to processing list") simple job queue, one job → one worker no real acks or consumer groups (this is what Celery uses, see Celery with Redis)
    ❝ Interview line

    "Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: no persistence or acks, and offline subscribers miss messages. I'd use it for real-time signals like WebSocket fan-out or cache invalidation. For durable jobs I'd use RabbitMQ (or Redis Streams if it's small and we already run Redis), and for durable, replayable event streams at scale, Kafka."

    ⚠ Common trap

    "We already have Redis, so let's use Pub/Sub as our queue." Messages get silently lost on any disconnect or deploy.

    ↑ Back to top⌂ Home
    ← PreviousThe 4-Step Framework (Alex Xu, with a News Feed Example)Next →Celery with Redis as Broker
    ← → to turn pages · / to search
    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.1 Fundamentals

    Celery with Redis as Broker

    CeleryKombuRedis brokerLPUSHBRPOPresult backendvisibility_timeoutunackedtask_acks_lateacks earlyworker_prefetch_multiplierETAcountdownidempotent taskstask priority
    See also Redis Pub/Sub vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka · Kafka vs RabbitMQ · Async / Await · How to Run a System Design Interview · V1·10 Notification System · Locking & Concurrency Control · Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async · Transactions & Migrations

    What: Celery talks to brokers through Kombu, which emulates RabbitMQ (AMQP) concepts on top of Redis: queues become Redis Lists, bindings are stored in Redis sets, and fanout exchanges become PUBLISH.

    your code                      Redis                               worker
add.delay(2, 3) ──LPUSH──► list "celery" [task3, task2, task1] ──BRPOP──► runs add(2, 3)
                                                                         │
            result: key "celery-task-meta-<id>" ◄────────── SET ─────────┘
    1. Send: add.delay(2, 3) serializes the task name, args and id into a message and runs LPUSH celery <msg>. The list name is the queue name (default celery).
    2. Receive: workers block on BRPOP, and Redis gives each message to exactly one worker (competing consumers).
    3. Result (optional): the worker stores the result under celery-task-meta-<task_id>, which expires after 1 day by default. AsyncResult.get() reads it and gets notified via Pub/Sub.

    Where Pub/Sub is used (all fine to lose occasionally):

    • Broadcast/control: celery inspect active, celery control revoke, and shutdown go to all workers.
    • Monitoring events: task-started / task-succeeded for Flower and celery events.
    • Result notifications to code waiting on .get().

    Fake acks: the tricky part. Redis has no acks, so when a worker takes a task, Kombu also copies it into an unacked hash, with a timestamp in a sorted set called unacked_index. The ack removes it. If the worker dies, the message is restored to the queue only after visibility_timeout (default 1 hour).

    Problem Why Fix
    A crashed worker's tasks reappear only after ~1h the visibility timeout is the only failure detection lower visibility_timeout (but keep it longer than your longest task)
    ETA/countdown tasks run multiple times apply_async(countdown=7200): the worker fetches the task now and holds it in memory until the ETA, so it stays unacked > 1h and gets restored to another worker visibility_timeout > the longest ETA, or avoid long countdowns (use a scheduler or DB)

    With RabbitMQ as the broker, neither happens: acks are tied to the worker's connection, so if a worker dies the connection drops and RabbitMQ redelivers immediately.

    When the ack happens (any broker):

    • Default task_acks_late=False: acked when the worker receives the task, before running it. A crash mid-task means the task is lost (at-most-once).
    • task_acks_late=True: acked after the task finishes. A crash means it runs again (at-least-once), so tasks must be idempotent (e.g. check "already charged?" before charging).
    • worker_prefetch_multiplier (default 4): each worker process reserves 4 tasks ahead. For long tasks, set it to 1 so one worker doesn't hoard jobs while others are idle.

    Other Redis-broker gotchas:

    • Durability: queued tasks live in Redis memory. If Redis restarts without AOF/RDB persistence, the queue is lost. RabbitMQ has durable queues on disk.
    • Priorities are emulated: Kombu uses a separate list per priority level (default 0, 3, 6, 9), and on Redis 0 is the highest priority, the opposite of RabbitMQ.
    • Memory: a big backlog uses RAM. Pass IDs, not big objects, in task args.
    ❝ Interview line

    "In Celery, Redis acts as the broker through Lists: LPUSH to send, BRPOP to receive, so each task goes to one worker. Pub/Sub is only used for broadcast commands, events and result notifications. Redis has no native acks, so Kombu emulates them with an unacked set and a visibility timeout (1h by default). That's why crashed tasks come back late and long ETA tasks can run twice. RabbitMQ handles acks natively, so it's the more robust broker. Redis is simpler if you already run it. Either way, use acks_late with idempotent tasks for anything important."

    ⚠ Common trap

    assuming Celery with defaults never loses tasks. With early acks, a worker crash (OOM kill, deploy) silently drops the task it was running.

    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.2 Case Studies › 4.2.1 Volume 1

    V1·4 Rate Limiter

    rate limiterthrottlingtoken bucketleaking bucketfixed windowsliding window logsliding window counterRedisINCR EXPIREHTTP 429API gatewayrace conditionLua scriptdistributed rate limiting
    See also Locking & Concurrency Control

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 4. · Your write-up: Rate Limiter

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a rate limiter. It limits how many requests a client can send in a time window and blocks the excess calls.

    Why it matters: it stops DoS attacks (Twitter: 300 tweets per 3 hours; Google Docs: 300 reads per user per 60 s), it cuts cost (fewer servers, fewer paid third-party API calls), and it keeps servers from overloading.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Client-side or server-side API rate limiter? Server-side API rate limiter
    Throttle by IP, user ID, or something else? Flexible: support different sets of throttle rules
    Scale? Startup or big company? Must handle a large number of requests
    Distributed environment? Yes
    Separate service or in application code? Your design decision
    Tell throttled users? Yes

    Requirements:

    • Functional: accurately limit excessive requests; support flexible rules; show clear exceptions to throttled users.
    • Non-functional:
    • Low latency: must not slow down HTTP response time.
    • Use as little memory as possible.
    • Distributed: shared across many servers or processes.
    • High fault tolerance: if the limiter has a problem (e.g. a cache server goes offline), the whole system keeps working.

    Estimates: the book gives none.

    Try it first: decide where the limiter sits, pick an algorithm, and sketch where the counters live and how two limiter servers share them.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Where to put it:

    • Client-side: unreliable. Requests can be forged, and you may not control the client.
    • Server-side: inside the API servers.
    • Middleware: a rate limiter in front of the API servers. In microservices this is often the API gateway (which also does SSL termination, auth, IP whitelisting).

    Example: the limit is 2 requests/second and a client sends 3. The first two reach the API servers. The middleware throttles the third and returns HTTP 429 (too many requests).

    Server-side vs gateway has no single answer. Guidelines:

    • Check your stack: is your language efficient enough to do it server-side?
    • Server-side gives full control of the algorithm. A third-party gateway may limit your choice.
    • Already have an API gateway for auth and IP whitelisting? Add the limiter there.
    • Building your own takes time. Without enough engineers, use a commercial API gateway.

    Where to store counters: not the database (disk is slow). Use an in-memory cache with time-based expiry. Redis has two useful commands:

    • INCR: increase the counter by 1.
    • EXPIRE: set a timeout; the counter is deleted when it expires.
    client ──► rate limiter middleware ──(under limit)──► API servers
                 │   ▲
                 ▼   │  fetch / increment counter
                 Redis
    • The client sends a request to the middleware.
    • The middleware fetches the counter from the right bucket in Redis and checks the limit.
    • Limit reached → reject the request.
    • Limit not reached → forward to the API servers, and increment the counter in Redis.

    Deep dives

    Rate limiting algorithms

    Token bucket (used by Amazon and Stripe)

    • A bucket has a fixed capacity. A refiller adds tokens at a preset rate. Extra tokens overflow.
    • Each request takes one token. No token → the request is dropped.
    • Example: size 4, refill 4 per minute. At 1:00:00 one request passes (3 left). At 1:00:05 three requests pass (0 left). At 1:00:20 a request is dropped. At 1:01:00 the bucket is refilled to 4.
    • Two parameters: bucket size and refill rate.
    • How many buckets? One per endpoint per user (1 post/s, 150 friends/day, 5 likes/s → 3 buckets per user). One per IP if throttling by IP. One global bucket for a system-wide cap like 10,000 req/s.

    Leaking bucket (used by Shopify)

    • A FIFO queue. If the queue is full, the request is dropped; otherwise it is queued.
    • Requests are pulled from the queue and processed at a fixed rate.
    • Two parameters: bucket size (queue size) and outflow rate.

    Fixed window counter

    • Split the timeline into fixed windows, one counter each. Each request adds 1. At the threshold, drop until the next window.
    • Problem: bursts at window edges. Limit 5/min, reset on the minute. 5 requests in 2:00:30–2:01:00 and 5 in 2:01:00–2:01:30 → 10 requests in one rolling minute, twice the limit.

    Sliding window log

    • Keep request timestamps (e.g. in a Redis sorted set).
    • On a new request: remove timestamps older than the window start, add the new timestamp, accept if the log size ≤ the limit.
    • Example, 2/min: 1:00:01 accepted; 1:00:30 accepted (size 2); 1:00:50 rejected (size 3, but the timestamp stays in the log); 1:01:40 removes 1:00:01 and 1:00:30 → size 2 → accepted.

    Sliding window counter (hybrid of fixed window + sliding log)

    • Requests in rolling window = current window + previous window × overlap % of the rolling window with the previous window.
    • Example, limit 7/min: 5 requests last minute, 3 this minute, new request at 30% into the minute → 3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5 → rounded down to 6 → allowed. One more request hits the limit.
    Algorithm Pros Cons
    Token bucket Easy; memory efficient; allows short bursts Bucket size and refill rate are hard to tune
    Leaking bucket Memory efficient (bounded queue); stable outflow rate A burst fills the queue with old requests, so new ones are dropped; two params hard to tune
    Fixed window counter Memory efficient; easy; reset at window end fits some cases Spikes at window edges let up to 2× the quota through
    Sliding window log Very accurate: never exceeds the limit in any rolling window Uses a lot of memory; rejected requests' timestamps are still stored
    Sliding window counter Smooths spikes; memory efficient Approximation (assumes the previous window was even); Cloudflare: only 0.003% of 400M requests wrong

    Rate limiting rules

    Example from Lyft's open-source limiter: rules live in config files on disk.

    domain: messaging
descriptors:
  - key: message_type
    value: marketing
    rate_limit:
      unit: day
      requests_per_unit: 5      # max 5 marketing messages per day
---
domain: auth
descriptors:
  - key: auth_type
    value: login
    rate_limit:
      unit: minute
      requests_per_unit: 5      # max 5 logins per minute

    Exceeding the limit

    • Return HTTP 429. Depending on the use case, enqueue the request for later (e.g. orders throttled during overload).
    • Response headers:
    • X-Ratelimit-Remaining: requests left in the window.
    • X-Ratelimit-Limit: calls allowed per window.
    • X-Ratelimit-Retry-After: seconds to wait before retrying.
    • A throttled user gets 429 plus X-Ratelimit-Retry-After.

    Detailed design

                                      Rules (disk) ◄── workers pull rules
                                                         │
                                                         ▼
                                                  Cached rules
                                                         ▲
client ──► rate limiter middleware ──────────────────────┘
                 │      │
                 │      ├──(success)──► API servers
                 │      └──► Redis (counters, last request timestamp)
                 │
                 └─(rate limited)─► 429 to client
                                    + option 1: drop the request
                                    + option 2: push to message queue
    • Workers pull rules from disk into a cache.
    • The middleware loads rules from the cache and counters + last request timestamp from Redis.
    • Not limited → forward to API servers. Limited → 429, and drop or enqueue the request.

    Distributed environment

    Race condition. The flow is read counter → check counter + 1 → write. Two concurrent requests both read 3 and both write 4; the correct value is 5. Locks fix it but slow the system a lot. Use a Lua script or Redis sorted sets instead.

    Synchronization. Many limiter servers are needed. The web tier is stateless, so a client's requests can hit different limiters; without sync, limiter 1 knows nothing about client 2.

    • Sticky sessions: not advisable; neither scalable nor flexible.
    • Centralized store (Redis) that all limiters share: the book's choice.
    client 1 ──► rate limiter 1 ──┐
                              ├──► Redis
client 2 ──► rate limiter 2 ──┘

    Performance optimization

    • Multi-data center / edge servers: latency is high for users far away. Route traffic to the closest edge (Cloudflare had 194 edge locations as of 5/20 2020).
    • Synchronize data with eventual consistency (see Ch 6, Key-Value Store).

    Monitoring

    Check that the algorithm and the rules are effective. Too strict rules drop valid requests → relax them. The limiter fails during sudden bursts like flash sales → switch to an algorithm that supports bursts; token bucket fits.

    Wrap-up

    • Hard vs soft limiting: hard never exceeds the threshold; soft can exceed it for a short time.
    • Other layers: this chapter is layer 7 (HTTP). You can also limit by IP at layer 3 with iptables.
    • Avoid being rate limited (client side): cache on the client, know the limits, catch errors to recover gracefully, add enough back-off time to retries.
    ✓ Key points
    • Put the limiter in middleware or the API gateway; reject with 429 and tell the client via X-Ratelimit-* headers.
    • Store counters in Redis (INCR + EXPIRE), not a database.
    • Compare the 5 algorithms; pick by need: bursts → token bucket, steady outflow → leaking bucket, accuracy → sliding log, cheap and close → sliding counter.
    • Rules live in config files, cached by workers; the middleware reads them from the cache.
    • Distributed: fix read-check-write races with Lua scripts or sorted sets, and share one central Redis instead of sticky sessions.
    ⚠ Common trap

    using a plain fixed window and missing that a burst across a window edge lets twice the limit through. Also: wrapping the counter in a lock, which kills latency.

    V1·5 Consistent Hashing

    consistent hashinghash ringrehashing problemmodulo hashingvirtual nodesvnodespartitioningshardingSHA-1cache misseshotspotDynamoCassandrahorizontal scaling
    See also SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 5.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a way to distribute keys across servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a few keys.

    This is a technique, not a product. The setting is a pool of cache (or data) servers that must scale horizontally and spread load evenly.

    Clarifying questions → answers: the chapter has no Q&A. These are the assumptions it works with:

    Question Answer
    What is being distributed? Cache keys (or data) across a pool of servers
    Does the pool change? Yes: servers are added and go offline
    What hurts when keys move? Clients hit the wrong server → a storm of cache misses

    Requirements:

    • Functional: map any key to exactly one server; look it up without a central table.
    • Non-functional:
    • Adding or removing a server moves only a small fraction of keys.
    • Keys spread evenly; no server gets most of the data.
    • Scales horizontally; helps with hotspot keys.

    Estimates: none. The only number to know is the goal: on resize, only k/n keys move on average (k = keys, n = slots).

    Try it first: show why hash(key) % N fails when one of 4 servers dies, then sketch a scheme where only that server's keys move.

    Solution

    High-level design

    The rehashing problem. With N servers, the simple method is serverIndex = hash(key) % N. It works only while N is fixed.

    4 servers, 8 keys. Then server 1 goes offline, so N = 3:

    key hash hash % 4 hash % 3
    key0 18358617 1 0
    key1 26143584 0 0
    key2 18131146 2 1
    key3 35863496 0 2
    key4 34085809 1 1
    key5 27581703 3 0
    key6 38164978 2 1
    key7 22530351 3 0

    With the 3 remaining servers re-indexed (0 = server 0, 1 = server 2, 2 = server 3), key0, key3, key4, key5 and key7 all change server. Only key0 and key4 were on server 1. Most keys move, not just the dead server's keys → cache-miss storm.

    Consistent hashing (Karger et al., MIT): when the table is resized, only k/n keys need to move on average. Traditional hashing remaps nearly all keys.

    The hash ring:

    • Take a hash function f, e.g. SHA-1. Its space is 0 … 2^160 − 1.
    • Join both ends of the space → a ring.
    • Hash each server (by IP or name) onto the ring with f.
    • Hash each key onto the same ring with f. There is no modulo.
    • Lookup: from the key's position, go clockwise to the first server. That server stores the key.
    ring, read clockwise (the end wraps back to the start):

  k0 ─► s0 ── k1 ─► s1 ── k2 ─► s2 ── k3 ─► s3 ──┐
  ▲                                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  key0 → s0, key1 → s1, key2 → s2, key3 → s3
    • Add a server: s4 lands between k0 and s0 (k0 ─► s4 ── s0). Only key0 moves (s0 → s4). k1, k2, k3 stay.
    • Remove a server: s1 is removed. Only key1 moves (s1 → s2). The rest stay.

    Deep dives

    Two issues with the basic approach

    1. Uneven partitions. A partition is the hash space between two adjacent servers. Servers come and go, so partition sizes drift. Example: remove s1, and s2's partition becomes twice as large as s0's and s3's.
    2. Non-uniform key distribution. If the servers cluster on one part of the ring, most keys land on one server. Example: s0, s1, s2, s3 bunched together → most keys go to server 2, and servers 1 and 3 get none.

    Virtual nodes

    • Each real server appears on the ring as many virtual nodes. Server 0 is s0_0, s0_1, s0_2; server 1 is s1_0, s1_1, s1_2. (3 is arbitrary; real systems use many more.)
    • Each server now owns many small partitions spread around the ring.
    • Lookup: go clockwise to the first virtual node, then map it to its server. Example: k0 → s1_1 → server 1.
    • More virtual nodes → smaller standard deviation → more balanced data.
    Virtual nodes per server Std dev of load (vs mean)
    100 ~10%
    200 ~5%
    • Trade-off: more virtual nodes need more space to store vnode metadata. Tune the count to your requirements.

    Find affected keys

    • Server added (s4): start at s4 and go anticlockwise until you hit a server (s3). Keys between s3 and s4 move to s4.
    • Server removed (s1): start at s1 and go anticlockwise until you hit a server (s0). Keys between s0 and s1 move to s2 (the next server clockwise).
    add s4:     s3 ──[keys here move to s4]── s4 ── s0 ...
remove s1:  s0 ──[keys here move to s2]── s1(x) ── s2

    Wrap-up

    Benefits:

    • Very few keys are redistributed when servers are added or removed.
    • Easy to scale horizontally because data is spread more evenly.
    • Mitigates hotspot keys: e.g. Katy Perry, Justin Bieber and Lady Gaga's data are less likely to land on the same shard.

    Real-world users:

    • Amazon Dynamo (partitioning)
    • Apache Cassandra (data partitioning across the cluster)
    • Discord chat
    • Akamai CDN
    • Google Maglev network load balancer
    ✓ Key points
    • Start with why % N fails: changing N remaps most keys and floods the backend with misses.
    • Servers and keys share one hash space (e.g. SHA-1, 0 … 2^160 − 1); a key goes to the first server clockwise.
    • Adding or removing a server moves only the keys in one arc, about k/n of them.
    • Basic ring has uneven partitions and skew; virtual nodes fix both (100 → ~10%, 200 → ~5% std dev), at the cost of metadata.
    • Affected range = from the changed node anticlockwise to the previous server.
    ⚠ Common trap

    saying "consistent hashing balances load" without virtual nodes. With one point per server, partitions are uneven and one server can own most keys.

    V1·6 Key-Value Store

    key-value storedistributed hash tableCAP theoremquorumeventual consistencyvector clockgossip protocolsloppy quorumhinted handoffMerkle treeSSTablebloom filterDynamoCassandraput get
    See also SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 6.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a distributed key-value store that supports two operations: put(key, value) and get(key).

    Keys are unique. A short key works better (plain text like last_logged_in_at or a hash like 253DDEC4). The value is an opaque object: a string, list, object, etc.

    Clarifying questions → answers: the book lists the scope directly. As Q&A:

    Question Answer
    How big is a key-value pair? Small: less than 10 KB
    How much data? Big data: more than one server can hold
    Availability? High: respond quickly, even during failures
    Scaling? High scalability, and automatic: add/remove servers based on traffic
    Consistency? Tunable
    Latency? Low

    Requirements:

    • Functional: put(key, value), get(key).
    • Non-functional: store big data, high availability, high and automatic scalability, tunable consistency, low latency.

    Estimates: the book gives none. A single server fills up fast even with compression and keeping only hot data in memory (the rest on disk), so the store must be distributed.

    Try it first: pick CP or AP, then sketch how keys are partitioned, how many copies you keep, and how a read and a write reach the replicas.

    Solution

    High-level design

    API: get(key) and put(key, value).

    Start from CAP. A distributed system can give at most two of:

    • Consistency: all clients see the same data at the same time, whatever node they hit.
    • Availability: every request gets a response, even if some nodes are down.
    • Partition tolerance: the system keeps working when nodes can't talk to each other.
    Type Keeps Gives up Note
    CP Consistency + partition tolerance Availability e.g. bank balances: return an error until consistent
    AP Availability + partition tolerance Consistency keep serving reads (maybe stale) and accepting writes; sync later
    CA Consistency + availability Partition tolerance cannot exist: network failure is unavoidable

    Example: data on n1, n2, n3; n3 goes down. CP blocks all writes to n1 and n2. AP keeps accepting writes on n1 and n2 and syncs n3 when the partition heals. Discuss the choice with the interviewer. The book's design goes AP with eventual consistency, like Dynamo and Cassandra.

    Architecture:

    ring of nodes n0 … n7 (consistent hashing); key's replicas = n0, n1, n2 (N = 3)

client ──read/write──► n6 (coordinator) ──► n0, n1, n2
       ◄───response──── n6               ◄── ACKs / data
    • Clients use a simple API: get(key) and put(key, value).
    • A coordinator node is a proxy between the client and the store.
    • Nodes sit on a ring via consistent hashing.
    • The system is fully decentralized, so adding and moving nodes can be automatic.
    • Data is replicated on multiple nodes.
    • No single point of failure: every node has the same jobs: client API, failure detection, conflict resolution, failure repair, replication, storage engine.

    Deep dives

    Data partition

    Two challenges: spread data evenly, and move little data when nodes join or leave. Consistent hashing solves both (see V1·5): put servers on a ring, hash the key, store it on the first server clockwise.

    • Automatic scaling: servers can be added and removed based on load.
    • Heterogeneity: virtual nodes per server are proportional to its capacity. Bigger servers get more.

    Data replication

    • Replicate asynchronously to N servers (N is configurable).
    • Pick them by walking clockwise from the key and taking the first N servers. N = 3: key0 → s1, s2, s3.
    • With virtual nodes, the first N nodes may belong to fewer than N physical servers. Choose only unique servers on the walk.
    • Nodes in one data center fail together (power, network, disasters). Place replicas in different data centers linked by fast networks.

    Consistency: quorum consensus

    • N = number of replicas.
    • W = write quorum: a write succeeds after W replicas acknowledge.
    • R = read quorum: a read waits for at least R replicas.
    • W = 1 does not mean data is written to one server. The coordinator sends to all N and waits for just 1 ACK.
    • Trade-off: W or R = 1 is fast (wait for any one replica). W or R > 1 is more consistent but slower (wait for the slowest replica).
    Setting Effect
    R = 1, W = N Optimized for fast reads
    W = 1, R = N Optimized for fast writes
    W + R > N Strong consistency: at least one overlapping node has the latest data (usually N = 3, W = R = 2)
    W + R ≤ N Strong consistency not guaranteed

    Consistency models:

    • Strong: a read always returns the latest write. Usually done by blocking reads/writes on a replica until all replicas agree on the current write. Bad for high availability.
    • Weak: later reads may not see the latest value.
    • Eventual: a weak form; given enough time, all replicas converge. The book's choice (as in Dynamo and Cassandra). Concurrent writes can create conflicting values; the client reads them and reconciles.

    Inconsistency resolution: vector clocks

    How conflicts arise: n1 and n2 both hold name = john. Server 1 sets johnSanFrancisco and server 2 sets johnNewYork at the same time → two conflicting versions v1 and v2, with no clear winner.

    Versioning: every change is a new immutable version. A vector clock is a list of [server, version] pairs on a data item: D([S1, v1], [S2, v2], …). On a write of D to server Si: increment vi if [Si, vi] exists, else add [Si, 1].

    D1([Sx,1])               write handled by Sx
   │
D2([Sx,2])               write handled by Sx (overwrites D1)
   ├──────────────────────┐
D3([Sx,2],[Sy,1])     D4([Sx,2],[Sz,1])    two clients update D2 via Sy and Sz → conflict
   └──────────┬───────────┘
D5([Sx,3],[Sy,1],[Sz,1])  client reconciles; written by Sx
    • Ancestor (no conflict): every counter in Y ≥ the matching counter in X. D([s0,1],[s1,1]) is an ancestor of D([s0,1],[s1,2]).
    • Sibling (conflict): some counter in Y is less than in X. D([s0,1],[s1,2]) vs D([s0,2],[s1,1]).
    • Downsides:
    • The client must implement conflict-resolution logic.
    • The pairs can grow fast. Cap the length and drop the oldest pairs. That can make reconciliation inaccurate, but per the Dynamo paper Amazon has not hit this in production.

    Failure detection: gossip

    • One server saying "X is down" is not enough. Usually you need at least two independent sources.
    • All-to-all multicasting works but is inefficient with many servers.
    • Gossip protocol (decentralized):
    • Each node keeps a membership list: member ID, heartbeat counter, time.
    • Each node increments its own heartbeat counter periodically.
    • Each node sends heartbeats to random nodes, which pass them on.
    • Nodes update their lists with the latest info.
    • If a member's heartbeat has not increased for a set period, it is offline.
    • Example: s0's list shows member 2 stuck at 9908 since 11:58:02 while others are around 10,230 at 12:00. s0 gossips this to random nodes; once others confirm, s2 is marked down and the news spreads.

    Temporary failures: sloppy quorum + hinted handoff

    • A strict quorum can block reads and writes when replicas are down.
    • Sloppy quorum: use the first W healthy servers for writes and the first R healthy servers for reads on the ring. Ignore offline servers.
    • Hinted handoff: if s2 is down, s3 handles its reads and writes for now. When s2 is back, s3 hands the data back to s2.

    Permanent failures: anti-entropy with Merkle trees

    • Anti-entropy: compare data on replicas and update each to the newest version.
    • A Merkle tree (hash tree): each non-leaf node is the hash of its children. It finds differences while moving little data.

    • Building one, key space 1–12: 1. Split the key space into buckets (4 here) to limit tree depth. 2. Hash each key in a bucket. 3. Make one hash node per bucket. 4. Build up to the root by hashing children.

    • Compare: if root hashes match, the replicas are the same. If not, compare left child, then right child, and walk down to the buckets that differ. Sync only those.

    • Data to sync is proportional to the differences, not the total data. Real config example: 1 million buckets for 1 billion keys → 1,000 keys per bucket.

    Data center outage

    Replicate data across multiple data centers. If one is fully offline, users read through the others.

    Write path (based on Cassandra)

    client ─write─► node
                 1. append to commit log (disk)
                 2. save in memory cache
                 3. when cache is full / hits threshold → flush to SSTable (disk)

    An SSTable (sorted-string table) is a sorted list of <key, value> pairs.

    Read path

    client ─read─► node
                 1. in memory cache? → return it
                 2. no → check bloom filter
                 3. bloom filter says which SSTables might have the key
                 4. SSTables return the data
                 5. return result to client

    Wrap-up

    The book's summary table:

    Goal / problem Technique
    Ability to store big data Consistent hashing to spread load across servers
    High availability reads Data replication; multi-data center setup
    Highly available writes Versioning and conflict resolution with vector clocks
    Dataset partition Consistent hashing
    Incremental scalability Consistent hashing
    Heterogeneity Consistent hashing
    Tunable consistency Quorum consensus
    Handling temporary failures Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff
    Handling permanent failures Merkle tree
    Handling data center outage Cross-data center replication
    ✓ Key points
    • Open with CAP: CA is impossible, so choose CP or AP with the interviewer. This design is AP with eventual consistency.
    • Partition with consistent hashing; replicate to N unique servers clockwise, spread across data centers.
    • Tune consistency with N, W, R; W + R > N gives strong consistency (N = 3, W = R = 2).
    • Resolve conflicting writes with vector clocks; the client reconciles siblings.
    • Failures: gossip to detect, sloppy quorum + hinted handoff for temporary, Merkle trees for permanent, cross-DC replication for outages.
    • Each node: commit log → memory cache → SSTables; reads use a bloom filter to skip SSTables.
    ⚠ Common trap

    thinking W = 1 means the data is written to only one server. The coordinator still sends to all N replicas; W is only how many ACKs it waits for.

    V1·7 Unique ID Generator

    unique ID generatordistributed IDTwitter snowflake64-bit IDUUIDticket serverFlickrmulti-master replicationauto_incrementsortable IDtimestamp bitssequence numbercustom epochclock synchronizationNTP
    See also SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 7.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a unique ID generator for a distributed system. A database auto_increment key does not work here: one DB server is not big enough, and keeping IDs unique across many DBs with low delay is hard.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    What are the characteristics of the IDs? Unique and sortable
    Does each new ID go up by exactly 1? No. IDs grow with time, not always by 1. Evening IDs > morning IDs on the same day.
    Numbers only? Yes
    Length? Must fit in 64 bits
    Scale? 10,000 IDs per second

    Example IDs from the book: 1227238262110117894, 1241107244890099715, 1567981766075453440.

    Requirements:

    • IDs are unique.
    • IDs are numeric only.
    • IDs fit in 64 bits.
    • IDs are ordered by date.
    • Generate over 10,000 unique IDs per second.

    Estimates: none beyond the 10,000 IDs/s target.

    Try it first: list 3–4 ways to generate IDs, check each against the 5 requirements, then draw the bit layout of a 64-bit ID that meets them all.

    Solution

    High-level design

    The book compares four options. Only the last one meets every requirement.

    1. Multi-master replication

    MySQL #1 ──► 1, 3, 5, ...  ──┐
                             ├──► Web servers
MySQL #2 ──► 2, 4, 6, ...  ──┘
    • Use each DB's auto_increment, but step by k (k = number of DB servers) instead of 1.
    • IDs scale with the number of DB servers.
    • Cons: hard to scale across multiple data centers; IDs do not go up with time across servers; adding or removing a server breaks the scheme.

    2. UUID

    Web server + ID generator   Web server + ID generator   ...
(each server makes its own IDs, no coordination)
    • 128-bit number, e.g. 09c93e62-50b4-468d-bf8a-c07e1040bfb2.
    • Collision chance is tiny: you need 1 billion UUIDs per second for ~100 years to reach a 50% chance of one duplicate.
    • Pros: simple; no coordination or sync between servers; scales with the web servers.
    • Cons: 128 bits (we need 64); not time-ordered; can be non-numeric.

    3. Ticket server (Flickr)

    Web Server   Web Server   Web Server   Web Server
      \           |           |           /
                 Ticket Server
     (one DB with a central auto_increment)
    • Pros: numeric IDs; easy to build; fine for small to medium scale.
    • Cons: single point of failure. More ticket servers fix that but bring data sync problems.

    4. Twitter snowflake (chosen)

    Split the 64-bit ID into sections ("divide and conquer"):

    | 1 bit | 41 bits    | 5 bits        | 5 bits     | 12 bits         |
|   0   | timestamp  | datacenter ID | machine ID | sequence number |
    • Sign bit (1): always 0. Reserved for future use (e.g. signed vs unsigned).
    • Timestamp (41): ms since the epoch. The book uses Twitter's default epoch 1288834974657 (Nov 04, 2010, 01:42:54 UTC).
    • Datacenter ID (5): 2^5 = 32 datacenters.
    • Machine ID (5): 2^5 = 32 machines per datacenter.
    • Sequence (12): +1 for each ID made on that machine/process; resets to 0 every ms.

    Deep dives

    Fixed vs runtime parts

    • Datacenter ID and machine ID are chosen at startup and normally stay fixed.
    • Change them only with careful review. An accidental change can cause ID conflicts.
    • Timestamp and sequence are produced at runtime.

    Timestamp

    • The 41 timestamp bits are the most significant part. Time grows, so IDs sort by time.
    • Decoding example (Figure 7-7):
    0-00100010101001011010011011000101101011000-01010-01100-000000000000
        41-bit timestamp → decimal 297616116568
        + Twitter epoch 1288834974657 = 1586451091225 ms
        → Apr 09 2020 16:51:31 UTC
    • Max value: 2^41 − 1 = 2,199,023,255,551 ms ≈ 69 years.
    • A custom epoch close to today delays overflow. After 69 years you need a new epoch or an ID migration.

    Sequence number

    • 12 bits = 2^12 = 4,096 values.
    • It stays 0 unless one server makes more than one ID in the same ms.
    • So one machine can make up to 4,096 IDs per ms in theory. That is far above 10,000/s.

    How the options compare (summary of the book's pros/cons):

    Option 64-bit numeric Time-ordered Scales / no SPOF
    Multi-master Yes No Hard across DCs, hard to add/remove servers
    UUID No (128-bit, may be non-numeric) No Yes
    Ticket server Yes Not discussed No, single point of failure
    Snowflake Yes Yes Yes

    Wrap-up

    Snowflake is chosen because it meets all the use cases and scales in a distributed setup. Extra talking points:

    • Clock synchronization. The design assumes all ID servers share one clock. That may be false across cores or machines. NTP is the most popular fix. The book leaves the details out of scope.
    • Section length tuning. Fewer sequence bits and more timestamp bits suit low-concurrency, long-lived apps.
    • High availability. The ID generator is mission-critical, so it must be highly available.
    ✓ Key points
    • Start by saying why auto_increment fails: one DB is not enough, and many DBs can't agree cheaply.
    • Walk through the 4 options and reject each with one requirement it breaks.
    • Draw the 1/41/5/5/12 layout and explain each field.
    • Quote the numbers: ~69 years of timestamps, 4,096 IDs per ms per machine, 32 × 32 machines.
    • Point out the IDs sort by time because the timestamp is in the high bits.
    • End with clock sync (NTP), bit tuning, and high availability.
    ⚠ Common trap

    Picking UUID because it is "simple and unique". It fails two hard requirements: 64 bits and time ordering. Also, forgetting that snowflake depends on synced clocks.

    V1·8 URL Shortener

    URL shortenerTinyURLshort URL301 vs 302 redirectbase 62hash collisionCRC32MD5SHA-1bloom filterunique ID generatorread-heavycacheredirecthashValue length
    See also Web & Networking Fundamentals · SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 8. · Your write-up: URL Shortener

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a URL shortening service like TinyURL. Given a long URL, return a short alias. Clicking the alias redirects to the original URL.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Example? https://www.systeminterview.com/q=chatsystem&c=loggedin&v=v3&l=long → https://tinyurl.com/y7keocwj
    Traffic? 100 million URLs generated per day
    How short? As short as possible
    Allowed characters? 0-9, a-z, A-Z
    Can short URLs be deleted or updated? No (keep it simple)

    Requirements:

    • Functional: shorten (long URL → short URL); redirect (short URL → original URL).
    • Non-functional: high availability, scalability, fault tolerance.

    Estimates:

    • Writes: 100M / 24 / 3600 ≈ 1,160/s.
    • Reads (10:1 read:write): 11,600/s.
    • Records over 10 years: 100M × 365 × 10 = 365 billion.
    • Average URL length: 100 bytes.
    • Storage over 10 years: the book says 365 TB. (Note: 365B × 100 bytes is ~36.5 TB; the book multiplies by 10 years twice. Either way, it is not small.)

    Try it first: write the two APIs, decide 301 or 302, compute the short-code length, and pick how to turn a long URL into that code.

    Solution

    High-level design

    API (REST):

    POST api/v1/data/shorten
  request:  {longUrl: longURLString}
  returns:  shortURL

GET api/v1/shortUrl
  returns:  longURL for HTTP redirection

    Redirect flow:

    Client ── GET https://tinyurl.com/qtj5opu ──► tinyurl server
Client ◄── 301, Location: <long URL> ──────── tinyurl server
Client ── GET <long URL> ───────────────────► amazon.com server

    301 vs 302:

    301 Moved Permanently 302 Found (temporary)
    Browser caches it? Yes No
    Later requests Go straight to the long URL Go through the shortener again
    Best for Lower server load Analytics (click rate, click source)
    • Simplest model: a hash table of <shortURL, longURL>; redirect = hashTable.get(shortURL).
    • Short URL format: www.tinyurl.com/{hashValue}.
    • The hash function must map each long URL to one hashValue, and each hashValue must map back to its long URL.

    Deep dives

    Data model

    • A hash table in memory is too costly at this size.
    • Store the mapping in a relational DB table url:
    url
  id        PK, auto increment
  shortURL
  longURL

    Hash value length

    • 62 characters: 10 digits + 26 lower + 26 upper.
    • Find the smallest n with 62^n ≥ 365 billion.
    n 62^n
    5 916,132,832
    6 56,800,235,584
    7 3,521,614,606,208 ≈ 3.5 trillion
    • So n = 7.

    Option A: hash + collision resolution

    • Use CRC32, MD5 or SHA-1. Even the shortest is too long for https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design:
    Hash Hex value
    CRC32 5cb54054
    MD5 5a62509a84df9ee03fe1230b9df8b84e
    SHA-1 0eeae7916c06853901d9ccbefbfcaf4de57ed85b
    • Take the first 7 characters. That can collide. On a collision, append a predefined string to the long URL and hash again, until there is no collision:
    longURL → hash → first 7 chars → exists in DB?
   ▲                               │ yes (collision)
   └──── longURL + predefined ◄────┘
                                   │ no
                                save to DB
    • Cost: a DB lookup per request. A bloom filter (fast, space-efficient, probabilistic set check) makes this cheaper.

    Option B: base 62 conversion

    • Map digits: 0–9 → 0-9, 10–35 → a-z, 36–61 → A-Z.
    • Example: 11157 = 2 × 62² + 55 × 62¹ + 59 × 62⁰ → [2, 55, 59] → 2TX.
    11157 / 62 = 179  rem 59 → X
  179 / 62 = 2    rem 55 → T
    2 / 62 = 0    rem 2  → 2      → read upward: 2TX
    • Short URL: https://tinyurl.com/2TX.

    Comparison

    Hash + collision resolution Base 62 conversion
    Fixed short URL length Length grows with the ID
    No unique ID generator needed Needs a unique ID generator
    Collisions possible; must resolve No collisions; IDs are unique
    Next short URL can't be guessed Next URL is easy to guess if IDs go +1 (security concern)

    Book's choice: base 62.

    URL shortening flow

    1. input longURL
2. longURL in DB? ── yes ──► 3. return existing shortURL
        │ no
4. generate a new unique ID (distributed ID generator, see Ch 7)
5. convert ID to shortURL with base 62
6. save (id, shortURL, longURL) to DB
    • Example: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design → ID 2009215674938 → zn9edcu.
    • Stored row: id=2009215674938, shortURL=zn9edcu, longURL=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design.

    URL redirecting flow

    User ─(1) GET tinyurl.com/zn9edcu─► Load balancer ─(2)─► Web servers
                                                         │(3)      │(4)
                                                       Cache    Database
User ◄──(5) return long URL ─────────────────────────────┘
    1. User clicks https://tinyurl.com/zn9edcu.
    2. The load balancer forwards to a web server.
    3. If the short URL is in the cache, return the long URL.
    4. On a cache miss, read the DB. If it is not in the DB, the short URL is probably invalid.
    5. Return the long URL to the user.
    • Reads far outnumber writes, so the cache is the key performance piece.

    Wrap-up

    • Rate limiter: stop abusers who flood the shorten API (filter by IP or other rules; see Ch 4).
    • Web tier scaling: it is stateless, so add or remove servers freely.
    • DB scaling: replication and sharding.
    • Analytics: how many clicks, and when.
    • Availability, consistency, reliability (Ch 1).
    ✓ Key points
    • Do the math first: 1,160 writes/s, 11,600 reads/s, 365B URLs → 7 base-62 chars.
    • Explain 301 vs 302 and pick based on load vs analytics.
    • Compare hash+collision with base 62; choose base 62 with a distributed ID generator.
    • Check "long URL already exists?" before creating a new row, so one long URL keeps one short URL.
    • Put a cache in front of the DB for redirects.
    • Mention rate limiting and the guessable-ID security concern.
    ⚠ Common trap

    Truncating MD5/SHA-1 to 7 chars and ignoring collisions. Also, using 301 when the product needs click analytics: the browser caches it and you never see repeat clicks.
