    V1·9 Web Crawler

    web crawlerspiderURL frontierpolitenessfront queuesback queuesBFS vs DFSrobots.txtDNS cachecontent seenURL seenbloom filterspider trapduplicate contentfreshnessPageRank
    See also Web & Networking Fundamentals

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 9.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a web crawler for a search engine. It starts from some URLs, downloads the pages, extracts links, and keeps going. Other uses are web archiving, web mining and web monitoring.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Main purpose? Search engine indexing
    Pages per month? 1 billion
    Content types? HTML only
    New or edited pages? Yes, handle them
    Store crawled HTML? Yes, up to 5 years
    Duplicate content? Ignore pages with duplicate content

    Requirements:

    • Functional: crawl 1B HTML pages/month; pick up new and edited pages; store HTML for 5 years; skip duplicates.
    • Scalability: the web is huge, so crawl in parallel.
    • Robustness: handle bad HTML, dead servers, crashes, malicious links.
    • Politeness: don't send too many requests to one site in a short time.
    • Extensibility: add new content types (e.g. images) without a redesign.

    Estimates:

    • QPS: 1,000,000,000 / 30 days / 24 h / 3600 s ≈ 400 pages/s. Peak = 2 × = 800.
    • Average page: 500 KB → 1B × 500 KB = 500 TB/month.
    • 5 years: 500 TB × 12 × 5 = 30 PB.

    Try it first: draw the crawl loop as boxes (where URLs wait, where pages are fetched, where duplicates are dropped), then think how to stop one host from being flooded.

    Solution

    High-level design

    seed URLs ─1─► URL Frontier ─2─► HTML Downloader ─4─► Content Parser ─5─► Content Seen? ◄─6─► Content Storage
                  ▲                    │3                                      │7
                  │               DNS Resolver                           Link Extractor
                  │                                                            │8
                  │                                                        URL Filter
                  │                                                            │9
                  └──────────────────11──────────────────────────────────  URL Seen? ◄─10─► URL Storage
    • Seed URLs: the starting points. Split the URL space by locality (country) or by topic (shopping, sports, …). No perfect answer; think out loud.
    • URL Frontier: URLs still to download. Think of it as a FIFO queue (refined in the deep dive).
    • HTML Downloader: fetches pages; asks the DNS Resolver for the IP first.
    • Content Parser: parses and validates pages. It is a separate component so it doesn't slow down crawl servers.
    • Content Seen?: drops pages whose content was already stored. Compare hashes of pages, not characters. About 29% of web pages are duplicates.
    • Content Storage: mostly on disk (too big for memory); popular content in memory for low latency.
    • URL Extractor: pulls links; turns relative paths into absolute URLs (e.g. add https://en.wikipedia.org).
    • URL Filter: drops some content types, file extensions, error links and blacklisted sites.
    • URL Seen?: skips URLs already visited or already in the frontier. Prevents extra load and infinite loops. Built with a bloom filter or hash table.
    • URL Storage: stores visited URLs.

    Workflow: (1) seeds go into the frontier → (2) downloader takes URLs → (3) resolves DNS and downloads → (4) parser validates → (5–6) Content Seen? drops known content → (7) links extracted → (8) filtered → (9–10) URL Seen? drops known URLs → (11) new URLs go back into the frontier.

    Deep dives

    DFS vs BFS

    • The web is a directed graph: pages are nodes, links are edges.
    • DFS is a bad fit because the depth can be huge. Crawlers use BFS with a FIFO queue.
    • Plain FIFO BFS has two problems:
    • Impolite: most links on a page point to the same host (e.g. all internal wikipedia links). Parallel downloads then flood that host.
    • No priority: every URL is treated the same, but pages differ in quality and importance.

    URL frontier

    The frontier fixes both problems. It handles politeness, priority and freshness.

    Politeness (back queues)

    • Download one page at a time per host, with a delay between downloads.
    • Keep a map from hostname to a queue; each worker thread reads from one queue.
             Queue router ──► Mapping table (host → queue)
        /     |      \       wikipedia.com → b1
      b1     b2 ...   bn     apple.com     → b2
        \     |      /       nike.com      → bn
         Queue selector
        /     |      \
  Worker 1  Worker 2 ... Worker N   (one host each, one page at a time)
    • Queue router: puts only one host's URLs in each queue b1…bn.
    • Queue selector: maps each worker thread to one queue.

    Priority (front queues)

    • A random forum post about Apple matters less than the Apple home page.
    • Prioritizer scores URLs by usefulness: PageRank, web traffic, update frequency, etc.
    • Queues f1…fn each have a priority. The queue selector picks randomly, biased toward high-priority queues.

    Full frontier = front queues + back queues:

    input URLs → Prioritizer → f1 … fn → Front queue selector
           → Back queue router (+ mapping table) → b1 … bn → Back queue selector
           → Worker threads
    • Front queues manage priority. Back queues manage politeness.

    Freshness

    • Pages are added, edited and deleted, so recrawl. Recrawling everything is too costly.
    • Recrawl based on each page's update history.
    • Recrawl important pages first and more often.

    Frontier storage

    • Real frontiers hold hundreds of millions of URLs. All in memory is not durable or scalable. All on disk is too slow.
    • Hybrid: most URLs on disk; in-memory buffers for enqueue/dequeue, flushed to disk periodically.

    HTML downloader

    Robots.txt (Robots Exclusion Protocol)

    • Sites list what crawlers may fetch. Check it before crawling a site and follow it.
    • Cache the file and re-download it periodically.
    • Example from amazon.com: User-agent: Googlebot, Disallow: /creatorhub/*, Disallow: /rss/people/*/reviews, …

    Performance optimizations

    1. Distributed crawl: many servers, many threads each. Partition the URL space so each downloader owns a subset.
    2. DNS cache: DNS takes 10–200 ms and many DNS interfaces are synchronous, so one lookup can block other threads. Keep a domain → IP cache, refreshed by cron jobs.
    3. Locality: place crawl servers (and cache, queue, storage) near the website hosts.
    4. Short timeout: set a max wait. If a host doesn't answer in time, move on to other pages.

    Robustness

    • Consistent hashing spreads load across downloaders and makes adding/removing one easy (Ch 5).
    • Save crawl state and data so a failed crawl restarts from saved state.
    • Exception handling: errors are normal at scale; don't crash.
    • Data validation to prevent system errors.

    Extensibility

    • Plug in new modules after "Content Seen?", next to the Link Extractor.
    • Examples: a PNG Downloader module for PNG files; a Web Monitor module for copyright and trademark checks.

    Problematic content

    Problem Fix
    Redundant content (~30% duplicates) Hashes or checksums
    Spider traps (e.g. /foo/bar/foo/bar/... forever) Max URL length; spot sites with an unusually large page count; manual review → exclude site or custom URL filter
    Data noise (ads, code snippets, spam URLs) Exclude when possible

    Wrap-up

    • Server-side (dynamic) rendering: JavaScript/AJAX builds links on the fly. Render the page before parsing to see them.
    • Filter unwanted pages: an anti-spam component saves storage and crawl resources.
    • DB replication and sharding for the data layer.
    • Horizontal scaling: hundreds or thousands of download servers; keep them stateless.
    • Availability, consistency, reliability (Ch 1).
    • Analytics for fine-tuning.
    ✓ Key points
    • Clarify scope first: purpose, 1B pages/month, HTML only, 5-year storage, dedup.
    • State the four qualities: scalable, robust, polite, extensible.
    • Draw the 11-step loop and name both dedup checks (content hash and URL seen).
    • Explain the frontier: front queues for priority, back queues for one-host-per-worker politeness.
    • List the speed-ups: distributed crawl, DNS cache, locality, short timeouts; and obey robots.txt.
    • Mention spider traps and freshness (recrawl by update history and importance).
    ⚠ Common trap

    Using a plain BFS queue with many threads. Most links point to the same host, so you end up hammering one site. Also, forgetting DNS as a bottleneck.

    V1·10 Notification System

    notification systempush notificationAPNsFCMSMSemailmessage queueworkersretrydedupenotification templateopt-outrate limitinganalyticssoft real-time
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ · Celery with Redis as Broker

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 10. · Your write-up: Notification System

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a scalable system that sends notifications to users as mobile push, SMS, and email. It must send millions of notifications a day.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Which notification types? Push, SMS, and email
    Real-time? Soft real-time: as soon as possible, but a slight delay under high load is OK
    Which devices? iOS, Android, and laptop/desktop
    What triggers a notification? Client apps, or a schedule on the server side
    Can users opt out? Yes. Opted-out users get nothing
    How many per day? 10M push, 1M SMS, 5M email

    Requirements:

    • Functional: send push (iOS/Android), SMS, and email. Accept triggers from other services and from schedules. Respect opt-out.
    • Non-functional: soft real-time, highly reliable (no lost notifications), scalable, and easy to add or remove a third-party provider.

    Estimates: 16M notifications per day in total (10M push, 1M SMS, 5M email). The book gives no further math.

    Try it first: sketch how one internal service's request becomes an iOS push, an SMS and an email. Then add what keeps one slow provider from blocking the rest, and what happens when a send fails.

    Solution

    High-level design

    How each channel works. We never deliver to devices ourselves. A third-party service does it.

    • iOS push: Provider → APNs → iOS device. The provider sends a device token (the unique device ID) and a JSON payload, e.g. {"aps": {"alert": {"title": "Game Request", "body": "Bob wants to play chess", "action-loc-key": "PLAY"}, "badge": 5}}.
    • Android push: Provider → FCM → Android device.
    • SMS: Provider → an SMS service such as Twilio or Nexmo → phone.
    • Email: Provider → a commercial email service such as SendGrid or Mailchimp → inbox. These give better delivery rates and analytics than running your own mail servers.

    Contact info gathering. When a user installs the app or signs up, the API servers store their contact info.

    user:   user_id bigint, email varchar, country_code int, phone_number int, created_at timestamp
device: id bigint, device_token varchar, user_id bigint, last_logged_in_at timestamp
        (one user → many devices; push goes to all of them)

    Send API (internal or verified clients only, to prevent spam). The book's email example (its URL says sms, but the body is an email):

    POST https://api.example.com/v/sms/send
{ "to": [{"user_id": 123456}],
  "from": {"email": "from_address@example.com"},
  "subject": "Hello, World!",
  "content": [{"type": "text/plain", "value": "Hello, World!"}] }

    Initial design: Service 1..N → one notification server → APNs/FCM/SMS/email → devices. It has three problems:

    • Single point of failure: one server.
    • Hard to scale: the DB, the cache and the processing parts cannot scale independently.
    • Performance bottleneck: building HTML and waiting on third parties is slow. One box overloads at peak.

    Improved design (Figure 10-10): move the DB and cache out, add more notification servers with auto horizontal scaling, and decouple with message queues.

    Service 1..N ─(1)─► Notification servers ─(2)─► Cache ─► DB
                           │(3)
         ┌─────────────────┼──────────────┬─────────────────┐
         ▼                 ▼              ▼                 ▼
     iOS PN queue    Android PN queue   SMS queue      Email queue
         │(4)              │              │                 │
      Workers ◄─retry   Workers        Workers           Workers
         │(5)              │              │                 │
       APNs              FCM         SMS service      Email service
         │(6)              │              │                 │
        iOS            Android          phone             inbox
    1. A service calls the notification servers' API.
    2. The servers validate (email, phone number), then fetch user info, device tokens and settings from the cache or DB.
    3. The servers put an event on the queue for that channel (e.g. iOS push → iOS PN queue).
    4. Workers pull events from the queues.
    5. Workers call the third-party service.
    6. The third party delivers to the device.
    • One queue per channel: an outage at one provider does not affect the other channels. The queues also buffer traffic spikes.
    • Cache: user info, device info, and notification templates. DB: users, notifications, settings.
    • Extensibility: it must be easy to plug a provider in or out. A provider may not exist in a new market. For example, FCM is not available in China, so you use Jpush or PushY there.

    Deep dives

    Reliability: no data loss

    • Notifications may be delayed or reordered, but never lost.
    • Workers write every notification to a notification log DB (Figure 10-11) and use a retry mechanism.

    Reliability: exactly once?

    • No. Most of the time a notification arrives once, but distribution can cause duplicates.
    • Dedupe: when an event arrives, check its event ID. If it was seen before, drop it. Otherwise send it.
    • This makes duplicates rare. It does not make exactly-once possible.

    Notification template

    • Most notifications share a format. A template is a preformatted message with parameters, styling and tracking links.
    • Example: BODY: You dreamed of it. We dared it. [ITEM NAME] is back — only until [DATE]. CTA: Order Now. Or, Save My [ITEM NAME]
    • Benefits: a consistent format, fewer errors, and less time spent.

    Notification setting

    • Users get fine-grained control. Table: user_id bigint, channel varchar (push/email/SMS), opt_in boolean.
    • Before sending, check that the user opted in to this channel.

    Rate limiting

    • Cap how many notifications one user receives. If we send too often, users turn notifications off completely.

    Retry mechanism

    • If a third party fails, the worker puts the notification back on the queue and retries a set number of times.
    • If the failure persists, alert the developers.

    Security

    • Push APIs are secured with an appKey/appSecret pair. Only authenticated or verified clients can send.

    Monitor queued notifications

    • Key metric: the total number of queued notifications. If it is large, workers are too slow. Add more workers.

    Events tracking

    • An analytics service tracks open rate, click rate and engagement.
    • Event lifecycle (Figure 10-13): start → pending → sent → deliver → click | unsubscribe. pending and sent can go to error.

    Updated design (Figure 10-14)

                       ┌──────────── Analytics service ◄────── click tracking ──┐
             send pending ▲                       ▲ sent                    │
                   │                              │                         │
Service N ─► Notification servers ─► iOS PN queue ─► Workers ─► APNs ─► iOS
             [authentication,          ▲            │  │
              rate limit]              └─ retry ────┘  ├─► Notification template
                   │                                   └─► Notification log
                 Cache ─► DB (device, setting, user info)
    • Notification servers gain authentication and rate limiting.
    • Failed sends go back to the queue, and workers retry a predefined number of times.
    • Templates make creating notifications consistent and fast.
    • Monitoring and tracking give health checks and data for improvements.

    Wrap-up

    • We support push, SMS and email, and use message queues to decouple the parts.
    • Reliability: a robust retry mechanism keeps the failure rate low.
    • Security: an appKey/appSecret pair lets only verified clients send.
    • Tracking and monitoring at every stage of the flow.
    • Respect user settings: check opt-out before sending.
    • Rate limiting: cap the frequency per user.
    ✓ Key points
    • Third parties deliver; your job is reliable, decoupled hand-off to them.
    • Give each channel its own queue and worker pool, so one provider's outage stays isolated.
    • Persist to a notification log and retry from the queue: "delayed or reordered, never lost."
    • Say exactly-once delivery is impossible, then show the event-ID dedupe.
    • Gate every send on opt-in settings and a per-user rate limit.
    • Watch queue depth, and scale workers when it grows.
    ⚠ Common trap

    one notification server that calls APNs/SMS/email inline. It is a single point of failure, and one slow provider stalls everything. Put queues between the servers and the senders.

    V1·11 News Feed System

    news feedtimelineFacebook feedTwitter timelineInstagram feedfanout on writefanout on readpush vs pullhybrid fanoutcelebrity problemhotkeygraph databasenews feed cachehydrationCDN
    See also The 4-Step Framework (Alex Xu, with a News Feed Example)

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 11. The worked example in The 4-Step Framework uses this same design.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a news feed like Facebook's: a constantly updating list of posts from friends on the home page. Similar asks: Instagram feed, Twitter timeline.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Mobile app, web app, or both? Both
    Most important features? Publish a post, and see friends' posts on the news feed page
    Feed order: reverse chronological or ranked (e.g. close friends score higher)? Reverse chronological, to keep it simple
    How many friends can a user have? 5,000
    Traffic? 10M DAU
    Text only, or media? Images and videos too

    Requirements:

    • Functional: publish a post; view a feed of friends' posts, newest first. Posts can hold images and videos.
    • Non-functional: fetching the feed must be fast. Scale to 10M DAU and users with up to 5,000 friends.

    Estimates: the book does no math here. Work from 10M DAU and up to 5,000 friends, which means one post can fan out to 5,000 feeds.

    Try it first: sketch the two flows (publish a post, read a feed). Then decide when a post gets copied into friends' feeds: at write time or at read time.

    Solution

    High-level design

    APIs (HTTP):

    POST /v1/me/feed   params: content (post text), auth_token
GET  /v1/me/feed   params: auth_token

    Feed publishing (Figure 11-2):

    User ──POST /v1/me/feed?content=Hello&auth_token=…──► Load balancer ► Web servers
   Web servers ─► Post service ─► Post cache ─► Post DB
               ─► Fanout service ─► News feed cache
               ─► Notification service

    News feed building (Figure 11-3):

    User ──GET /v1/me/feed──► Load balancer ► Web servers ► News feed service ► News feed cache
    • Load balancer spreads traffic over the web servers. Web servers route requests to internal services.
    • Post service saves the post in the DB and the cache.
    • Fanout service pushes the new post into friends' feeds, which live in a cache for fast reads.
    • Notification service tells friends there is new content and sends push notifications.
    • News feed service reads the feed from the news feed cache, which holds the IDs needed to render it.

    Deep dives

    Feed publishing (Figure 11-4)

    User ─► Load balancer ─► Web servers [authentication, rate limiting]
          ├─► Post service ─► Post cache ─► Post DB
          ├─► Notification service
          └─► Fanout service ─(1) get friend IDs──► Graph DB
                    ├─(2) get friends' data──► User cache ─► User DB
                    └─(3)─► Message queue ─(4)─► Fanout workers ─(5)─► News feed cache

    Web servers also enforce:

    • Authentication: only signed-in users with a valid auth_token can post.
    • Rate limiting: cap posts per user per time window, to stop spam and abuse.

    Fanout service. Fanout delivers a post to all friends. The book compares two models:

    Fanout on write (push) Fanout on read (pull)
    When the feed is built At write time; post goes into friends' caches right away At read time, on demand when the user loads the home page
    Pros Real-time; feed can be pushed to friends at once. Fast reads, since the feed is precomputed No wasted work on inactive users. No hotkey problem, since nothing is pushed
    Cons Hotkey problem: a user with many friends makes fetching the list and writing all feeds slow. Wasted work for inactive users Slow reads, since the feed is not precomputed

    The book's choice: hybrid. Fast feed reads are crucial, so use push for most users. For celebrities or users with very many friends/followers, followers pull that content on demand, which avoids overload. Consistent hashing helps with hotkeys by spreading requests and data more evenly.

    Fanout steps (Figure 11-5):

    1. Get friend IDs from the graph DB. Graph DBs suit friend relations and friend recommendations.
    2. Get friends' info from the user cache. Filter by user settings: a muted friend's posts stay hidden, and a post may be shared only with chosen friends.
    3. Send the friend list and the new post ID to the message queue.
    4. Fanout workers read from the queue.
    5. Workers append <post_id, user_id> to the news feed cache (Figure 11-6).
    • Store only IDs. Whole user and post objects would use too much memory.
    • Keep a configurable limit on feed length. Few users scroll through thousands of posts; most want the latest. So the cache miss rate stays low.

    News feed retrieval (Figure 11-7)

    User ─(1) GET /v1/me/feed─► Load balancer ─(2)─► Web servers [auth, rate limiting]
                                                     │(3)          ▲ (6) JSON
                                                     ▼             │
                                              News feed service ───┘
                          (4) post IDs ◄─ News feed cache
                          (5) hydrate  ◄─ User cache ─► User DB
                                       ◄─ Post cache ─► Post DB
User ◄── images/videos ── CDN
    1. The user sends GET /v1/me/feed.
    2. The load balancer sends it to a web server.
    3. The web server calls the news feed service.
    4. The service gets a list of post IDs from the news feed cache.
    5. A feed needs more than IDs: username, profile picture, post text, post image. The service hydrates the feed with full user and post objects from the user cache and post cache.
    6. The fully hydrated feed goes back to the client as JSON.

    Media (images, videos) is stored in a CDN for fast retrieval.

    Cache architecture (Figure 11-8)

    The cache is central to a feed system. The book splits it into 5 layers:

    Layer Holds
    News feed IDs of news feed items
    Content Every post's data. Popular posts go in a hot cache, the rest in normal
    Social graph Relationships: follower, following
    Action Whether a user liked, replied to, or did something else to a post
    Counters Like, reply, follower, following, and other counts

    Wrap-up

    There is no perfect design; fit it to the company's constraints and know your trade-offs. If time is left, talk about scale.

    • Scaling the database: vertical vs horizontal scaling, SQL vs NoSQL, master-slave replication, read replicas, consistency models, sharding.
    • Other points: keep the web tier stateless, cache as much as you can, support multiple data centers, loosely couple components with message queues.
    • Monitor key metrics: for example, peak-hour QPS and the latency when users refresh their feed.
    ✓ Key points
    • Split the problem into two flows, publishing and retrieval, and design each one.
    • Compare push and pull out loud, then choose hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities.
    • Fan out async through a message queue and workers, so the post request returns fast.
    • Store only IDs in the feed cache. Cap its length, and hydrate from the user and post caches at read time.
    • Put authentication and rate limiting at the web servers, and media on a CDN.
    ⚠ Common trap

    pure fanout on write. One celebrity post then becomes millions of cache writes (the hotkey problem). Say "hybrid" and explain why.

    V1·12 Chat System

    chat systemmessengerWhatsAppWebSocketlong pollingpresenceheartbeatservice discoveryZooKeeperkey-value storemessage IDmessage sync queuegroup chatmulti-device syncpush notification
    See also Web & Networking Fundamentals · Redis Pub/Sub vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 12. · Your write-up: Chat System

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a chat app like Facebook Messenger. It must support 1-on-1 chat, small group chat, and online status.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    1-on-1 or group? Both
    Mobile, web, or both? Both
    Scale? 50M DAU
    Group member limit? 100 people
    Key features? Attachments? 1-on-1 chat, group chat, online indicator. Text only
    Message size limit? Text under 100,000 characters
    End-to-end encryption? Not now; discuss if time allows
    How long to keep history? Forever

    Requirements:

    • Functional: 1-on-1 chat with low delivery latency; small group chat (max 100); online presence; multiple devices per account logged in at once; push notifications.
    • Non-functional: 50M DAU, low latency, chat history stored forever.

    Estimates: if each connection needs ~10 KB of server memory, 1M concurrent users need only ~10 GB. In theory one box could hold them all, but a single server is a single point of failure. Start with one server only if you say it is a starting point. Messenger and WhatsApp together process ~60B messages a day.

    Try it first: decide how the server pushes a message to a receiver who sent no request. Then sketch where messages are stored, and how a sender's message reaches an online receiver and an offline one.

    Solution

    High-level design

    The chat service must: receive messages from clients, find the recipients and relay to them, and hold messages for offline recipients until they come online.

    Protocol choice. Sending is client-initiated, so HTTP with keep-alive works (early Facebook used it). Receiving is the hard part, because the server must push:

    Technique How Problems
    Polling Client asks "anything new?" on a timer Wastes server resources; most answers are "no"
    Long polling Client holds the request open until a message arrives or a timeout, then reconnects Sender and receiver may hit different stateless servers; the server cannot tell when a client disconnected; still reconnects after timeouts for quiet users
    WebSocket Starts as HTTP, then upgrades. Bi-directional and persistent Connections are stateful, so you must manage them carefully on the server

    Choice: WebSocket for both sending and receiving. It uses ports 80/443, so it usually passes firewalls. One protocol on both sides keeps the client and server simpler. Everything else (signup, login, profile) stays plain HTTP request/response.

    Three groups of services (Figure 12-7):

    • Stateless (behind a load balancer, HTTP): service discovery, authentication, group management, user profile. Service discovery gives the client the DNS host names of the chat servers it can use.
    • Stateful: the chat service. Each client keeps a persistent connection to one chat server and stays on it while that server is up.
    • Third party: push notification, to reach users when the app is not running (see Ch 10).

    Adjusted design (Figure 12-8):

    User ──http──► Load balancer ─► API servers ─► Notification servers
  │                                 ▲   ▲
  └──ws──► Real-time service ───────┘   │
           [Chat servers | Presence servers]
                       │
   API servers, notification servers, chat servers, presence servers ─► KV stores
    • Chat servers send and receive messages. Presence servers manage online/offline status.
    • API servers handle login, signup, profile changes and the rest.
    • Notification servers send push notifications.
    • KV store holds chat history, so a user who comes online sees all past messages.

    Storage. There are two kinds of data:

    • Generic data (profiles, settings, friend lists): a relational DB, with replication and sharding.
    • Chat history: huge volume; mostly recent chats are read, but random access is needed for search, mentions and jump-to-message; the read/write ratio is about 1:1 for 1-on-1 chat.

    Choice for chat history: a key-value store. It scales horizontally with ease and has very low latency. Relational DBs handle the long tail of data badly: when indexes grow large, random access is expensive. Proven in practice: Facebook Messenger uses HBase, Discord uses Cassandra.

    Data models:

    message (1-on-1):   message_id bigint PK, message_from bigint, message_to bigint,
                    content text, created_at timestamp
group_message:      channel_id bigint, message_id bigint   PK = (channel_id, message_id)
                    user_id bigint, content text, created_at timestamp
                    channel_id is the partition key: every group query is per channel
    • Order by message_id, not created_at: two messages can have the same timestamp.

    Message ID. It must be unique and sortable by time (newer rows get higher IDs). Options:

    Option Verdict
    auto_increment (MySQL) NoSQL stores usually do not have it
    Global 64-bit generator like Snowflake (Ch 7) Works
    Local sequence number, unique only within a channel Enough, since order only matters inside one 1-on-1 or group channel. Easier than a global ID

    Deep dives

    Service discovery (Figure 12-11)

    It picks the best chat server for a client by criteria such as location and server capacity. Apache ZooKeeper registers all chat servers and chooses one.

    1. User A logs in.
    2. The load balancer sends the login to the API servers.
    3. After authentication, service discovery picks a chat server (say server 2) and returns its info.
    4. User A opens a WebSocket to chat server 2.

    1-on-1 message flow (Figure 12-12)

    User A ─(1)─► Chat server 1 ─(2)─► ID generator
                   │(3)
                   ▼
          Message sync queue ─(4)─► KV store
                   ├─(5a online)──► Chat server 2 ─(6)─► User B
                   └─(5b offline)─► PN servers (push notification)
    1. User A sends a message to chat server 1.
    2. Chat server 1 gets a message ID from the ID generator.
    3. It sends the message to the message sync queue.
    4. The message is stored in the KV store.
    5. If B is online, the message goes to chat server 2, where B is connected. If B is offline, the PN servers send a push notification.
    6. Chat server 2 sends it to B over B's WebSocket.

    Multi-device sync (Figure 12-13)

    • User A's phone and laptop each hold a WebSocket to chat server 1.
    • Each device keeps its own cur_max_message_id: the latest message ID it has (e.g. phone 653, laptop 842).
    • A message is new for a device if its recipient ID = the logged-in user and its message ID > cur_max_message_id.
    • So each device just pulls its new messages from the KV store.

    Small group chat (Figures 12-14, 12-15)

    • When A sends to a group {A, B, C}, the message is copied into each member's message sync queue: one for B, one for C.
    • Think of the sync queue as each recipient's inbox. It holds messages from many senders and groups.
    • Good for small groups: each client checks only its own inbox, and a copy per member is cheap when groups are small.
    • WeChat does this and caps groups at 500. For very large groups, a copy per member is not acceptable.

    Online presence

    • Login: after the WebSocket is up, save A's online status and last_active_at in the KV store.
    • Logout: set the status to offline in the KV store.
    • Disconnection: marking offline on every drop makes the indicator flicker (e.g. a user in a tunnel). Use a heartbeat instead. The client sends one periodically, e.g. every 5 s. If no heartbeat arrives within x seconds (the book's example: 30 s), the user is offline.
    • Status fanout: presence servers use pub/sub with one channel per friend pair. A's change is published to channels A-B, A-C and A-D, which B, C and D subscribe to. Clients get updates over WebSocket.
    • This works for small groups (WeChat caps at 500). For a group of 100,000 members, each change would make 100,000 events. Instead, fetch status only when a user enters a group or refreshes the friend list.

    Wrap-up

    The design: WebSocket for real-time traffic, chat servers, presence servers, push notification servers, KV stores for history, and API servers for the rest. Extra talking points:

    • Media files: much larger than text. Discuss compression, cloud storage and thumbnails.
    • End-to-end encryption: as in WhatsApp, only sender and recipient can read messages.
    • Client-side message cache to cut data transfer.
    • Faster load time: Slack built a geo-distributed cache for users' data and channels.
    • Chat server failure: a server may hold hundreds of thousands of connections. If it dies, service discovery (ZooKeeper) gives clients a new server to reconnect to.
    • Message resend: use retry and queueing.
    ✓ Key points
    • Compare polling, long polling and WebSocket, then pick WebSocket for both directions and keep HTTP for everything else.
    • Split services into stateless (behind a load balancer), stateful (chat servers, chosen by service discovery) and third party (push).
    • Store history in a KV store and justify it: scale, latency, long tail, a 1:1 read/write ratio, and HBase/Cassandra in production.
    • Order by a time-sortable message_id, not a timestamp. A per-channel local sequence is enough.
    • Presence = heartbeat with a timeout + pub/sub per friend pair. Fall back to fetch-on-open for huge groups.
    ⚠ Common trap

    marking a user offline on every socket drop. Flaky networks make the indicator flicker. Use a heartbeat with a grace timeout.

    V1·13 Search Autocomplete

    search autocompletetypeaheadtop ktrieprefix treedata gatheringaggregationtrie cacheshard map managerbrowser cachedata samplingquery servicetrending queries

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 13.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a search autocomplete system ("typeahead", or "top k most searched queries"). As the user types, show the most popular queries that start with what they typed.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Match only at the start of the query, or in the middle too? Only at the start
    How many suggestions? 5
    How do we pick the 5? By popularity: historical query frequency
    Spell check / autocorrect? No
    Language? English. Multi-language if time allows
    Capitals and special characters? No. All queries are lowercase a–z
    Users? 10M DAU

    Requirements:

    • Functional: given a prefix, return the top 5 queries by frequency, sorted.
    • Fast: results within 100 ms (Facebook's figure), or typing stutters.
    • Relevant and sorted by popularity (or another ranking model).
    • Scalable to high traffic. Highly available when parts fail or slow down.

    Estimates:

    • 10M DAU, 10 searches per user per day.
    • A query is 4 words × 5 chars = 20 bytes (ASCII, 1 byte per char).
    • One request per typed character: about 20 requests per search (search?q=d, search?q=di, … search?q=dinner).
    • QPS = 10M × 10 × 20 / 86,400 ≈ 24,000. Peak ≈ 48,000.
    • 20% of queries are new: 10M × 10 × 20 B × 20% = 0.4 GB new data per day.

    Try it first: sketch the data structure that returns the top 5 for a prefix in O(1), and the pipeline that keeps it fresh without slowing reads.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Two services:

    • Data gathering service: collects user queries and counts them. The naive version updates a frequency table in real time.
    • Query service: given a prefix, return the 5 most searched queries.

    Naive version: one frequency table (query, frequency). Example rows: twitter 35, twitch 29, twilight 25, twin peak 21, twitch prime 18, twitter search 14, twillo 10, twin peak sf 8. Typing "tw" returns the top 5 of these.

    SELECT * FROM frequency_table
WHERE query LIKE 'prefix%'
ORDER BY frequency DESC
LIMIT 5;
    • This works for a small data set.
    • At scale the database becomes the bottleneck. The deep dive fixes both services.

    Deep dives

    Trie data structure

    A trie (prefix tree, from "retrieval") stores strings compactly.

    • The root is the empty string. Each node is one character and has up to 26 children.
    • Each node is a word or a prefix. Add the frequency to nodes that end a real query.

    Basic top-k algorithm (p = prefix length, n = nodes, c = children of a node):

    Step Cost
    1. Find the prefix node O(p)
    2. Traverse its subtree to collect all valid queries O(c)
    3. Sort them and take top k O(c log c)

    Example, k = 2, prefix "tr": valid nodes are tree:10, true:35, try:29 → return true, try.

    This is too slow: in the worst case you walk the whole trie. Two optimizations:

    1. Limit the prefix length. Users rarely type long queries. Cap p at about 50. Finding the prefix becomes O(1).
    2. Cache the top k queries at every node. Node "be" stores [best:35, bet:29, bee:20, be:15, beer:10]. This costs a lot of space. Fast response is worth it.

    After both: find prefix O(1) + return cached top k O(1) = O(1).

    Data gathering service

    Updating the trie on every query is impractical:

    • Users send billions of queries a day. Constant updates slow down the query service.
    • Top suggestions do not change much once the trie is built.

    How fresh it must be depends on the product. Twitter needs near real time. Many Google keywords barely change day to day. The data source is the same either way: analytics logs.

    Analytics Logs ─► Aggregators ─► Aggregated Data ─► Workers ──update weekly──► Trie DB
                                                                                   │
                                                              weekly snapshot of DB
                                                                                   ▼
                                                                              Trie Cache
    • Analytics logs: raw (query, time) rows. Append-only, not indexed.
    • Aggregators: turn huge raw logs into counts. Short windows for real-time apps; weekly is enough for many. Ask the interviewer. The book assumes a weekly rebuild.
    • Aggregated data: (query, time = week start, frequency), e.g. tree / 2019-10-01 / 12000.
    • Workers: async jobs at fixed intervals. They build the trie and store it in Trie DB.
    • Trie Cache: distributed in-memory cache of the trie. Takes a weekly snapshot of the DB.
    • Trie DB: persistent storage. Two options:
    Option How
    Document store (e.g. MongoDB) Serialize the weekly trie snapshot and store it
    Key-value store Each prefix is a key; the node's data (its top-k list) is the value

    Key-value example: b → [be:15, bee:20, beer:10, best:35], bee → [bee:20, beer:10], best → [best:35].

    Query service

    User (web / mobile)
   │ 1
   ▼
Load balancer ─2─► API servers ─3─► Trie Cache ─4 (on miss)─► Trie DB
    1. The query goes to the load balancer.
    2. It routes to an API server.
    3. The API server reads trie data from Trie Cache and builds the suggestions.
    4. On a cache miss, reload the data from Trie DB into the cache. Misses happen when a cache server is out of memory or offline.

    Optimizations:

    • AJAX requests: fetch results without reloading the page.
    • Browser caching: suggestions change slowly. Google caches them in the browser for an hour: Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600. private = one user only, no shared caches.
    • Data sampling: logging every query is expensive. Log only 1 out of every N requests.

    Trie operations

    • Create: workers build it from aggregated data (from the analytics log/DB).
    • Update, option 1: rebuild weekly and replace the old trie. This is the default.
    • Update, option 2: update a single node in place. Slow, so avoid it. OK only if the trie is small. You must also update every ancestor up to the root, because ancestors cache the top queries of their children. Example: "beer" 10 → 30 changes "beer" in the node and in all its ancestors.
    • Delete: remove hateful, violent, sexually explicit or dangerous suggestions. Put a filter layer between Trie Cache and API servers. Filter rules are flexible. Delete the bad data from the DB asynchronously, so the next weekly build is clean.
    Trie Cache ─► Filter Layer ─► API servers

    Scale the storage

    When the trie does not fit on one server, shard it.

    • First-level sharding by first letter: 2 servers = a–m, n–z. 3 servers = a–i, j–r, s–z. Up to 26 servers.
    • Beyond 26: shard on the 2nd or 3rd letter. Example: "a" split into aa–ag, ah–an, ao–au, av–az.
    • Problem: far more words start with "c" than "x". Shards are uneven.
    • Fix: analyze historical distribution. A shard map manager keeps a lookup DB of which shard holds which prefixes. Example: if "s" has as many queries as u–z combined, use one shard for "s" and one for "u–z".
    Web servers ─1. which shard?─► Shard map manager
            ─2. read data────► Shard 1 | Shard 2 | Shard ...

    Wrap-up

    • Multiple languages: store Unicode characters in trie nodes.
    • Different top queries per country: build a trie per country. Store tries in CDNs for speed.
    • Trending (real-time) queries: the weekly design fails. Workers are not scheduled yet, and a rebuild takes too long. Ideas:
    • Shard to shrink the working data set.
    • Change the ranking model to weight recent queries more.
    • Treat data as streams: Hadoop MapReduce, Spark Streaming, Storm, Kafka. The book does not go deeper.
    ✓ Key points
    • Split the problem into a read path (query service) and a write path (data gathering). Optimize them separately.
    • Trie + capped prefix length + top k cached per node makes reads O(1). Say the space cost out loud.
    • Rebuild the trie offline (weekly) from aggregated logs. Serve it from an in-memory Trie Cache backed by Trie DB.
    • Cut load with browser caching, AJAX, and log sampling.
    • Shard by prefix using a shard map manager based on real distribution, not plain alphabet ranges.
    ⚠ Common trap

    updating the trie on every search. It kills read latency, and an in-place update must rewrite every ancestor's cached top k.

    V1·14 YouTube

    YouTubevideo streamingNetflixvideo uploadtranscodingencodingDAGGOPblob storageCDNpre-signed URLMPEG-DASHHLSDRMlong tailcompletion queueresumable upload
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 14.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design YouTube: creators upload videos and viewers watch them. The same design applies to Netflix or Hulu.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Most important features? Upload a video and watch a video
    Clients? Mobile apps, web browsers, smart TV
    DAU? 5 million
    Average daily time on the product? 30 minutes
    International users? Yes, a large share
    Supported resolutions / formats? Most resolutions and formats
    Encryption? Yes
    File size limit? Small and medium videos; max 1 GB
    Use existing cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure)? Yes, recommended. Don't build everything from scratch

    Requirements:

    • Functional: upload videos fast; stream smoothly; change video quality.
    • Clients: mobile, web, smart TV.
    • Non-functional: low infrastructure cost; high availability, scalability and reliability.

    Estimates:

    • 5M DAU. Each user watches 5 videos per day.
    • 10% of users upload 1 video per day. Average video = 300 MB.
    • Storage per day: 5M × 10% × 300 MB = 150 TB.
    • CDN (Amazon CloudFront, all traffic from the US, average $0.02/GB): 5M × 5 × 0.3 GB × $0.02 = $150,000 per day. Streaming only.
    • So CDN cost is the big number. The deep dive reduces it.

    Try it first: sketch the upload path (where the raw file goes, how it becomes many formats, how metadata learns it is ready) and the watch path.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Use existing cloud services: blob storage and CDN. In an interview, picking the right tool matters more than explaining how it works inside. Even Netflix (AWS) and Facebook (Akamai CDN) do not build everything.

    Three parts:

    • Client: computer, phone, smart TV.
    • CDN: stores videos and streams them when you press play.
    • API servers: everything else. Feed recommendations, upload URLs, metadata DB and cache, sign-up.

    Upload flow (two processes run in parallel):

    User ──(a) upload video──► Original storage (blob)
                                │
                                ▼
                       Transcoding servers ──transcoding complete──► Completion queue
                                │                                         │
                                ▼                                         ▼
                       Transcoded storage ─► CDN                 Completion handler
                                                                   │            │
User ──(b) metadata──► Load balancer ─► API servers ─► Metadata cache  +  Metadata DB

    • Flow a, upload the video: 1. Upload to original storage. 2. Transcoding servers fetch it and transcode. 3. In parallel: 3a. transcoded files go to transcoded storage, then to the CDN. 3b. a completion event goes to the completion queue. Completion-handler workers pull events and update the metadata DB and cache. 4. API servers tell the client the video is uploaded and ready to stream.

    • Flow b, update metadata: while the file uploads, the client sends metadata (file name, size, format, …). API servers write it to the metadata cache and DB.

    • Metadata DB is sharded and replicated. Metadata cache holds video metadata and user objects.

    Streaming flow:

    Client (web / mobile / TV) ──streaming video──► CDN (nearest edge server)
    • Streaming = the client loads a little data at a time and plays right away. Downloading = copy the whole file first.
    • Streaming protocols: MPEG-DASH, Apple HLS, Microsoft Smooth Streaming, Adobe HDS. Names don't matter much. What matters: each supports different encodings and players, so pick one that fits.
    • Video comes from the nearest CDN edge, so latency is low.

    Deep dives

    Video transcoding

    Why transcode:

    • Raw video is huge. One hour of HD at 60 fps can be a few hundred GB.
    • Devices and browsers support only some formats.
    • Send high resolution to high-bandwidth users and low resolution to low-bandwidth users.
    • Networks change, especially on mobile. Switch quality automatically or manually to keep playback smooth.

    An encoding format has two parts:

    • Container: the "basket" for video, audio and metadata. Seen in the extension: .avi, .mov, .mp4.
    • Codec: compression algorithm. Most used: H.264, VP9, HEVC.

    DAG model

    Transcoding is slow and expensive, and creators want different steps (watermarks, own thumbnails, HD or not). So let programmers define tasks as a directed acyclic graph (like Facebook's streaming video engine). Tasks run in stages, in sequence or in parallel.

                    ┌─► Video ──► [Inspection | Video transcoding | Thumbnail | … | Watermark] ─┐
Original video ─┼─► Audio ──► Audio encoding ───────────────────────────────────────────────┼─► Assemble
                └─► Metadata
    • Inspection: check quality; reject malformed files.
    • Video encoding: many resolutions, codecs and bitrates, e.g. 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K .mp4.
    • Thumbnail: uploaded by the user or generated.
    • Watermark: image overlay with identifying info.

    Video transcoding architecture

    Preprocessor ─► DAG scheduler ─► Resource manager ─► Task workers ─► Encoded video
     │                                                    │
     └──────────────────► Temporary storage ◄─────────────┘

    • Preprocessor: 1. Splits the video into GOP (Group of Pictures) chunks. A GOP is a few seconds of frames that play on their own. 2. Does the splitting for old clients that cannot split. 3. Generates the DAG from config files programmers write. Example: task download-input (type Download, output inputVideo, next transcode) → task transcode (type Transcode, input inputVideo + transConfig). That is 2 nodes and 1 edge. 4. Caches GOPs and metadata in temporary storage, so a failed encode can retry from them.

    • DAG scheduler: splits the DAG into stages and puts tasks in the resource manager's task queue. Example: stage 1 = video, audio, metadata. Stage 2 = video encoding + thumbnail (from video), audio encoding (from audio).

    • Resource manager: three queues + a task scheduler.
    • Task queue: priority queue of tasks.
    • Worker queue: priority queue of worker utilization.
    • Running queue: current task/worker pairs.
    • Scheduler loop: take the highest-priority task → pick the best worker → tell it to run → record in running queue → remove when done.
    • Task workers: run the DAG tasks. Different worker types: watermark, encoder, thumbnail, merger, ….
    • Temporary storage: pick by data type, size, access rate, lifetime. Metadata is small and hot → memory cache. Video/audio → blob storage. Freed when processing finishes.
    • Encoded video: the output, e.g. funny_720p.mp4.

    Speed optimizations

    • Parallelize uploads: the client splits the video into GOP chunks. Upload is faster and resumable after a failure.
    • Upload centers near users: use the CDN as upload centers (North America, Asia, …).
    • Parallelism everywhere: original storage → download module → encoding module → upload module → encoded storage → CDN. Each step waits on the last. Put a message queue between every pair. Then, e.g., the encoding module no longer waits for the download module; it processes queued events in parallel.

    Safety optimizations

    • Pre-signed upload URL: only authorized users upload, and only to the right place. 1. Client: POST /upload to API servers. 2. API servers return a pre-signed URL (S3 term; Azure calls it "Shared Access Signature"). 3. Client uploads the video to original storage with that URL.

    • Protect videos (pick one):

    • DRM: Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine, Microsoft PlayReady.
    • AES encryption: encrypt the video with an authorization policy; decrypt on playback.
    • Visual watermark: logo or company name overlaid on the video.

    Cost-saving optimizations

    YouTube views follow a long-tail distribution: a few videos get most views, many get almost none.

    1. Serve only popular videos from the CDN. Serve the rest from high-capacity video servers.
    2. For unpopular content, store fewer encoded versions. Encode short videos on demand.
    3. Some videos are popular in one region only. Don't distribute them elsewhere.
    4. Build your own CDN and partner with ISPs (Comcast, AT&T, Verizon), like Netflix. A huge project, but it makes sense for large streaming companies.

    Analyze historical viewing patterns before doing any of this.

    Error handling

    • Recoverable (e.g. a segment fails to transcode): retry a few times. If it keeps failing, return an error code.
    • Non-recoverable (e.g. malformed video): stop the video's tasks and return an error code.
    Component Playbook
    Upload Retry a few times
    Split video Old client can't split by GOP → send the whole file; split on the server
    Transcoding Retry
    Preprocessor Regenerate the DAG
    DAG scheduler Reschedule the task
    Resource manager queue down Use a replica
    Task worker down Retry the task on a new worker
    API server down Stateless → route to another server
    Metadata cache down Data is replicated; read other nodes, start a new cache server
    Metadata DB master down Promote a slave to master
    Metadata DB slave down Read from another slave; replace the dead one

    Wrap-up

    • Scale the API tier: stateless, so scale horizontally.
    • Scale the database: replication and sharding.
    • Live streaming: also needs upload, encoding and streaming, but:
    • Stricter latency → maybe a different streaming protocol.
    • Less need for parallelism; small chunks are processed in real time.
    • Different error handling; slow recovery is not acceptable.
    • Video takedowns: remove copyright, pornographic or illegal videos. Catch some at upload; others via user flagging.
    ✓ Key points
    • Lean on managed blob storage + CDN. Only API traffic hits your servers; video bytes go to/from storage and CDN.
    • Upload and metadata update run in parallel. A completion queue tells metadata when transcoding is done.
    • Transcoding is a DAG of tasks on GOP chunks, run by a scheduler, resource manager and worker pool.
    • Put message queues between pipeline stages to decouple them and run them in parallel.
    • Pre-signed URLs for safe uploads; DRM / AES / watermark to protect content.
    • CDN is the main cost. Use the long tail to decide what goes on the CDN.
    ⚠ Common trap

    streaming every video through the CDN without looking at the cost. The estimate shows ~$150K/day, and most videos are rarely watched.

    V1·15 Google Drive

    Google DriveDropboxfile synccloud storageblock serverdelta synccompressionS3cold storagemetadata databasestrong consistencysync conflictlong pollingresumable uploadfile versionsdeduplication
    See also Transactions & Isolation Levels · Web & Networking Fundamentals

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 1, Ch 15.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design Google Drive: a file storage and sync service. Users store files in the cloud, reach them from any device, and share them.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Most important features? Upload and download files, file sync, notifications
    Mobile, web, or both? Both
    File formats? Any type
    Encryption? Yes, files in storage must be encrypted
    File size limit? Yes, 10 GB or smaller
    Users? 10M DAU

    Requirements:

    • Functional: add files (drag and drop); download files; sync across devices; see file revisions; share files; notify when a file is edited, deleted or shared with you.
    • Out of scope: Google Docs-style real-time collaborative editing.
    • Non-functional:
    • Reliability: data loss is unacceptable.
    • Fast sync. Slow sync makes users leave.
    • Low bandwidth use, especially on mobile data.
    • Scalability and high availability.

    Estimates:

    • 50M signed-up users, 10M DAU. Each user gets 10 GB free.
    • 2 uploads per user per day, average file 500 KB. Read:write = 1:1.
    • Total space allocated: 50M × 10 GB = 500 PB.
    • Upload QPS: 10M × 2 / 86,400 ≈ 240. Peak ≈ 480.

    Try it first: sketch how a file gets from one device to the cloud and to the user's other devices, and what you store as metadata vs. as file content.

    Solution

    High-level design

    The book starts with one server and scales it up.

    Single server: Apache web server, MySQL for metadata, and a drive/ directory with 1 TB. Under drive/ there is one namespace (folder) per user. A file is identified by namespace + relative path, e.g. drive/user1/recipes/….

    APIs (all need authentication and HTTPS/SSL):

    API Params
    https://api.example.com/files/upload?uploadType=resumable uploadType=resumable, data (local file)
    https://api.example.com/files/download path, e.g. /recipes/soup/best_soup.txt
    https://api.example.com/files/list_revisions path, limit (e.g. 20)
    • Two upload types: simple (small files) and resumable (large files, flaky network).
    • Resumable upload: 1) get a resumable URL, 2) upload and monitor state, 3) resume if interrupted.

    Move away from a single server:

    • Disk fills up (10 MB left). First fix: shard storage by user_id.
    • Still risky: a server outage can lose data. Move files to Amazon S3. Use same-region and cross-region replication (a bucket is like a folder).
    • Load balancer in front; add/remove web (API) servers with load.
    • Metadata DB moves off the server, with replication and sharding.
    • File storage = S3, replicated in two regions.

    Sync conflicts: two users change the same file at the same time. The first version processed wins. The later one gets a conflict. The system shows user 2 both copies (local and latest server version). User 2 merges them or overrides one.

    Final high-level design:

                             User (browser / mobile)
           ┌──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐ long polling
           ▼                      ▼                         ▼
     Block servers          Load balancer          Notification service ─► Offline backup queue
           │                      │                         ▲
           ▼                      ▼                         │
     Cloud storage ──callback──► API servers ───────────────┘
           │                      │
           ▼               ┌──────┴──────┐
     Cold storage    Metadata cache   Metadata DB
    • Block servers: split files into blocks and upload them to cloud storage. Each block has a hash, stored in the metadata DB. Blocks are joined in order to rebuild a file. Max block size 4 MB (Dropbox).
    • Cloud storage: holds the blocks. Cold storage: holds files not used for a long time.
    • API servers: everything except uploading: auth, user profile, file metadata.
    • Metadata DB + cache: users, files, blocks, versions. Only metadata; content lives in the cloud.
    • Notification service: pub/sub. Tells clients when a file is added, edited or removed elsewhere, so they pull changes.
    • Offline backup queue: holds changes for offline clients until they reconnect.

    Deep dives

    Block servers

    Sending the whole file on every edit wastes bandwidth. Two fixes:

    • Delta sync: upload only the changed blocks (rsync-style algorithm). Example: only block 2 and block 5 changed → only those two upload.
    • Compression: per file type. gzip/bzip2 for text; other algorithms for images and video.

    Block server pipeline for a new file:

    file ─split─► Block 1..N ─compress─► ─encrypt─► Cloud storage

    Block servers do the heavy lifting: split, compress, encrypt, upload only modified blocks.

    High consistency requirement

    • Strong consistency by default. Different clients must not see a file differently at the same time. This applies to both the metadata cache and DB.
    • Memory caches are eventually consistent by default. To fix this: keep cache replicas consistent with the master, and invalidate the cache on every DB write.
    • Relational DBs give ACID natively. NoSQL does not; you would have to build it into the sync logic. Choice: relational database.

    Metadata database

    Simplified schema:

    Table Key fields
    user user_id, user_name, created_at
    device device_id (uuid), user_id, last_logged_in_at (plus push_id for mobile push)
    workspace (namespace) id, owner_id, is_shared, created_at
    file id, file_name, relative_path, is_directory, latest_version, checksum, workspace_id, created_at, last_modified
    file_version id, file_id, device_id, version_number, last_modified
    block block_id, file_version_id, block_order
    • user 1 → * devices; user 1 → * workspaces; workspace 1 → * files; file 1 → * versions; version 1 → * blocks.
    • Namespace / workspace = a user's root directory.
    • file holds the latest version. file_version holds history; its rows are read-only to protect history.
    • Any version can be rebuilt by joining its blocks in block_order.

    Upload flow

    Client 1 sends two requests in parallel:

    Add metadata:
 1. Client 1 ─add file metadata─► API servers
 2. API servers ─► Metadata DB: status = "pending"
 3. ─► Notification service
 4. Notification service ─► Client 2: "file is being uploaded"

Upload content:
 2.1 Client 1 ─upload file─► Block servers
 2.2 Block servers: chunk, compress, encrypt ─► Cloud storage
 2.3 Cloud storage ─upload completion callback─► API servers
 2.4 API servers ─► Metadata DB: status = "uploaded"
 2.5 ─► Notification service
 2.6 Notification service ─► Client 2: "file fully uploaded"

    Editing a file follows the same flow.

    Download flow

    A client learns about changes in one of two ways:

    • Online: the notification service tells it to pull.
    • Offline: changes are saved (in the cache); it pulls them when it comes back online.
    1. Notification service ─► Client 2: changes exist
2. Client 2 ─get changes─► API servers
3–4. API servers ◄─► Metadata DB
5. API servers ─► Client 2: metadata
6. Client 2 ─download blocks─► Block servers
7–8. Block servers ◄─► Cloud storage
9. Block servers ─► Client 2: blocks; client rebuilds the file

    Notification service

    Options: long polling (Dropbox uses it) or WebSocket (persistent, bi-directional).

    Choice: long polling, because:

    • Communication is one-way: server tells client about changes, not the reverse.
    • WebSocket suits real-time two-way traffic like chat. Drive notifications are infrequent, with no bursts.

    How it works: each client holds a long-poll connection. When a change is detected, the connection closes and the client fetches the latest changes from the metadata server. After a response or a timeout, the client immediately opens a new long-poll request.

    Save storage space

    Many versions across many data centers fill storage fast. Three techniques:

    • De-duplicate blocks at the account level. Same hash = same block.
    • Smart backup strategy:
    • Set a limit on versions per file. At the limit, the oldest is replaced.
    • Keep valuable versions only. A heavily edited doc could save 1000+ versions in a short time. Weight recent versions more. Experiment to find the right number.
    • Move cold data to cold storage (not touched for months or years). S3 Glacier is much cheaper than S3.

    Failure handling

    Failure Handling
    Load balancer Secondary takes over. LBs check each other via heartbeat
    Block server Other servers pick up unfinished or pending jobs
    Cloud storage S3 buckets are replicated across regions; fetch from another region
    API server Stateless; LB redirects traffic
    Metadata cache Replicated; read other nodes, start a replacement
    Metadata DB master Promote a slave to master; add a new slave
    Metadata DB slave Read from another slave; replace the failed one
    Notification service Each server holds many long-poll connections (Dropbox 2012: 1M+ per machine). If one dies, all its clients must reconnect elsewhere. Reconnecting them all is slow
    Offline backup queue Queues are replicated; consumers re-subscribe to the backup queue

    Wrap-up

    • The design has two flows: manage file metadata and file sync. The notification service (long polling) keeps clients current.
    • What makes it interesting: strong consistency + low bandwidth + fast sync.
    • Alternative: upload straight from the client to cloud storage. Faster: the file travels once, not client → block server → cloud. Drawbacks:
    • Chunking, compression and encryption must be built on every platform (iOS, Android, web). Error-prone and costly. Block servers keep it in one place.
    • Clients can be hacked, so client-side encryption is not ideal.
    • Presence service: move online/offline tracking out of the notification servers, so other services can use it.
    ✓ Key points
    • Separate metadata (relational DB + cache) from content (blocks in S3).
    • Files become ≤ 4 MB blocks; block servers compress and encrypt; delta sync sends only changed blocks.
    • Upload metadata and content in parallel; status goes pending → uploaded via the storage callback.
    • Strong consistency: ACID DB, invalidate cache on write.
    • Long polling for change notifications; offline backup queue for offline clients.
    • Save space with block dedup, version limits, and cold storage.
    ⚠ Common trap

    re-uploading the whole file on every edit. It wastes bandwidth, which is one of the stated requirements. Also: saying "WebSocket" for notifications without noting that traffic is one-way and infrequent.

    V2·1 Proximity Service

    proximity serviceYelpnearby searchlocation-based serviceLBSgeospatial indexgeohashquadtreeGoogle S2Hilbert curvek-nearestread replicasRedis cachegeofencing
    See also Indexes · SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 1.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a proximity service like Yelp's "nearby": given a user's location and a radius, return nearby businesses (restaurants, hotels, gas stations).

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Can the user set a radius? Expand if too few results? Yes. Only care about the radius; expanding is a bonus topic
    Max radius? 20 km (12.5 miles)
    Radius options in the UI? 0.5 km, 1 km, 2 km, 5 km, 20 km
    Must business adds/edits/deletes show in real time? No. Agreed upfront: changes take effect the next day
    Refresh results as the user moves? No. Assume users move slowly

    Requirements:

    • Functional: return businesses for a (latitude, longitude) + radius; owners add, update or delete businesses (not real-time); customers view business details.
    • Non-functional: low latency; data privacy (location is sensitive; comply with GDPR, CCPA); high availability and scalability for peak hours in dense areas.

    Estimates: 100M DAU, 200M businesses. A day ≈ 10^5 seconds. 5 searches per user per day → search QPS = 100M × 5 / 10^5 = 5,000.

    Try it first: write the search API, then explain how you would index 200M points so "everything within 1 km of me" does not scan the whole table.

    Solution

    High-level design

    API:

    GET /v1/search/nearby?latitude=..&longitude=..&radius=..   (radius optional, default 5000 m)
  → { "total": 10, "businesses": [ {business object} ] }   (paginate in real life)

GET    /v1/businesses/{:id}   business details
POST   /v1/businesses         add a business
PUT    /v1/businesses/{:id}   update a business
DELETE /v1/businesses/{:id}   delete a business

    The search result object has enough to render the list. The detail page (photos, reviews, rating) needs a second call.

    Data model. Reads are high (search, view details); writes are low. A relational DB like MySQL fits.

    business:      business_id PK, address, city, state, country, latitude, longitude
geo index:     covered in the deep dive (geohash table)

    Architecture (Figure 2):

                  User
               │
         Load balancer
     /search/nearby   /businesses/{:id}
        │                    │
       LBS            Business service
        │ read               │ write
   ┌────▼──── Database cluster ───▼────┐
   │ Replica  Replica  Replica  Primary│  (primary replicates to replicas)
   └───────────────────────────────────┘
    • Load balancer: one DNS entry point; routes by URL path.
    • LBS (location-based service): finds nearby businesses. Read-only, high QPS at peak, stateless, so it scales horizontally.
    • Business service: owner writes (low QPS) and detail views (high QPS at peak).
    • DB cluster: primary takes writes, replicas take reads. Replication lag is fine, since updates need not be real-time.
    • Both services are stateless: add servers at mealtime, remove them at night. Use multiple regions and AZs.

    Algorithms to fetch nearby businesses. Real systems use Redis geohash or PostGIS. In the interview, explain how the index works instead of naming a DB.

    Option Idea Verdict
    1. 2D search WHERE lat BETWEEN lat±r AND lng BETWEEN lng±r Full scan. Indexes on lat and lng each return a huge set; intersecting them is slow. An index helps only one dimension
    2. Even grid Split the world into equal cells Data is very uneven (NYC vs ocean). Finding neighbor cells is hard
    3. Geohash Recursively halve lat and lng, interleave bits, base32-encode Simple, widely used
    4. Quadtree In-memory tree; split a cell into 4 until ≤ 100 businesses Adapts to density
    5. Google S2 Map the sphere to 1D on a Hilbert curve (close on the curve = close in space) Powerful but hard to explain

    The shared idea: divide the map into small areas and index them (hash-based: even grid, geohash, cartesian tiers; tree-based: quadtree, S2, R-tree).

    Geohash. Split the planet at the equator and prime meridian: lat [-90,0]→0, [0,90]→1; lng [-180,0]→0, [0,180]→1. Keep splitting, alternating longitude and latitude bits. Encode in base32. Example: Google HQ = 9q9hvu, Facebook HQ = 9q9jhr. There are 12 lengths; only 4–6 are useful here.

    Geohash length Grid size
    4 39.1 km × 19.5 km
    5 4.9 km × 4.9 km
    6 1.2 km × 609.4 m
    7 152.9 m × 152.4 m

    Pick the shortest geohash whose cell covers the whole search circle:

    Radius 0.5 km 1 km 2 km 5 km 20 km
    Geohash length 6 5 5 4 4

    Geohash boundary issues:

    • A longer shared prefix means closer. The reverse is false. Issue 1: two places can be close with no shared prefix (they sit on either side of the equator or prime meridian). La Roche-Chalais (u000) is 30 km from Pomerol (ezzz). So WHERE geohash LIKE '9q8zn%' misses results.
    • Issue 2: two points can share a long prefix yet sit in different cells.
    • Fix: query the current cell plus its 8 neighbors. Neighbor geohashes are computed in constant time.
    • Not enough results? Option 1: return only what is in the radius (easy, but may be too few). Option 2: drop the last geohash character to widen the cell, and repeat until there are enough.

    Quadtree.

    • Root = the whole world. Split any node with > 100 businesses into 4 children (buildQuadtree recursion). It is an in-memory structure on each LBS server, built at start-up, not a database.
    • Leaf node: 4 coordinates (32 B) + up to 100 IDs × 8 B = 832 B. Internal node: 32 B coords + 4 child pointers (32 B) = 64 B.
    • Leaves ≈ 200M / 100 = 2M; internal nodes ≈ 2M / 3 ≈ 0.67M. Memory ≈ 2M × 832 B + 0.67M × 64 B ≈ 1.71 GB. Fits in one server, but you may still need several for CPU or bandwidth.
    • Build time ≈ (n/100) log(n/100): a few minutes for 200M.
    • Search: walk from the root to the leaf with the user's location. If it has 100 businesses, return it; otherwise add neighbors until there are enough.
    • Operations: a server cannot serve while it builds. Roll out to a few servers at a time. Blue/green would make a whole new cluster load 200M rows from the DB at once. Updates: rebuild incrementally (some servers stale for a while, acceptable given the next-day rule), or update on the fly (needs locking in a multi-threaded tree, much harder). A nightly cache refresh can invalidate many keys at once and load the cache servers.

    S2 advantages: great for geofencing (cover any area at varying levels and notify users who leave it), and the Region Cover algorithm (set min level, max level, max cells instead of one fixed precision).

    Who uses what: Geohash: Bing Maps, Redis, MongoDB, Lyft. Quadtree: Yext. Both: Elasticsearch. S2: Google Maps, Tinder. In an interview, pick geohash or quadtree.

    Geohash Quadtree
    Implementation Easy, no tree Harder, must build a tree
    Query type Within a radius k-nearest (e.g. nearest k gas stations, however far)
    Grid size Fixed per precision Adapts to density (Denver example)
    Updates Easy: delete the (geohash, business_id) row O(log n) walk from root; locking with threads; rebalancing (over-allocate ranges)

    Deep dives

    Scale the database

    • Business table: too big for one server. Shard by business_id: even load, easy to operate.
    • Geo index table (geohash as the example). Option 1: one row per geohash holding a JSON array of business IDs. Updates must scan the array, check duplicates, and lock the row. Option 2 (chosen): one row per business, compound key (geohash, business_id). Adds and removes are simple, with no locks.
    geohash | business_id
32feac  | 343
32feac  | 347
f3lcad  | 112
    • Don't rush to shard the geo index. It is small (≈1.71 GB for quadtree, similar for geohash) and fits in one DB's working set. Sharding adds app-level logic for no strong reason. Use read replicas to spread the read load.

    Caching

    • First ask if a cache is even a win. The dataset fits in memory, so queries are not I/O bound, and replicas can add read throughput. Justify it with benchmarks and cost.
    • Cache key: not raw lat/lng. Phone coordinates are noisy and change slightly as users move. Use the geohash, so nearby points map to the same key.
    • Two caches:
    Key Value Name in final diagram
    geohash list of business IDs in the grid "Geohash" Redis
    business_id business object (name, address, image URLs) "Business info" Redis
    • On a miss: SELECT business_id FROM geohash_index WHERE geohash LIKE '{geohash}%', then Cache.set(key, ids, "1d"). On add/edit/delete, update the DB and invalidate the cache. Easy, since writes are rare and geohash needs no locks.
    • Cache all three precisions (geohash_4, _5, _6). Memory = 8 B × 200M × 3 ≈ 5 GB. One Redis server is enough by memory, but deploy the same copy globally for availability and lower cross-continent latency.

    Regions and availability zones

    • Users connect to a nearby region (US West, Europe).
    • Spread dense areas (Japan, Korea) into their own regions or several AZs.
    • Privacy laws: some countries require local data. Put a region there and use DNS routing to keep that country's requests inside it.

    Filter by time or type

    "Open now" or "restaurants only": each grid returns few businesses, so return IDs, hydrate the objects, then filter in memory. This assumes opening time and type are in the business table.

    Final design (Figure 21)

    User ─► Load balancer ─┬─ /search/nearby ──► LBS ──read──► Redis cluster [Business info | Geohash]
                       └─ /businesses/{:id} ─► Business service ─read─► Redis cluster
                                                        └─write─► DB primary ─► replicas
                                               DB cluster ──sync──► Redis cluster

    Search flow (restaurants within 500 m):

    1. Client sends lat/lng (37.776720, -122.416730) and radius 500 m to the load balancer.
    2. The load balancer forwards to the LBS.
    3. LBS maps 500 m to geohash length 6.
    4. LBS computes the 8 neighbors: [my_geohash, neighbor1 … neighbor8].
    5. LBS fetches business IDs for each geohash from "Geohash" Redis, in parallel.
    6. LBS hydrates businesses from "Business info" Redis, computes distances, ranks, and returns.

    View/edit flow: the business service reads "Business info" Redis, falling back to the DB and filling the cache. Because changes take effect next day, a nightly job updates cached business data.

    Wrap-up

    • Covered indexes: 2D search, even grid, geohash, quadtree, S2. Geohash was used as the worked example.
    • Caching cuts latency: what to cache and how to use it.
    • Scale the DB with replication (geo index) and sharding (business table).
    • Multi-region and multi-AZ deployment for availability, proximity to users, and local privacy laws.
    ✓ Key points
    • Explain why a 2D lat/lng index fails, then map 2D → 1D with grid cells.
    • Know geohash: precision vs radius, the boundary issues, the 8-neighbor fix, and dropping a character to widen the search.
    • Know quadtree: the 100-per-leaf rule, ~1.71 GB memory, start-up build time, and that it suits k-nearest.
    • The geo index is small: use read replicas, not sharding. Shard the business table by ID.
    • Cache by geohash, not exact coordinates.
    ⚠ Common trap

    jumping to sharding the geo index, or querying only the user's own geohash cell. The index fits in memory, and a prefix-only query misses businesses just across a cell edge.
