    V2·2 Nearby Friends

    nearby friendslocation sharingWebSocketRedis pub/sublocation cacheTTLconsistent hashinghash ringservice discoveryetcdZooKeeperCassandrageohash channelErlangfan-outstateful servers
    See also Redis Pub/Sub vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka · Concurrency Models (GIL, Threads, Processes, asyncio)

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 2.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design the backend for a "Nearby Friends" feature. An opt-in user sees a list of friends who are close by, with distance and last-updated time.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    What counts as "nearby"? 5 miles; configurable
    Straight-line distance? Yes (ignore rivers and roads)
    How many users? 1B users; 10% use this feature
    Store location history? Yes, e.g. for machine learning
    Inactive friends? Hide a friend inactive for more than 10 minutes
    Privacy laws (GDPR, CCPA)? Ignore for now

    Requirements:

    • Functional: see nearby friends, each with a distance and a last-updated timestamp; the list refreshes every few seconds.
    • Non-functional: low latency; reliable overall, but losing an occasional data point is fine; eventual consistency (replicas a few seconds behind is fine).

    Estimates:

    • Refresh every 30 s (walking is 3–4 mph, so 30 s barely changes anything).
    • 100M DAU; concurrent = 10% → 10M. 400 friends per user on average; 20 shown per page.
    • Location update QPS = 10M / 30 ≈ 334,000.
    • Forwarding: if ~10% of friends are online and nearby, 333K × 400 × 10% ≈ 13M updates/s to forward.

    Try it first: decide how a location update from one user reaches each online friend within seconds, and where the "current location" lives. Then estimate how many pub/sub servers you need.

    Solution

    High-level design

    The book designs the high level before the API, because the protocol is not plain HTTP: the server must push.

    Peer-to-peer (each phone connects to each nearby friend) is not practical on flaky mobile networks and a tight battery budget. So a shared backend does three things: receive every active user's updates; for each update, find the active friends who should get it; and drop it if the distance is over the threshold.

    Mobile users ──WebSocket──► Load balancer ──http──► API servers ─► User DB
                                │                    (friends, profile, auth)
                                ▼
                       WebSocket servers (stateful, bi-directional)
                 │            │                 │                  │
           Redis pub/sub  Location cache   Location history DB   User DB
           (publish; subscribers' handlers get updates back)
    • Load balancer: in front of the stateless REST API servers and the stateful WebSocket servers.
    • REST API servers: add/remove friends, update profiles. Standard work.
    • WebSocket servers: one persistent connection per client. They push friends' updates and seed a new client with nearby online friends.
    • Redis location cache: latest location per active user, with a TTL. Each update refreshes the TTL. When it expires, the user is inactive and drops out.
    • User DB: profiles and friendships (relational or NoSQL).
    • Location history DB: not on the critical path.
    • Redis pub/sub: a very light message bus. Channels are cheap; a server with GBs of memory can hold millions of channels. Each user publishes to their own channel. Each online friend's WebSocket handler subscribes to it.

    Periodic location update (Figure 7):

    1. The client sends an update to the load balancer.
    2. The load balancer forwards it to the client's persistent connection on a WebSocket server.
    3. The server saves it to the location history DB.
    4. The server updates the location cache (refreshing the TTL) and stores the location in the connection handler's variable.
    5. The server publishes it to the user's channel in Redis pub/sub. Steps 3–5 can run in parallel.
    6. Redis broadcasts it to all subscribers: the handlers of the user's online friends.
    7. Each friend's handler computes the distance between the sender (from the message) and the friend (from the handler's variable).
    8. If within the radius, it sends the new location and timestamp to the friend's client. Otherwise it drops the update.

    With 400 friends and 10% online and nearby, each update fans out to about 40 friends.

    API (WebSocket):

    API Request Response
    Periodic location update lat, lng, timestamp nothing
    Client receives updates (server push) friend location + timestamp —
    WebSocket init lat, lng, timestamp friends' locations
    Subscribe to a new friend (server sends) friend ID friend's latest lat, lng, timestamp
    Unsubscribe a friend (server sends) friend ID nothing

    HTTP APIs (add/remove friends, profiles) are standard.

    Data model:

    Location cache (Redis):   key = user_id   value = {latitude, longitude, timestamp}
Location history:         user_id | latitude | longitude | timestamp
    • Why not a DB for current location? Only the current location matters, one per user. Redis is very fast and has TTL for auto-purging inactive users. It need not be durable. If Redis dies, start an empty one and let updates refill it. Users miss an update cycle or two, which is acceptable.
    • Location history: heavy writes, must scale horizontally. Cassandra is a good fit. A relational DB also works but must be sharded by user ID.

    Deep dives

    How each component scales

    • API servers: stateless; auto-scale on CPU, load or I/O.
    • WebSocket servers: auto-scaling is easy, but they are stateful. To remove a node, mark it "draining" at the load balancer so no new connections arrive. Remove it when its connections close (or after a long wait). Deploys need the same care. Good cloud load balancers handle this well.
    • User DB: profiles and friendships will not fit one instance. Shard by user ID. At this scale a dedicated team may expose it through an internal API. Same function and performance either way.
    • Location cache: 10M users × ≤ 100 B fits easily in one Redis by memory. But 334K writes/s is too much for one server. Shard by user ID (each user's data is independent). Replicate each shard to a standby for availability.

    Client initialization

    When a client opens its WebSocket and sends its first location, the handler:

    1. Updates the user's location in the location cache.
    2. Saves it in a handler variable.
    3. Loads all friends from the user DB.
    4. Batch-fetches friends' locations from the cache. Inactive friends have expired (TTL = inactivity timeout), so they are missing.
    5. For each friend within the radius, returns profile, location and timestamp to the client.
    6. Subscribes to every friend's channel, active or not. Inactive channels cost a little memory but no CPU or I/O until the friend publishes.
    7. Publishes the user's current location to the user's own channel.

    Redis pub/sub: why and how many

    • A channel is created on first subscribe. Publishing to a channel with no subscribers just drops the message. A channel costs a small hash table and linked list, and no CPU while idle.
    • So: one channel per user, and subscribe to all friends at start-up. The backend never has to subscribe or unsubscribe as friends go online or offline. This trades more memory for a simpler design.
    Resource Math Servers
    Memory 100M channels × 100 active friends × 20 B per subscriber ≈ 200 GB ≈ 2 (100 GB each)
    CPU 13M pushes/s ÷ ~100K pushes/s per server (conservative, gigabit NIC) ≈ 130
    • The bottleneck is CPU, not memory. We need a distributed pub/sub cluster.

    Distributed pub/sub cluster

    • Channels are independent, so shard by the publisher's user ID.
    • Add service discovery (etcd or ZooKeeper). It only needs to store a config value and let clients subscribe to changes:
    Key:   /config/pub_sub_ring
Value: ["p_1", "p_2", "p_3", "p_4"]      ← consistent-hash ring of pub/sub servers
    • To publish (Figure 10): (1) the WebSocket server looks up hash(channel) on the ring. It keeps a local cached copy of the ring and subscribes to ring updates. (2) It publishes to that pub/sub server. Subscribing uses the same lookup.

    Scaling and operating the pub/sub cluster

    • Messages are not stored, so the data path is stateless. But each channel's subscriber list is state. If a channel moves, every subscriber must unsubscribe from the old server and resubscribe on the new one.
    • So treat it as a stateful cluster, like storage. Over-provision for daily peak plus headroom. Do not scale it up and down every day.
    • Resizing (e.g. [p_1..p_4] → [p_1..p_6]) moves many channels and causes a flood of resubscribes. Some updates are missed. Do it at the lowest-traffic time. Steps: provision new servers, update the ring key, watch for a CPU spike on the WebSocket cluster.
    • Replacing a dead server is much safer: only its channels move. The on-call operator swaps p_1 → p_1_new in the ring. WebSocket servers are notified. Each handler checks its subscribed channels against the new ring and resubscribes only the moved ones.

    Adding or removing friends

    The app registers callbacks. On "friend added", the client asks the WebSocket server to subscribe to the friend's channel. The server returns the friend's latest location if active. On "friend removed", it unsubscribes. The same callbacks handle a friend opting in or out.

    Users with many friends

    Friend counts are capped (Facebook: 5,000), and friendships are two-way, unlike a celebrity follower model. A user's subscribers spread across many WebSocket servers. Their channel adds some load to one of tens of pub/sub servers. These "whales" are spread out, so there are no hotspots.

    Nearby random person (extra credit)

    • Add a pool of pub/sub channels per geohash cell.
    • On update, the handler computes the user's geohash and publishes to that cell's channel. Everyone in the cell (except the sender) receives it.
    • For border cases, each client subscribes to its cell plus the 8 surrounding cells.

    Alternative: Erlang

    • The book argues Erlang is better than Redis pub/sub here, but it is niche and hard to hire for.
    • The Erlang ecosystem: Erlang/Elixir language, BEAM VM, OTP libraries. An Erlang process is ~300 bytes, with millions per server. It uses no CPU when idle.
    • Design: write the WebSocket service in Erlang and replace the Redis pub/sub cluster with a distributed Erlang app. Each user is an Erlang process. It gets the user's updates and subscribes to friends' processes (native in OTP), forming a mesh that routes updates.

    Wrap-up

    Core parts: WebSocket for real-time traffic, Redis for fast location reads and writes, and Redis pub/sub as the routing layer. We built a small-scale design, then scaled the API servers, WebSocket servers, data layer and pub/sub servers. We also covered the Erlang alternative, users with many friends, and "nearby random person".

    ✓ Key points
    • Say why this differs from proximity search: dynamic locations make it a fan-out problem.
    • Put current locations in Redis with a TTL equal to the inactivity timeout. Keep history in Cassandra.
    • One pub/sub channel per user. The subscriber's handler does the distance filter, so far-away updates are dropped on the server.
    • Do the memory vs CPU math: CPU (~13M pushes/s) drives the server count.
    • Shard channels with a consistent-hash ring in etcd/ZooKeeper. Resize rarely and off-peak; replacing a node is cheap.
    ⚠ Common trap

    treating the pub/sub cluster as stateless and auto-scaling it daily. Each resize moves channels and forces mass resubscribes. Also, storing current locations in a durable DB is unnecessary.

    V2·3 Google Maps

    Google MapsnavigationETAmap renderingmap tilesrouting tileszoom levelsCDNgeohashgeocodingA* searchDijkstraCassandraKafkaadaptive ETAreroutingvector tilesWeb Mercator
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ · SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 3.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a simple Google Maps for mobile phones: track user locations, give directions with an ETA, and render the map.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    DAU? 1 billion
    Which features? Location update, navigation, ETA, map rendering
    Road data? We already have it from several sources: TBs of raw data
    Consider traffic? Yes, it is key to accurate ETAs
    Travel modes? Support several (driving, walking, bus…)
    Multi-stop directions? Nice to have; not the focus
    Businesses and photos? Out of scope

    Requirements:

    • Functional: user location update; navigation service including ETA; map rendering. Main clients are mobile phones.
    • Non-functional: accuracy (no wrong directions); smooth map rendering; low data and battery usage; general availability and scalability.

    Map 101 (the concepts the design needs):

    • Projection: 3D globe → 2D plane always distorts. Google uses Web Mercator.
    • Geocoding: address → lat/lng (reverse geocoding goes the other way). One method is interpolation over GIS street data.
    • Geohashing: recursively split a flat 20,000 × 10,000 km map into 4 sub-grids, each named 0–3, until a size threshold. Used here for tiling.
    • Map tiles: the world is cut into 256×256 PNG tiles per zoom level. The client downloads only the tiles it needs and stitches them. Fully zoomed out = one tile.
    • Routing: routing algorithms (Dijkstra and A variants) run on a graph: intersections = nodes, roads = edges. Their speed depends heavily on graph size. So split the road network into routing tiles: geohash-like grids, each a small graph with references to the tiles it connects to*. Map tiles are PNGs; routing tiles are binary road data.
    • Hierarchical routing tiles: 3 levels. Small tiles with local roads; bigger tiles with arterial roads; large tiles with highways. Edges link levels (e.g. local street A → freeway F). Cross-country routing uses the coarse level.

    Estimates:

    • Map storage: zoom 21 has ~4.4 trillion tiles. × 100 KB ≈ 440 PB. About 90% of the world is ocean, desert or mountains, which compress well, so cut by 80–90% → 44–88 PB, call it 50 PB. Each lower level has 4× fewer tiles: 50 + 50/4 + 50/16 + … ≈ 67 PB, so roughly 100 PB in total. Routing tiles: TBs. Metadata: negligible.
    • Navigation: 1B DAU × 5 sessions/week, 35 min/week → 5B minutes/day. QPS = 1B × 5 / 7 / 10^5 ≈ 7,200; peak (5×) 36,000.
    • Location updates: sending GPS every second = 5B min × 60 = 300B/day = 3M QPS. Batch on the client and send every 15 s → 200K QPS; peak 1M QPS. Send less often when the user is stuck in traffic.

    Try it first: sketch how the phone gets map images without the server drawing them, how a route is computed over a road graph too big for memory, and where 1M location writes per second go.

    Solution

    High-level design

                   Mobile user ───────────────► CDN ─► Static map images (object storage)
                    │
              Load balancer
           ┌────────┴─────────┐
   Navigation service    Location service
     │           │              │
 Geocoding DB  Routing tiles   User location DB
               (object storage)

    Location service.

    • The client records GPS every second but sends a batch every 15 s. This cuts traffic a lot.
    • Why collect it: live traffic, detecting new or closed roads, personalization, better ETAs and rerouting.
    • Writes stay huge, so use a write-optimized, scalable DB (Cassandra). Also log to Kafka for stream processing.
    • Protocol: HTTP with keep-alive (efficient).
    POST /v1/locations
  locs: JSON array of (latitude, longitude, timestamp) tuples

    Navigation service. Find a reasonably fast route from A to B. Some latency is fine. It need not be the fastest, but it must be accurate.

    GET /v1/nav?origin=1355+market+street,SF&destination=Disneyland
→ { distance: {text: "0.2 mi", value: 259}, duration: {text: "1 min", value: 83},
    start_location, end_location, html_instructions, polyline: {points: "..."},
    geocoded_waypoints: [...], travel_mode: "DRIVING" }

    Rerouting and traffic changes are handled later by adaptive ETA.

    Map rendering. 100 PB cannot live on the client. Fetch tiles on demand when the user zooms or pans, or moves into a nearby tile during navigation.

    Option How Verdict
    1. Build tiles on the fly Server renders per location + zoom Huge server load; endless combinations make caching hard
    2. Pre-generated static tiles Fixed grid per zoom level, one tile per geohash, served by a CDN Chosen. Served from the nearest POP; static files cache very well

    Data usage per client (no client cache): moving at 30 km/h, with each 256×256 tile (~100 KB) covering 200 m × 200 m. 1 km² = 25 tiles = 2.5 MB. 30 km/h → 75 MB/h ≈ 1.25 MB/min. Daily routes repeat, so client caching cuts this a lot.

    CDN traffic: 5B nav minutes/day × 1.25 MB = 6.25B MB/day → 62,500 MB/s. With 200 POPs, each serves only a few hundred MB/s.

    Tile URLs. The client can compute the geohash from lat/lng + zoom, e.g. zoom-7 tile at Google HQ 9q9heb → https://cdn.map-provider.com/tiles/9q9heb.png.

    • Trade-off: that algorithm is hardcoded in every client. Changing the encoding means shipping app updates on every platform, which is slow and risky.
    • Alternative: a tiny map tile service builds the URLs. It adds operational flexibility. Flow: (1) the client calls the map tile service via the load balancer, (2) the LB forwards it, (3) the service takes location + zoom and returns 9 tile URLs (the tile plus 8 neighbors), (4) the client downloads them from the CDN.

    Deep dives

    Data model

    Data Store Why
    Routing tiles Binary adjacency lists in object storage (S3), keyed by geohash; cached aggressively on the routing service Too big for memory (else no tiling needed). A DB would only be costly storage; no DB features needed. Geohash gives fast lookup by lat/lng
    User location Cassandra Write-heavy, scales horizontally
    Geocoding Redis (KV) Frequent reads, rare writes. Converts origin and destination to lat/lng
    Precomputed map images CDN backed by S3 Rendering roads into images is heavy and repeated. Compute once per zoom level
    • A routing tile processing service is an offline pipeline that runs periodically. It turns the raw road data (names, county, lat/lng; not a graph) into the 3 levels of routing tiles. Collected user locations improve the data over time.

    Location service

    • 1M writes/s, and a location is stale as soon as the next one arrives. Favor availability over consistency (AP in CAP). Cassandra fits.
    • Key = (user_id, timestamp): user_id is the partition key, timestamp the clustering key. You can read a user's latest position fast, and a time-range read is efficient because rows are stored together, sorted by time.
    user_id | timestamp | lat  | long | user_mode | navigation_mode
51      | 132053000 | 21.9 | 89.8 | active    | driving
    • Also write every update to Kafka. Consumers include:
    Location service ─► User location DB
        └─► Kafka ─┬─► Traffic update service ─► Traffic DB
                   ├─► ML personalization ─► Personalization DB
                   ├─► Routing tile processing ─► Routing tiles (S3): new/closed roads
                   └─► Analytics ─► Analytics DB

    Map rendering

    • 21 zoom levels (as Google uses). Level 0 = 1 tile of 256×256. Each level doubles the tiles in both directions: level 1 = 2×2 (512×512 px), level 2 = 4×4 (1024×1024 px). Each level has 4× the pixels. The client picks the level that matches its viewport and zoom.
    • Optimization: vector tiles. With WebGL, send paths and polygons instead of images, and the client draws them. Vectors compress much better (big bandwidth savings). Zooming is also smooth: raster tiles stretch and pixelate between levels, while vectors scale each element.

    Navigation service (Figure 17)

    Mobile user ─► Navigation service ─► Geocoding service ─► Geocoding DB
                       │
               Route planner service
          ┌────────────┼──────────────┐
       Ranker    Shortest-path svc   ETA service
         │             │                 │
   Filter service   Routing tiles     Traffic DB ◄─ Update traffic service ◄─ Location DB
  (avoid tolls…)    (object storage)
    • Geocoding service: resolves a place name or address to lat/lng (like Google's geocode API: address=1600+Amphitheatre+Parkway… → lat 37.4224764, lng -122.0842499). It runs on origin and destination first.
    • Route planner: finds a route optimized for travel time under current traffic, by calling the services below.
    • Shortest-path service: returns the top-k shortest paths without traffic. It depends only on road structure, which rarely changes, so cache routes. It runs an A* variant on routing tiles: convert origin and destination to geohashes, load those tiles, then traverse and hydrate neighbor tiles from S3 (or a local cache) as the search grows. Links between levels let it "enter" highway-only tiles.
    • ETA service: ML prediction from live and historical traffic for each candidate route. The hard part is predicting traffic 10–20 minutes ahead (out of scope).
    • Ranker: applies user filters (avoid tolls, avoid freeways), sorts fastest first, and returns the top-k.
    • Updater services consume Kafka: routing tile processing (new roads and closures → more accurate paths) and traffic update (→ live traffic DB → better ETAs).

    Adaptive ETA and rerouting

    The server must track active navigating users and update their ETA when traffic changes. How do we find affected users fast among millions of routes?

    • Naive: store each user's route as a list of routing tiles (user_1: s_1, s_2, …, s_k). On an incident in s_2, scan every row: O(n × m) (n users, m tiles per route).
    • Better: for each user, store the current tile and its enclosing tiles at the coarser levels: user_1, s_1, super(s_1), super(super(s_1)), …. An incident tile is checked against the last (largest) tile of each row. If it is not inside, the user is unaffected. This filters out most users quickly.
    • When traffic clears: keep all possible routes per user, recompute ETAs regularly, and notify the user if a faster route appears.

    Delivery protocol (server → client):

    Option Verdict
    Mobile push notification Payload too small (4,096 bytes on iOS); no web support
    Long polling Heavier on servers than WebSocket
    Server-Sent Events Works, but one-way only
    WebSocket Chosen: light on servers and bi-directional (features like last-mile delivery may need it)

    Final design = Figure 17 plus an Adaptive ETA and rerouting service. It is called by the navigation service, reads the traffic DB, and keeps an Active users store.

    Wrap-up

    We designed location updates, ETAs, route planning and map rendering. Extension: multi-stop navigation for enterprise customers (find the best order to visit a set of destinations under live traffic), useful for DoorDash, Uber, Lyft.

    ✓ Key points
    • Learn the vocabulary: projection, geocoding, geohash, map tiles vs routing tiles, zoom levels.
    • Pre-generate static map tiles per zoom level and serve them from a CDN. Discuss client-side URL computation vs a map tile service.
    • Break the road graph into hierarchical routing tiles in object storage. A* loads them lazily and jumps to highway tiles for long trips.
    • Batch GPS on the client (15 s). Store it in Cassandra keyed by (user_id, timestamp), and fan it out through Kafka to traffic, routing-tile and ML updaters.
    • Separate shortest path (static, cacheable) from ETA (traffic-aware ML) and ranking (user filters).
    ⚠ Common trap

    rendering map tiles on demand on the server, or loading the whole world's road graph into memory. Both fail at this scale. Pre-render to a CDN and tile the graph.

    V2·4 Distributed Message Queue

    message queueevent streamingKafkatopicpartitionbrokerconsumer groupoffsetwrite-ahead logsegmentin-sync replicasISRackpull vs pushrebalancingdelivery semanticsexactly once
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 4.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a distributed message queue. It should also have event-streaming features: long retention and repeated consumption of messages (like Kafka or Pulsar).

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Message format and size? Text only, in the KB range
    Can messages be consumed repeatedly? Yes, by different consumers (an added feature; a traditional MQ drops a message once delivered)
    Consumed in the order produced? Yes (added feature; traditional MQs usually don't guarantee order)
    Persist data? Retention? Yes, 2 weeks (added feature)
    How many producers and consumers? The more the better
    Delivery semantics? At-least-once for sure; ideally all three, configurable
    Throughput and latency? High throughput for log aggregation; low latency for classic MQ use cases

    Requirements:

    • Functional: producers send messages; consumers consume them; messages can be consumed repeatedly or once; old data can be truncated; KB-sized messages; delivery in the order added; configurable at-least / at-most / exactly once.
    • Non-functional: high throughput or low latency (configurable per use case); scalable and able to absorb sudden surges; persistent and durable (on disk, replicated across nodes).

    Estimates: the book gives none.

    Traditional MQ note: RabbitMQ-style queues keep messages in memory only until consumed (small on-disk overflow) and usually don't keep order. That makes the design much simpler.

    Try it first: sketch how one topic is split across servers, how a message is stored on disk, how consumers share work without breaking order, and how a message survives a broker crash.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Messaging models:

    • Point-to-point: a message goes to a queue and one consumer gets it. It is removed after the ACK. No retention.
    • Publish-subscribe: a message goes to a topic and every subscriber gets it.
    • This design supports both. Topics give pub/sub. Consumer groups simulate point-to-point.

    Core concepts:

    • Topic: a named category of messages, unique across the service.
    • Partition: a topic is sharded into partitions. Each one is a FIFO queue, so order is kept inside a partition. Add partitions to scale a topic.
    • Offset: the position of a message in its partition.
    • Broker: a server that holds partitions.
    • Message key: same key (e.g. user ID) → same partition. No key → random partition.
    • Consumer group: consumers that share the work for a topic. Each group keeps its own offsets (e.g. one group for billing, one for accounting).
    • Rule: a partition is consumed by only one consumer in a group. Two consumers on one partition would break order. If a group has more consumers than partitions, some sit idle.
    • Put all consumers in one group → point-to-point. Allocate many more partitions than consumers up front, then scale by adding consumers.

    Architecture:

                     Metadata storage        Coordination service
                        ▲                (ZooKeeper / etcd)
                        │                       ▲
Producers ──────► Brokers ─────────────────────────────► Consumer groups
                  ├─ data storage (partitions)
                  └─ state storage (consumer offsets)
    • Producer pushes messages to a topic. Consumer group subscribes and consumes.
    • Broker holds partitions.
    • Data storage: messages, per partition. State storage: consumer state (offsets). Metadata storage: topic config and properties.
    • Coordination service: service discovery (which brokers are alive) and leader election. One broker is the active controller; it assigns partitions.

    Deep dives

    Three choices drive throughput: an on-disk structure built for sequential access and the OS disk cache; a message format that passes from producer to queue to consumer with no changes (no copying); and batching everywhere.

    Data storage

    Traffic: write-heavy and read-heavy, no updates or deletes, mostly sequential access.

    Option Verdict
    Database (SQL table per topic, or NoSQL collection) Hard to support write-heavy + read-heavy at scale; becomes a bottleneck
    Write-ahead log (WAL) Chosen. Append-only file, pure sequential read/write (like MySQL redo log, ZooKeeper WAL)
    • New messages are appended to the tail of a partition with an increasing offset.
    • A file can't grow forever, so split it into segments. Only the active segment takes writes. When it hits a size limit, a new active segment starts. Old segments serve reads only and are truncated past the retention or capacity limit.
    • Layout: Topic-A/Partition-1/segment-1, segment-2, ….
    • Disk note: rotational disks are slow only for random access. Sequential access on RAID disks gives several hundred MB/s, cheaply. The OS also caches disk data in free memory very aggressively.

    Message data structure

    A shared contract between producer, queue, and consumer. If any part disagrees, messages get mutated, which means expensive copying.

    Field Type Note
    key byte[] picks the partition: hash(key) % numPartitions (or a custom mapping)
    value byte[] payload: plain text or compressed binary
    topic string
    partition integer
    offset long topic + partition + offset locate a message
    timestamp long when stored
    size integer
    crc integer integrity check
    • The key is not the partition number. Partition numbers are internal and not exposed to clients.
    • Unlike a KV store, message keys need not be unique or even present.
    • Optional fields (e.g. tags) can be added for features like filtering.

    Batching

    • Groups messages into one network request, so fewer round trips.
    • The broker writes large chunks: bigger sequential writes and bigger contiguous disk-cache blocks.
    • Trade-off: bigger batch = higher throughput but higher latency. For a low-latency queue, use smaller batches. When tuned for throughput, you may need more partitions per topic.

    Producer flow

    • Option 1: routing layer. The producer sends to a router. The router reads the replica plan from metadata storage (cached) and forwards to the partition's leader replica. Followers pull from the leader. Once "enough" replicas sync, the leader commits and replies. Drawbacks: an extra network hop, and no batching.
    • Option 2 (chosen): routing + buffer inside the producer client library. Fewer hops (lower latency), the producer can choose its own partition logic, and the buffer sends larger batches (higher throughput).
    • Batch size is the classic throughput vs latency knob; producers tune it per use case.

    Consumer flow: push vs pull

    The consumer gives an offset in a partition and gets back a chunk of events from that position.

    Push Pull
    Pros Low latency: broker sends at once Consumer controls rate; real-time and batch consumers can coexist; slow consumers scale out or catch up; better for aggressive batching (pull everything after the current offset)
    Cons Consumers can be overwhelmed; hard to serve consumers with different speeds Wasted pulls when no data; fix with long polling

    Choice: pull (what most MQs do). Pull flow:

    1. A new consumer joins group 1 for topic A. It finds its broker by hashing the group name. That broker is the group's coordinator (not the same as the cluster coordination service).
    2. The coordinator confirms membership and assigns a partition (round-robin, range, etc.).
    3. The consumer fetches from the last consumed offset in state storage.
    4. It processes messages and commits the offset. The order of process vs commit sets the delivery semantics.

    Consumer rebalancing

    Decides which consumer owns which partitions. Triggers: a consumer joins, leaves, crashes, or partitions change.

    • The coordinator gets heartbeats from consumers and manages their offsets.
    • When the member list changes, the coordinator elects a group leader (a consumer). The leader builds the partition dispatch plan; the coordinator broadcasts it.
    • Join: B asks to join → coordinator tells A (on its next heartbeat) to rejoin → all rejoin → leader elected → leader sends plan → everyone consumes new partitions.
    • Leave: A asks to leave → B is told to rejoin → same steps.
    • Crash: no heartbeat from A within the timeout → A marked dead → rebalance.

    State and metadata storage

    • State storage: partition ↔ consumer mapping, and each group's last consumed offset per partition (e.g. group 1 at 6, group 2 at 13). A replacement consumer resumes from it.
    • Access: frequent small reads/writes, frequent updates, rare deletes, random access, consistency matters → a KV store like ZooKeeper. (Kafka later moved offsets into the brokers.)
    • Metadata storage: partition count, retention, replica distribution. Small, rarely changes, needs strong consistency → ZooKeeper.
    • Simplified design: ZooKeeper holds metadata, state, and coordination (leader election). Brokers keep only message data.

    Replication and in-sync replicas

    • Each partition has 3 replicas on different brokers: one leader, two followers.
    • Producers write only to the leader. Followers pull from it. The leader ACKs once "enough" replicas have the message.
    • The replica distribution plan (e.g. "topic A partition 1: leader broker 1, followers 2 and 3") is made by the controller broker and saved in metadata storage.
    • ISR (in-sync replicas): followers that are close enough to the leader, set by topic config (e.g. replica.lag.max.messages = 4: up to 3 behind is still in sync). The leader is always in ISR. The leader tracks each replica's lag.
    • Committed offset: every message up to it is on all ISRs. Example: leader has 10–15, committed = 13; replica-2 and replica-3 are in ISR; replica-4 (only 10–11) is out until it catches up.
    • Why ISR: waiting for all replicas is safest, but one slow replica would stall the partition.
    ACK setting Producer gets ACK when Trade-off Use case
    ACK=all all ISRs have it (needs ISR count ≥ min.insync.replicas) slowest, strongest durability no loss allowed
    ACK=1 leader persisted it lost if leader dies before followers copy low latency, rare loss OK
    ACK=0 never; no retry lowest latency, may lose data metrics, logging
    • Consumers read from the leader. It is simple, one consumer per partition per group keeps connections low, and hot topics scale by adding partitions. Exception: a consumer in another data center can read from the closest ISR.

    Scalability

    • Producers: no group coordination; add or remove instances.
    • Consumers: groups are isolated; rebalancing handles add, remove, and crash.
    • Broker failure: 4 brokers, broker 3 crashes. The controller sees it and makes a new plan. Each partition gets a new replica on a live broker (e.g. topic B partition 1: broker 4 becomes leader, new replica on broker 2). New replicas catch up as followers.
    • Higher min ISR is safer but slower.
    • Never put replicas of one partition on the same node.
    • Cross-data-center replicas are safer but add latency and cost. Data mirroring is out of scope.
    • Adding a broker: don't just reshuffle. Temporarily allow more replicas than configured. E.g. partition 2 moves to brokers (2, 3, 4); broker 4 copies from leader 2; then the extra replica on broker 1 is removed. No data loss. Removing a broker works the same way.
    • Adding partitions: old messages stay where they are (no migration); new messages spread over all partitions. Producers learn of it from any broker; consumers rebalance.
    • Removing partitions: harder. The decommissioned partition stops receiving writes but stays readable until retention expires; then it is truncated and groups rebalance. It doesn't free space quickly.

    Delivery semantics

    Semantic Producer Consumer Result Use case
    At-most once async, ack=0, no retry commits offset before processing may lose, never duplicates monitoring metrics
    At-least once ack=1 or all, retries on failure/timeout commits offset after processing no loss, possible duplicates most cases; dedupe with a unique key in the DB
    Exactly once guaranteed once guaranteed once no loss, no duplicates; high cost in performance and complexity payments, trading, accounting, when downstream isn't idempotent

    Advanced features

    • Message filtering: e.g. payments only want checkout and refund events from the orders topic.
    • A dedicated topic per consumer wastes storage and couples producers to consumers.
    • Filtering in the consumer wastes traffic.
    • Choice: filter on the broker by tags in the message metadata. The broker must not decrypt or deserialize the payload (slow, and sensitive data should stay unreadable). Several tags allow multi-dimension filters. Complex formulas would need a parser, which is too heavy.
    • Delayed / scheduled messages: e.g. close an order if unpaid after 30 minutes. Send the message now to temporary storage (special topics) on the broker; deliver it to the real topic when time is up. Timing options: fixed delay levels (RocketMQ: 1s, 5s, 10s, 30s, 1m … 2h) or a hierarchical time wheel. Scheduled messages work the same way.

    Wrap-up

    • Protocol: must cover produce, consume, heartbeat; move large volumes; verify integrity. Examples: AMQP, Kafka protocol.
    • Retry consumption: send failed messages to a dedicated retry topic so they don't block new ones.
    • Historical archive: for replaying truncated data, archive old messages to HDFS or object storage.
    ✓ Key points
    • Say early whether you're designing a classic queue or a streaming platform; retention and ordering change the whole design.
    • Partitions are the unit of scale and of order. Key → partition; one consumer per partition per group.
    • Store messages as segmented append-only logs on disk. Sequential I/O, OS cache, zero-copy format, and batching give throughput.
    • Replicate each partition (leader + followers), track ISR, and let producers pick ACK=0/1/all.
    • Consumers pull with long polling; the group coordinator runs rebalancing.
    • Delivery semantics come from ACK settings plus when the consumer commits its offset.
    ⚠ Common trap

    expecting global order across a topic. Order holds only within a partition, and only if a single consumer in the group reads that partition.

    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.2 Case Studies › 4.2.2 Volume 2

    V2·5 Metrics Monitoring and Alerting

    metrics monitoringalertingtime-series databaseInfluxDBPrometheuspull vs pushservice discoverymetrics collectorKafkadownsamplingdelta encodingalert managerGrafanaobservability
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 5.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a scalable metrics monitoring and alerting system for internal use at a large company (like Datadog or Prometheus, but in-house).

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    In-house or SaaS? Internal use only
    Which metrics? Operational: CPU load, memory, disk; also requests/sec, running server count. No business metrics
    Scale? 100M DAU, 1,000 server pools, 100 machines per pool
    Retention? 1 year
    Lower resolution for old data? Raw for 7 days; 1-minute resolution for 30 days; 1-hour after that
    Alert channels? Email, phone, PagerDuty, webhooks
    Logs (error/access)? No
    Distributed tracing? No

    Requirements:

    • Functional: collect many kinds of metrics (CPU, request count, memory, queue message count); store them with the retention policy; alert to several channels; visualize.
    • Non-functional: scalable (growing metrics and alerts), low query latency for dashboards and alerts, reliable (never miss a critical alert), flexible (easy to plug in new tech).
    • Out of scope: log monitoring (ELK) and distributed tracing.

    Estimates: 1,000 pools × 100 machines × 100 metrics per machine ≈ 10 million metrics. 1-year retention with the downsampling policy above.

    Try it first: sketch the path from a server's CPU number to a stored data point and to an alert. Decide pull or push, what database stores it, and how you survive a database outage.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Five components: data collection, data transmission, data storage, alerting, visualization.

    Data model: a time series is identified by a name and optional labels. Each holds <value, timestamp> pairs.

    Part Type
    Metric name String
    Tags/labels List of <key:value> pairs
    Values Array of <value, timestamp> pairs

    Example point: cpu.load, labels host:i631,env:prod, timestamp 1613707265, value 0.29.

    Average CPU on us-west web servers over 10 minutes = average the values of lines like this (the line protocol, used by Prometheus and OpenTSDB):

    CPU.load host=webserver01,region=us-west 1613707265 50
CPU.load host=webserver02,region=us-west 1613707265 43
...

    Access pattern: writes are heavy and constant (10M metrics, many at high frequency). Reads are spiky (dashboards and alert queries come in bursts).

    Storage choice:

    Option Verdict
    Relational DB (MySQL) Needs expert tuning at this scale; rolling-window queries are messy SQL; an index per tag; weak under constant heavy writes
    General NoSQL (Cassandra, Bigtable) Works, but you need deep internals knowledge to design a time-series schema
    Time-series DB Chosen. Far fewer servers for the same data; time-series query languages; built-in retention and aggregation
    • OpenTSDB runs on Hadoop/HBase (extra complexity). Twitter uses MetricsDB; Amazon has Timestream.
    • Most popular: InfluxDB and Prometheus. Both use an in-memory cache plus on-disk storage. InfluxDB with 8 cores and 32 GB RAM handles over 250,000 writes/sec.
    • A good TSDB indexes labels for fast lookup. Keep each label low cardinality (few possible values).
    • In the interview you don't need TSDB internals. Say "metrics are time series, so use a TSDB like InfluxDB."

    Architecture:

    Metrics source ──► Metrics collector ──► Time-series DB ◄── Query service ◄──┬── Alerting system ──► email / phone / PagerDuty / webhooks
(app servers,                                                                └── Visualization system
 SQL DBs, queues)
    • Metrics source: app servers, SQL databases, message queues, etc.
    • Metrics collector: gathers metrics and writes them to the TSDB.
    • Time-series DB: stores series, offers a custom query interface, indexes labels.
    • Query service: a thin wrapper over the TSDB; could be replaced by the TSDB's own interface.
    • Alerting system: sends notifications. Visualization system: graphs and charts.

    Deep dives

    Metrics collection: pull vs push

    For counters and CPU usage, losing a point now and then is fine, so clients can fire and forget.

    Pull model: dedicated collectors pull from each app's HTTP endpoint (e.g. /metrics, exposed by a client library).

    1. The collector gets endpoint config from service discovery (etcd, ZooKeeper): pull interval, IPs, timeout, retries.
    2. It pulls metrics over HTTP.
    3. It registers for change events (or polls) so it sees new and removed servers.
    • A static file of IPs is hard to keep current as servers come and go; service discovery fixes that.
    • One collector can't handle thousands of servers, so use a pool. To stop two collectors pulling the same server, put collectors on a consistent hash ring and map each server by name. Each server then has exactly one collector (e.g. collector 2 owns servers 1 and 5).

    Push model: a collection agent on every server pushes metrics to the collector.

    • The agent can pre-aggregate (e.g. a counter per minute) to cut volume.
    • If the collector rejects pushes, the agent can buffer locally and resend. In auto-scaling groups servers disappear, so buffered data can be lost.
    • Put collectors behind a load balancer in an auto-scaling cluster (scale on CPU) so they don't fall behind.
    Pull Push
    Easy debugging /metrics can be viewed any time, even on a laptop. Pull wins
    Health check No response to a pull → server is down. Pull wins Missing metrics might just be a network issue
    Short-lived jobs Jobs may end before a pull (fix: push gateway) Push wins
    Firewalls / complex networks Every endpoint must be reachable; hard across data centers Collector behind LB + auto-scaling receives from anywhere. Push wins
    Performance Usually TCP Usually UDP, lower latency (counter: TCP setup is small next to the payload)
    Data authenticity Targets are listed in config, so data is authentic Anyone can push; fix with whitelists or auth
    • Examples: pull = Prometheus; push = Amazon CloudWatch, Graphite.
    • Knowing the trade-offs matters more than picking a winner. A large org probably needs both, especially with serverless, where you may not be able to install an agent.

    Scaling the transmission pipeline

    • The collector cluster auto-scales in both models. But if the TSDB is down, data is lost.
    • Add a queue: collector → Kafka → consumers / stream processors (Storm, Flink, Spark) → TSDB.
    • Kafka is reliable and scalable.
    • It decouples collection from processing.
    • It keeps data while the DB is unavailable.
    • Scale through Kafka partitions:
    • Set the partition count from throughput needs.
    • Partition by metric name so consumers can aggregate per metric.
    • Further partition by tags/labels.
    • Categorize and prioritize so important metrics go first.
    • Alternative: running Kafka at production scale is hard. Facebook's Gorilla in-memory TSDB has no queue and stays write-available during partial network failures; arguably as reliable.

    Where aggregation happens

    Place How Trade-off
    Collection agent Simple logic only, e.g. aggregate a counter each minute Limited
    Ingestion pipeline Stream processing (Flink) before writing Much less write volume; but late events are hard, and raw data and flexibility are lost
    Query side Aggregate raw data at query time No data loss; slower queries over the whole dataset

    Query service

    • A cluster of query servers between the TSDB and the visualization/alert systems. It decouples them so either side can be swapped.
    • Add a cache layer for query results to cut TSDB load.
    • The case against it: most visualization and alert tools already have plugins for popular TSDBs, and a good TSDB needs no extra cache.
    • Query language: Prometheus and InfluxDB don't use SQL. An exponential moving average is hard to read in SQL but one line in Flux:
    from(db:"telegraf") |> range(start:-1h) |> filter(fn: (r) => r._measurement == "foo") |> exponentialMovingAverage(size:-10s)

    Storage layer

    • Pick the TSDB carefully: per a Facebook paper, at least 85% of queries hit data from the past 26 hours. A TSDB that exploits this performs much better.
    • Delta encoding and compression: 1610087371 and 1610087381 differ by 10 s, which needs 4 bits, not 32. Store a base and deltas: 1610087371, 10, 10, 9, 11.
    • Downsampling: convert old high-resolution data to lower resolution. Rules per metric, e.g. 7 days raw; 30 days at 1 minute; 1 year at 1 hour.
    • Example (10 s → 30 s, host-a cpu): values 10, 16, 20 at 19:00:00–19:00:20 → 19 at 19:00:00; values 30, 20, 30 at 19:00:30–19:00:50 → 25 at 19:00:30.
    • Cold storage: move rarely used data to much cheaper storage.

    Alert system

    Rule config files ─1─► Cache ◄─2─► Alert manager ◄─3─► Query service
                                        │ ▲
                                      5 │ └─4─► Alert store (Cassandra)
                                        ▼
                                      Kafka ─6─► Alert consumers ─7─► email / text / PagerDuty / HTTPS endpoints
    1. Alert rules live as config files (YAML) and are loaded into a cache. Example:
    - name: instance_down
  rules:
  # Alert for any instance that is unreachable for >5 minutes.
  - alert: instance_down
    expr: up == 0
    for: 5m
    labels:
      severity: page
    1. The alert manager reads rule configs from the cache.
    2. It queries the query service on a set interval. A threshold violation creates an alert event. It also: - Filters, merges, and dedupes (e.g. three disk_usage > 90% events on instance 1 → one alert). - Enforces access control on alert management. - Retries, checking alert state, so each notification goes out at least once.
    3. The alert store (a KV DB like Cassandra) keeps each alert's state: inactive, pending, firing, resolved.
    4. Eligible alerts go into Kafka.
    5. Alert consumers pull from Kafka.
    6. They send notifications to email, text, PagerDuty, or HTTP endpoints.

    Build vs buy: many off-the-shelf alert systems integrate tightly with popular TSDBs and channels. Building your own is hard to justify. For senior roles, be ready to defend the choice.

    Visualization

    Metrics and alerts dashboards over different time ranges. A good one is hard to build, so the case for buying is strong: Grafana integrates with many popular TSDBs.

    Wrap-up

    Topics covered: pull vs push collection, scaling with Kafka, choosing a TSDB, downsampling, and build vs buy for alerting and visualization.

    Final design:

    Metrics source ─► Metrics collector ─► Kafka ─► Consumers ─► Time-series DB ◄── Query service ◄── Visualization system
                                                                                 │    ▲
                                                                              Cache   └── Alert system ─► email / text / PagerDuty / HTTPS
    ✓ Key points
    • Pin the scope first: operational metrics only, no logs, no tracing. ~10M metrics, 1-year retention with rollups.
    • Metrics are time series with labels; the load is write-heavy and read-spiky, so use a TSDB with low-cardinality labels.
    • Compare pull vs push with the trade-off table. Pull uses service discovery plus a consistent hash ring of collectors; push uses agents plus an auto-scaled, load-balanced collector cluster.
    • Put Kafka between collectors and the TSDB, partitioned by metric name, so a DB outage loses nothing.
    • Cut storage with delta encoding, downsampling, and cold storage. Recent data (past 26 h) gets most queries.
    • Alerting: YAML rules → alert manager (dedupe/merge, state in a KV store) → Kafka → channel consumers. Prefer buying alerting and dashboards.
    ⚠ Common trap

    declaring pull or push the "right" answer. The book's point is that both are used widely; explain the trade-offs and note a big company likely needs both.

    V2·6 Ad Click Event Aggregation

    ad click aggregationreal-time biddingRTBstream processingMapReduceKafkaFlinkwatermarktumbling windowsliding windowexactly-oncelambda architecturekappa architecturereconciliationhotspotstar schematop N
    See also Kafka vs RabbitMQ

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 6.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design an ad click event aggregation system at Facebook or Google scale. Its results drive ad billing and real-time bidding (RTB), so they must be correct.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Input format? Log files on many servers. New click events are appended. Fields: ad_id, click_timestamp, user_id, ip, country
    Data volume? 1 billion clicks per day, 2 million ads. Clicks grow 30% per year
    Queries? (1) clicks for one ad in the last M minutes; (2) top 100 most clicked ads in the past 1 minute (both configurable, aggregate every minute); (3) filter both by ip, user_id or country
    Edge cases? Late events, duplicate events, any part may fail. Handle all of them
    Latency? A few minutes end to end. (RTB itself needs < 1 s, but aggregation is for billing and reporting)

    Requirements:

    • Functional: count clicks of an ad_id in the last M minutes; return the top 100 most clicked ads every minute; filter by attributes; Facebook/Google scale.
    • Non-functional: correct results (used for RTB and billing); handle late and duplicate events; resilient to partial failures; end-to-end latency of a few minutes at most.

    Estimates:

    • 1B DAU, 1 click each per day → 1B events/day.
    • QPS = 10^9 / 10^5 s = 10,000. Peak = 5× = 50,000 QPS.
    • 0.1 KB per event → 100 GB/day, about 3 TB/month.

    Try it first: sketch the path from log files to a dashboard, how you count per minute and get the top N, and how you avoid counting a click twice after a crash.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Query API (clients are dashboard users: data scientists, advertisers, PMs). Filtering is a query parameter, so two APIs cover all three use cases.

    API Params Response
    GET /v1/ads/{:ad_id}/aggregated_count from (start minute, default now − 1 min), to (end minute, default now), filter (e.g. 001 = drop non-US clicks) ad_id, count
    GET /v1/ads/popular_ads count (top N), window (M minutes), filter ad_ids (array)

    Data model:

    • Raw event: [AdClickEvent] ad001, 2021-01-01 00:00:01, user 1, 207.148.22.22, USA. Columns: ad_id, click_timestamp, user_id, ip, country.
    • Aggregated: ad_id | click_minute | count, e.g. ad001 | 202101010000 | 5.
    • With filters: ad_id | click_minute | filter_id | count. A separate filter table maps filter_id to criteria (region, IP, user_id), e.g. 0012 = region US.
    • Top N: most_clicked_ads(window_size int, update_time_minute timestamp, most_clicked_ads array of ad IDs in JSON).

    Raw vs aggregated data:

    Raw data only Aggregated data only
    Pros Full data set; supports filters and recalculation Smaller data set; fast query
    Cons Huge storage; slow query Data loss: it is derived (10 entries → 1)

    Store both. Raw data is the backup: use it for debugging and to recalculate after a bug. Move old raw data to cold storage. Aggregated data is the active data, tuned for queries.

    Database choice:

    • Raw data: write-heavy (10K–50K QPS), rarely read. Relational DBs struggle to scale writes. Cassandra or InfluxDB fit (write-optimized, time-range queries). Another option: S3 with columnar files (ORC, Parquet, AVRO), capped at ~10 GB per file. The book uses Cassandra.
    • Aggregated data: time series, read- and write-heavy. Dashboards query every ad every minute (2M ads). The service writes every minute. Same DB type works.

    Architecture. A synchronous chain breaks when producers outrun consumers (OOM, shutdowns) or when one part dies. So add Kafka to decouple stages and scale them independently.

    Log watcher ─► MQ #1 ─► Data aggregation service ─(ad count / min, top 100 / min)─► MQ #2
                 │                                                                   │
                 ▼                                                                   ▼
           DB writer ─► Raw data DB                                   DB writer ─► Aggregation DB
                                                                                     ▲
                                                                     Query service (dashboard)
    • MQ #1 holds raw click events: ad_id, click_timestamp, user_id, ip, country.
    • MQ #2 holds per-minute results: ad_id, click_minute, count and update_time_minute, most_clicked_ads.
    • Why MQ #2 instead of writing to the DB directly? It gives end-to-end exactly-once (atomic commit across MQ #1 → aggregation → MQ #2).

    Aggregation service = a DAG of Map / Aggregate / Reduce nodes (MapReduce, really map-reduce-reduce):

    • Map: reads, cleans, normalizes, and routes by ad_id (e.g. ad_id % 3). Why not let Kafka partition it? Input may need cleaning, and you may not control producers, so the same ad_id can land in different partitions.
    • Aggregate: counts clicks per ad_id in memory every minute.
    • Reduce: merges results from all Aggregate nodes.
    • Nodes talk over TCP (separate processes) or shared memory (threads).

    Use cases:

    1. Click count: map by ad_id, each Aggregate node counts its ads.
    2. Top N: each Aggregate node keeps a heap of its local top 3. Reduce merges 3 × 3 = 9 candidates into the global top 3 each minute.
    3. Filtering: pre-aggregate per dimension, e.g. ad001 | 202101010001 | USA | 100, GPB | 200, others | 3000. This is a star schema; filter fields are dimensions. Simple, reuses the same service, fast reads. Cost: many more buckets and records.

    Deep dives

    Streaming vs batching

    Services (online) Batch (offline) Streaming (near real-time)
    Responsiveness Respond fast No client response No client response
    Input User requests Bounded, large Unbounded streams
    Output Responses Materialized views, aggregates Materialized views, aggregates
    Measured by Availability, latency Throughput Throughput, latency
    Example Online shopping MapReduce Flink
    • Lambda: batch path + streaming path. Downside: two codebases.
    • Kappa: one streaming engine does both real-time and reprocessing. The design uses Kappa.
    • Data recalculation (replay): after a bug, (1) a recalculation service reads raw data in a batch job, (2) sends it to a dedicated aggregation service so live traffic is not affected, (3) writes results to MQ #2 → aggregation DB.

    Time: event time vs processing time

    Pros Cons
    Event time More accurate; the client knows when the click happened Client clocks can be wrong or forged
    Processing time Server clock is reliable Wrong if the event arrives much later (e.g. 5 hours)
    • Choice: event time, because accuracy matters.
    • Watermark: extend each window by e.g. 15 s (tunable) to catch slightly late events. Longer = more accurate but more latency.
    • Very late events are rare. Do not build complex logic for them; fix with end-of-day reconciliation.

    Aggregation window

    Four types (Kleppmann): tumbling, hopping, sliding, session.

    • Tumbling (fixed): equal, non-overlapping chunks. Fits "clicks per minute" (use case 1).
    • Sliding: a window slides over the stream, may overlap. Fits "top N in the last M minutes" (use case 2).

    Delivery guarantees and deduplication

    • At-least-once is normally fine, but here a few percent error = millions of dollars. Use exactly-once.
    • Duplicate sources: clients resending (malicious ones go to ad fraud / risk control), and server outages.
    • Outage case: Aggregator consumes offsets 100–110, sends results downstream, gets the ack, then dies before acking upstream with offset 110. A new node re-reads from 100 → duplicates.
    • Fix 1: store the offset in HDFS/S3 and check it before processing. If the offset is saved before sending downstream and the send fails, events 100–110 are lost.
    • Fix 2: save the offset after the downstream ack. Crash before saving → resend → duplicates again.
    • Final: put send result + save offset + ack in one distributed transaction. Any failure rolls back all.
    Upstream Kafka ─1 poll / 2 consume @100─► Aggregator ─3.1 verify offset─► HDFS/S3
                                          3 aggregate 100..110
                     ┌──── distributed transaction ─────────────────┐
                     │ 4 send result ─► Downstream Kafka             │
                     │ 5 save offset ─► HDFS/S3                      │
                     │ 6 ack back ◄─ Downstream                      │
                     └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Upstream ◄─7 ack with new offset 110─ Aggregator

    Scale the system

    Growth is 30%/year (2× every ~3 years). MQ, aggregation service and DB are decoupled, so scale each alone.

    • Kafka consumers: add consumers to the group; rebalance spreads partitions. With hundreds of consumers, rebalance can take minutes, so add them off-peak.
    • Kafka brokers:
    • Hash key = ad_id, so one ad's events go to one partition.
    • Pre-allocate enough partitions. Changing the count remaps ad_ids.
    • Shard topics by geography (topic_north_america, …) or business (topic_web_ads, topic_mobile_ads). Pro: more throughput, faster rebalances. Con: more complexity and maintenance.
    • Aggregation service: horizontal. Two ways to raise throughput: (1) different ad_ids on different threads (simpler); (2) run nodes on a resource provider like Hadoop YARN (multi-processing). Option 2 is more common because you just add compute.
    • Database: Cassandra scales horizontally with virtual nodes on a hash ring. A new node triggers automatic rebalancing. No manual resharding.
    • Hotspots: big advertisers get far more clicks. Example: a node handles 100 events but gets 300 for ad1. It asks the resource manager for more nodes, splits the events into 3 groups of 100, and the reduced result returns to the original node. More advanced: Global-Local Aggregation, Split Distinct Aggregation (Flink).

    Fault tolerance

    • Aggregation is in memory, so a crash loses state. Replaying Kafka from the start is slow.
    • Save a snapshot of system state: the upstream offset plus state like the top-N data (e.g. top 3 of the last 5 minutes with per-minute counts per ad).
    • Failover: start a new node, load the latest snapshot, replay events after the snapshot from Kafka.

    Monitoring and reconciliation

    • Monitor: latency per stage (track timestamps as events flow); Kafka records-lag (not "queue size"); CPU, disk, JVM on aggregation nodes.
    • Reconciliation: no third party to compare with. A batch job sorts each partition's events by event time at end of day and compares with the real-time result. Use a smaller window (e.g. 1 hour) for more accuracy. Small mismatches remain because of late events.

    Final design:

    Log watcher ─► MQ ─► Aggregation service ─► MQ ─► DB writer ─► Aggregation DB ◄─ Query service
               │                             ▲                      ▲               (dashboard)
               ▼                             │                      │
          DB writer               Aggregation service               │
               │                  (recalculation only)              │
               ▼                             ▲                      │
          Raw data DB ◄─── read ── Recalculation service            │
               ▲                                                    │
               └──────────────── Reconciliation ────────────────────┘

    Alternative design: Log watcher → MQ → risk control engine → Hive (+ ElasticSearch for data scientist queries) and ClickHouse (or Druid) OLAP for merchant-facing analytics. In a generalist interview a generic design with clear trade-offs is enough.

    Wrap-up

    Covered: data model and API; MapReduce aggregation; scaling MQ, aggregation service and DB; hotspots; monitoring; reconciliation; fault tolerance. Knowing Kafka, Flink or Spark makes this design easier.

    ✓ Key points
    • Two Kafka queues decouple ingestion, aggregation and storage, and enable exactly-once end to end.
    • Aggregate with Map → Aggregate → Reduce; use local heaps + a reducer for top N.
    • Keep raw data for replay and reconciliation; serve queries from aggregated data.
    • Event time + watermark; tumbling window for counts, sliding window for top N.
    • Partition by ad_id, pre-allocate partitions, handle hot ads with extra nodes.
    • Snapshots (offset + in-memory state) make failover fast.
    ⚠ Common trap

    settling for at-least-once delivery. Duplicates here are billing errors worth millions. Also, saving the offset before the downstream ack loses data.

    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.2 Case Studies › 4.2.2 Volume 2

    V2·7 Hotel Reservation System

    hotel reservationMarriottAirbnbbookingdouble bookingidempotency keyoverbookingroom type inventorypessimistic lockingoptimistic lockingdatabase constraintSELECT FOR UPDATErace conditionshardingRedis cacheCDC2PCsaga
    See also Transactions & Isolation Levels · Locking & Concurrency Control

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 7.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a hotel reservation system for a hotel chain like Marriott. The same ideas apply to Airbnb, flight booking and movie ticket booking.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Scale? Hotel chain website: 5,000 hotels, 1 million rooms
    When do customers pay? In full, when they reserve
    Booking channels? Hotel website or app only (no phone)
    Can customers cancel? Yes
    Anything else? Allow 10% overbooking (sell more rooms than exist, expecting cancellations)
    Room search? Out of scope
    Pricing? Dynamic. The price can differ each day, based on expected occupancy

    Requirements:

    • Functional: show hotel page; show room detail page; reserve a room; admin panel to add/remove/update hotel or room info; support overbooking.
    • Non-functional: high concurrency (many people booking the same popular room in peak season); moderate latency (a few seconds to process a reservation is fine).

    Estimates:

    • Daily reservations: 1M × 70% / 3 days ≈ 233,333 → ~240,000.
    • Reservations per second: 240,000 / 10^5 ≈ 3 TPS. Not high.
    • Funnel (10% move to the next step, no prefetching): view hotel/room detail 300 QPS → order confirmation page 30 QPS → reserve 3 QPS.

    Try it first: sketch the services, the tables (think: what does a guest actually reserve?), and how you stop two people from getting the last room.

    Solution

    High-level design

    API (RESTful; search APIs are out of scope):

    API Detail
    GET /v1/hotels/ID Hotel details
    POST / PUT / DELETE /v1/hotels[/ID] Add / update / delete a hotel (staff only)
    GET /v1/hotels/ID/rooms/ID Room details
    POST / PUT / DELETE /v1/hotels/ID/rooms[/ID] Add / update / delete a room (staff only)
    GET /v1/reservations Reservation history of the logged-in user
    GET /v1/reservations/ID Reservation details
    POST /v1/reservations Make a reservation
    DELETE /v1/reservations/ID Cancel a reservation

    POST /v1/reservations body: startDate, endDate, hotelID, roomID, reservationID. The reservationID is the idempotency key that prevents double booking.

    Database: relational.

    • Read-heavy, write-light: far more people browse than book. NoSQL is usually optimized for writes.
    • ACID matters: it prevents negative balance, double charges and double reservations, and keeps app code simple.
    • The data is clearly relational and stable (hotel, room, room_type, …).

    First schema (one service per box):

    • Hotel service: hotel(hotel_id PK, name, address, location), room(room_id PK, room_type_id, floor, number, hotel_id, name, is_available).
    • Rate service: room_type_rate(hotel_id PK, date PK, rate).
    • Reservation service: reservation(reservation_id PK, hotel_id, room_id, start_date, end_date, status, guest_id).
    • Guest service: guest(guest_id PK, first_name, last_name, email).
    • Reservation status: pending → paid → refunded, or pending → cancelled, or pending → rejected.

    Problem with this schema: it works for Airbnb, where the user picks a specific listing. Hotel guests reserve a room type (standard, king, two queens). The room number is assigned at check-in. Fixed in the deep dive.

    Architecture (microservices):

    User ─► CDN (static assets)                         │ Admin (hotel staff)
User ─► Public API gateway                          │   │
          ├─► Hotel service ──► Hotel cache + Hotel DB    ▼
          ├─► Rate service ───► Rate DB             │ Internal API (VPN)
          ├─► Reservation service ─► Reservation DB │   │
          └─► Payment service ───► Payment DB       │   ▼
                                                    │ Hotel management service
    • API gateway: managed; rate limiting, auth, routes by endpoint.
    • Hotel service: hotel and room info. Mostly static, so cache it.
    • Rate service: room prices for future dates (price depends on expected occupancy).
    • Reservation service: takes reservations and tracks room inventory on book/cancel. Calls the rate service to compute the total charge.
    • Payment service: charges the customer; sets status to paid on success or rejected on failure.
    • Hotel management service: staff only; view upcoming reservations, book for a customer, cancel. Forwards changes to the service that owns the data.
    • Services talk over an RPC framework like gRPC.

    Deep dives

    Improved data model

    • The reservation API uses roomTypeID instead of roomID, plus roomCount.
    • reservation now stores room_type_id instead of room_id.
    • New table in the reservation service:
    room_type_inventory
  hotel_id          ┐
  room_type_id      ├ composite primary key
  date              ┘
  total_inventory   -- total rooms minus rooms taken off for maintenance
  total_reserved    -- rooms booked for this hotel, room type and date
    • One row per date makes date-range bookings and queries easy.
    • Rows are pre-populated for 2 years. A daily job adds new dates.
    • Size: 5,000 hotels × 20 room types × 2 years × 365 days = 73M rows. One DB is enough; replicate across regions/AZs for availability.

    Check availability (input: start/end date, room type, hotel, number of rooms):

    SELECT date, total_inventory, total_reserved
FROM room_type_inventory
WHERE room_type_id = ${roomTypeId} AND hotel_id = ${hotelId}
  AND date BETWEEN ${startDate} AND ${endDate}
-- then, for every row:
--   total_reserved + ${numberOfRoomsToReserve} <= total_inventory
-- with 10% overbooking:
--   total_reserved + ${numberOfRoomsToReserve} <= 110% * total_inventory

    If reservation data outgrows one DB:

    • Keep only current and future reservations. Archive history, some to cold storage.
    • Shard by hotel_id (hash(hotel_id) % servers): both making and looking up a reservation start from a hotel.

    Concurrency 1: the same user clicks "book" twice

    • Client side: gray out / disable the button. Not reliable (JavaScript disabled, network retries).

    • Idempotency key (chosen): 1. User fills details → reservation service generates a reservation order. 2. It returns a review page with a unique reservation_id from a global ID generator. 3. 3a: submit with reservation_id. 3b: a second submit hits the unique constraint on the primary key and fails.

    • The key doesn't have to be reservation_id; it is used because it already exists.

    Concurrency 2: two users want the last room

    Race (isolation below serializable; 100 rooms, 99 reserved): T1 and T2 both check total_reserved + 1 <= 100 → both true. Both update total_reserved to 100 and commit. Two bookings for one room.

    Reserve-room pseudo-code (one transaction):

    # step 1: check inventory
SELECT date, total_inventory, total_reserved FROM room_type_inventory WHERE ... date range
if ((total_reserved + ${numberOfRoomsToReserve}) > 110% * total_inventory) { Rollback }
# step 2: reserve
UPDATE room_type_inventory SET total_reserved = total_reserved + ${numberOfRoomsToReserve}
WHERE room_type_id = ${roomTypeId} AND date BETWEEN ${startDate} AND ${endDate}
Commit

    Three fixes:

    Option How Pros Cons
    Pessimistic locking SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the rows; T2 waits for T1, then sees 100 and rolls back Easy; serializes updates; good under heavy contention Deadlocks with many locked resources; not scalable, long locks hurt DB performance
    Optimistic locking Add a version column. Read version, write version + 1. DB rejects the write if the version is not exactly current + 1; client retries No DB locks (app logic only); fast when conflicts are rare Poor under heavy contention: everyone reads the same version, one wins, the rest retry again and again → bad UX
    Database constraint CHECK (total_inventory - total_reserved >= 0); T2 makes it 101 → violates → rollback Easy; fine under low contention Many failures under contention ("rooms shown, then none"); constraints are hard to version-control; not all DBs support them (migration risk)
    • Version numbers beat timestamps for optimistic locking, because server clocks drift.
    • Book's choice: not pessimistic. Optimistic locking or the DB constraint are both good, because reservation QPS is low.

    Scalability (e.g. booking.com / expedia.com, 1,000× QPS)

    • Services are stateless → add servers. The database is the bottleneck.
    • Sharding by hotel_id: e.g. 16 shards; 30,000 QPS / 16 = 1,875 QPS per shard, fine for one MySQL server.
    • Inventory cache (Redis): only current and future inventory matters, so use TTL to expire old data and LRU eviction.
    • Key: hotelID_roomTypeID_{date} → value: number of available rooms.
    • Reservation service queries inventory in the cache, updates inventory in the DB. The DB then updates the cache asynchronously (from app code or via CDC, e.g. Debezium).
    • Most ineligible requests stop at the cache. Reads outnumber writes by an order of magnitude.
    • The cache can be stale. That is fine: the DB is the source of truth and re-validates every booking. Worst case, the user sees "someone just booked the last room."
    • Pros: much lower DB load; fast in-memory reads. Con: keeping cache and DB consistent is hard; think about its UX impact.
                  Reservation service
         query inventory │   │ update inventory
                         ▼   ▼
   Inventory cache (Redis) ◄── async update (app or CDC) ── Inventory DB (shard N)

    Data consistency among services

    • The design is hybrid: the reservation service owns both the reservation and inventory tables in one relational DB, so ACID handles the concurrency issues above.
    • A microservice purist wants one DB per service. Then one logical operation spans services and DBs; no single transaction. If the reservation DB update fails, the inventory DB change must be rolled back. One happy path, many failure paths.
    • Options:
    • Two-phase commit (2PC): atomic commit across nodes. Blocking: one node failure stalls everyone. Not performant.
    • Saga: a chain of local transactions, each publishing a message to trigger the next. On failure, run compensating transactions. Eventually consistent.
    • Book's choice: not worth the complexity here. Keep reservation and inventory in the same relational DB.

    Wrap-up

    Covered: requirements and estimates; API, first data model, architecture; switching to room-type-level reservations; race conditions and three fixes (pessimistic, optimistic, constraint); scaling with sharding and a Redis cache; data consistency across microservices (2PC, Saga).

    ✓ Key points
    • Guests reserve a room type. Model inventory as room_type_inventory, one row per (hotel, room type, date).
    • Load is tiny (~3 TPS) but bursty and contended. Pick a relational DB for ACID.
    • reservation_id as an idempotency key stops double submits.
    • Low contention → optimistic locking or a CHECK constraint; avoid pessimistic locks (deadlocks, poor scaling).
    • Overbooking is just 110% * total_inventory in the check.
    • At booking.com scale: shard by hotel_id, cache inventory in Redis, but always re-check in the DB.
    ⚠ Common trap

    modeling reservations per specific room_id (the Airbnb model). Hotels sell room types, and room numbers are assigned at check-in. Another trap: trusting the cache count without re-validating in the DB.
