    V2·8 Distributed Email Service

    email serviceGmailOutlookSMTPIMAPPOPMX recordwebmailWebSocketattachment storeS3metadata databaseBigtabledenormalizationread unreadconversation threadsdeliverabilitySPF DKIM DMARCElasticsearchLSM tree
    See also SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 8.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a large-scale email service like Gmail, Outlook or Yahoo Mail.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    How many users? 1 billion
    Features? Send and receive email; fetch all emails; filter by read/unread; search by subject, sender, body; anti-spam and anti-virus. Authentication is out of scope
    How do clients connect? Traditionally SMTP, POP, IMAP and vendor protocols. Here, assume HTTP
    Attachments? Yes

    Requirements:

    • Functional: the feature list above.
    • Non-functional:
    • Reliability: never lose email data.
    • Availability: replicate email and user data across nodes; keep working through partial failures.
    • Scalability: performance must not drop as users and emails grow.
    • Flexibility and extensibility: easy to add features. POP/IMAP are too limited, so custom protocols may be needed.

    Estimates:

    • Send QPS: 10^9 users × 10 emails / 10^5 s = 100,000.
    • Received: 40 emails/user/day. Metadata (everything except attachments) = 50 KB.
    • Metadata per year: 1B × 40 × 365 × 50 KB = 730 PB.
    • 20% of emails have an attachment, avg 500 KB. Attachments per year: 1B × 40 × 365 × 20% × 500 KB = 1,460 PB.
    • So: a distributed database is needed.

    Try it first: sketch the send flow and the receive flow (with queues and spam checks), then the metadata tables for "folders", "emails in a folder" and "unread emails".

    Solution

    High-level design

    Email 101:

    • SMTP: sends mail between servers.
    • POP: downloads mail to one device and deletes it from the server. Downloads the whole email, even big attachments.
    • IMAP: keeps mail on the server, downloads a message only when opened (headers first). Works on many devices. Most used for personal accounts.
    • HTTPS: not a mail protocol, but used by webmail (e.g. Outlook's ActiveSync for mobile).
    • DNS MX records: find the recipient's mail server. Lower priority number = preferred (e.g. gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com priority 5, then alt1… priority 10).
    • Attachments: Base64-encoded, sent with MIME. Limits: Outlook 20 MB, Gmail 25 MB (June 2021).

    Traditional mail servers (Alice on Outlook → Bob on Gmail):

    1. Outlook client → Outlook mail server (SMTP).
    2. Outlook server looks up Gmail's SMTP server via DNS and sends the email (SMTP).
    3. Gmail server stores it.
    4. Bob's client fetches it via IMAP/POP.
    • Storage was Maildir: one file per email in per-user directories. Fine for few users. At billions of emails, disk I/O becomes the bottleneck, backups are hard, and a dead disk loses data.
    • Old protocols were not built for threading, search, labels or billions of users.

    Webmail API (HTTP):

    Endpoint Purpose
    POST /v1/messages Send to recipients in To, Cc, Bcc
    GET /v1/folders All folders: [{id, name, user_id}]. Defaults (RFC 6154): All, Archive, Drafts, Flagged, Junk, Sent, Trash
    GET /v1/folders/{folder_id}/messages Messages in a folder. Real version needs consecutive paging (1–50, 51–100) and range paging (73–87)
    GET /v1/messages/{message_id} One message: user_id, from {name, email}, to [{name, email}], subject, body, is_read

    Distributed architecture:

                        Webmail
          https │            │ WebSocket
                ▼            ▼
          Web servers    Real-time servers
                └─────┬──────┘
                      ▼
   Storage layer: Metadata DB | Attachment store | Distributed cache | Search store
    • Web servers: all API requests (send, load folders, load emails) plus login, signup, profile.
    • Real-time servers: push new mail. Stateful (persistent connections). WebSocket, with long polling as fallback for old browsers. Example: Apache James uses JMAP over WebSocket.
    • Metadata DB: subject, body, from, to, … (chosen in the deep dive).
    • Attachment store: S3. Attachments up to 25 MB. Not Cassandra: its blob limit is 2 GB in theory but < 1 MB in practice, and big blobs prevent using the row cache.
    • Distributed cache: Redis. Recent emails are loaded again and again. Redis has lists and scales easily.
    • Search store: distributed document store with an inverted index for full-text search.

    Sending flow:

    Webmail ─1 HTTPS─► LB ─2─► Web servers ─4a─► Outgoing queue ─5─► SMTP outgoing ─7─► Internet
                               │      └─4b─► Error queue        (check spam, virus, retry)
                               3 (same domain: store directly)        │ 6 store in "Sent"
                               ▼                                      ▼
          Storage: metadata DB | search store | object store (attachments) | cache (latest email)
    1. User sends → load balancer.
    2. LB applies the rate limit and routes to web servers.
    3. Web servers do basic validation (e.g. size limit). If the recipient is on the same domain, store directly in DB, cache and object store; done.
    4. Valid → outgoing queue; invalid → error queue.
    5. SMTP outgoing workers pull, check spam and viruses.
    6. Store the email in the Sent folder.
    7. Send to the recipient's mail server.
    • The queue decouples web servers from SMTP workers, so workers scale alone. Each message holds all metadata to build the email.
    • Monitor the outgoing queue size. Stuck mail means: the recipient server is down (retry with exponential backoff) or too few consumers (add more).

    Receiving flow:

    Mail ─1─► SMTP LB ─2─► SMTP servers (acceptance policy) ─4─► Incoming queue ─5─► Mail processing ─7─► Real-time servers ─8 WebSocket─► Webmail
                           │ 3 big attachment → S3                          │ (spam, virus)                                  ▲
                           ▼                                                ▼ 6                                               │ 9 HTTPS
                        Storage layer ◄──────────────────────────────────────────────── 10 ── Web servers ◄─────────────────┘
    • 1–2: LB spreads mail across SMTP servers. An acceptance policy at SMTP-connection level bounces invalid mail early.
    • 3: attachments too big for the queue go to S3.
    • 4: the incoming queue decouples SMTP servers from processing workers and buffers surges.
    • 5: workers filter spam and viruses.
    • 6: store in mail storage, cache and object store.
    • 7–8: recipient online → push via real-time (WebSocket) servers.
    • 9–10: recipient offline → mail waits in storage. When back, the client calls web servers (REST), which pull new mail.

    Deep dives

    Metadata database

    Characteristics:

    • Headers: small, read often. Bodies: any size, read rarely (usually once).
    • Operations are per user: a user only touches their own mail.
    • Recency matters: 82% of reads are for data younger than 16 days.
    • No data loss allowed.

    Options:

    Option Verdict
    Relational (MySQL, PostgreSQL) Indexes make simple search fast, but emails are big (100 KB+ with HTML). Search over BLOBs is slow. Not a good fit
    Distributed object storage (S3) Good for backup. Hard to support mark-as-read, keyword search, threading
    NoSQL Gmail uses Bigtable (not open source). Cassandra could work, but no big provider is known to use it

    Big providers build custom DBs to cut IOPS. In an interview, describe the needed properties instead:

    • A single column can be single-digit MB.
    • Strong consistency.
    • Designed to reduce disk I/O.
    • Highly available and fault-tolerant.
    • Easy incremental backups.

    Data model

    • Partition key = user_id: one user's data sits on one shard (messages are not shared between users, which is fine here). Partition key spreads data; clustering key sorts inside a partition.
    folders_by_user:   user_id UUID (K), folder_id UUID, folder_name TEXT
emails_by_folder:  user_id UUID (K), folder_id UUID (K), email_id TIMEUUID (C↓),
                   from TEXT, subject TEXT, preview TEXT, is_read BOOLEAN
emails_by_user:    user_id UUID (K), email_id TIMEUUID (C↓), from TEXT, to LIST<TEXT>,
                   subject TEXT, body TEXT, attachments LIST<filename|size>
attachments:       email_id TIMEUUID, filename TEXT, url TEXT
read_emails / unread_emails: user_id (K), folder_id (K), email_id TIMEUUID (C↓), from, subject, preview
    • Q1 folders for a user: folders_by_user, partition user_id.
    • Q2 emails in a folder: composite partition <user_id, folder_id>. email_id is a TIMEUUID clustering key, so emails sort newest first.
    • Q3 get an email: SELECT * FROM emails_by_user WHERE email_id = 123; Attachments are fetched by email_id + filename.
    • Q4 read/unread: WHERE … AND is_read = true is fine in SQL, but NoSQL only queries partition and clustering keys, so it rejects this. Fetching the whole folder and filtering in the app does not scale. Fix: denormalize into read_emails and unread_emails. Mark as read = delete from unread_emails + insert into read_emails. Query: SELECT * FROM unread_emails WHERE user_id = ? AND folder_id = ? ORDER BY email_id; More complex code, much faster reads.
    • Bonus, threads: headers carry Message-Id (set by the sending client), In-Reply-To (parent's Message-Id) and References (IDs in the thread). With the reply chain preloaded, the client rebuilds the thread (e.g. JWZ algorithm).

    Consistency trade-off: correctness matters, so each mailbox has a single primary. During failover the mailbox is unavailable and sync pauses. Consistency over availability.

    Email deliverability

    Sending is easy; landing in the inbox is hard. Over 50% of all email is spam, and a new server has no reputation.

    • Dedicated IPs for sending; providers distrust new IPs with no history.
    • Classify emails: send marketing and important mail from different IPs, or ISPs may mark everything promotional.
    • Warm up new IPs slowly with Gmail, Office365, Yahoo: about 2–6 weeks (Amazon SES).
    • Ban spammers quickly before they hurt reputation.
    • Retries: after max retries, park the event in a queue and monitor it.
    • Feedback loops with ISPs: route to separate queues for hard bounces (invalid address), soft bounces (temporary, e.g. ISP busy) and complaints ("report spam").
    • Email authentication against phishing (93% of breaches, Verizon 2018): SPF, DKIM, DMARC.

    Search

    Email search reindexes on every send, receive and delete, but runs only when the user clicks search. So it is write-heavy.

    Scope Sorting Accuracy
    Google search Whole internet Relevance Indexing takes time; new items can lag
    Email search User's own mailbox Time, has attachment, date, unread, … Near real-time and accurate
    • Option 1: Elasticsearch. Partition documents by user_id. Search is sync (user waits). Send/receive/delete events go async through Kafka → consumers → reindex. Challenge: keep the primary store and ES in sync.
    • Option 2: custom search in the datastore. Main bottleneck is disk I/O (PB/day of new data; accounts with 500K+ emails). Use an LSM tree: writes go to an in-memory level 0, then merge down; only sequential writes. Also separate data that changes often (folders, filter rules) from data that doesn't (email bodies).
    Feature Elasticsearch Custom search engine
    Scalability Scalable to some extent Easier; tuned for email
    System complexity Two systems: datastore + ES One system
    Data consistency Two copies; hard to keep in sync Single copy in the metadata store
    Data loss possible No; rebuild index from primary storage No
    Development effort Easy to integrate; large scale may need a dedicated ES team Significant engineering effort
    • Rule of thumb: small scale → Elasticsearch. Gmail/Outlook scale → native search embedded in the DB.

    Scalability and availability

    • Users' access patterns are independent, so most components scale horizontally.
    • Replicate data across multiple data centers. Users talk to the nearest one. During a network partition, they reach their mail through another data center.

    Wrap-up

    Extra talking points:

    • Fault tolerance: node failures, network issues, event delays.
    • Compliance: store EU PII per GDPR; lawful intercept.
    • Security: phishing protection, safe browsing, proactive alerts, account safety, confidential mode, encryption.
    • Optimization: a group email stores the same attachment many times in S3. Check if it already exists before the expensive save.
    ✓ Key points
    • Storage dominates: ~2.2 EB/year (730 PB metadata + 1,460 PB attachments). Attachments go to S3, not the metadata DB.
    • Queues on both send and receive paths decouple web/SMTP servers from workers and absorb spikes.
    • Real-time servers push new mail over WebSocket; offline users pull via REST.
    • Partition metadata by user_id, sort by TIMEUUID, and denormalize for read/unread.
    • Single primary per mailbox → consistency over availability.
    • Deliverability and search (Elasticsearch vs native, LSM for writes) are the hard parts at scale.
    ⚠ Common trap

    treating email as "just SMTP + a database." The hard parts are storage scale, keeping mail out of spam (reputation, warm-up, SPF/DKIM/DMARC), and write-heavy search indexing.

    V2·9 S3-like Object Storage

    S3object storageblob storagebucketmetadata storedata storeplacement servicereplicationerasure codingchecksumdurabilitymultipart uploadversioninggarbage collectioncompactionsharding
    See also SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases · Indexes

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 9.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design an object storage service like Amazon S3: users create buckets and store objects of any size through a RESTful API.

    Background: three kinds of storage

    Block storage File storage Object storage
    Mutable content Yes Yes No (versioning yes, in-place update no)
    Cost High Medium to high Low
    Performance Medium to very high Medium to high Low to medium
    Consistency Strong Strong Strong
    Data access SAS / iSCSI / FC CIFS/SMB, NFS RESTful API
    Scalability Medium High Vast
    Good for VMs, databases General file access Binary, unstructured data

    Object storage trades performance for durability, scale and low cost. Data lives as objects in a flat structure (no directories).

    Terms: bucket = logical container, globally unique name. Object = data (payload) + metadata (name-value pairs). Versioning = keep many variants of an object, enabled per bucket. Each resource has a URI.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Features? Create bucket; upload/download objects; object versioning; list objects in a bucket (like aws s3 ls)
    Data size? Both huge objects (GBs) and many small ones (tens of KB)
    Data per year? 100 PB
    Durability / availability? 6 nines (99.9999%) / 4 nines (99.99%)

    Requirements:

    • Functional: the four features above.
    • Non-functional: 100 PB; 6 nines durability; 4 nines availability; storage efficiency (lower cost, still reliable and fast).

    Estimates: bottleneck is disk capacity or disk IOPS.

    • Object mix: 20% small (< 1 MB, median 0.5 MB), 60% medium (1–64 MB, median 32 MB), 20% large (> 64 MB, median 200 MB).
    • One SATA 7200 rpm disk: 100–150 IOPS.
    • At 40% storage usage: (10^11 MB × 0.4) / (0.2×0.5 + 0.6×32 + 0.2×200) ≈ 0.68 billion objects.
    • Metadata ~1 KB per object → ~0.68 TB of metadata.

    Try it first: sketch the upload and download paths, and decide where object names live versus where the bytes live.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Properties that shape the design: immutable objects (replace whole, no incremental change); a key-value store (URI → data); write once, read many (LinkedIn: 95% reads); both small and large objects.

    Like a UNIX file system: the inode holds metadata and block pointers; data sits elsewhere on disk. Here, the metadata store plays the inode, and the data store plays the disk. The metadata store finds data by object ID over the network. Separation lets each part be built and tuned on its own: data is immutable, metadata is mutable.

    APIs:

    PUT /bucket-to-share/script.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: foo.s3example.org
Authorization: authorization string
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Length: 4567
x-amz-meta-author: Alex

[4567 bytes of object data]

GET /bucket-to-share/script.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: foo.s3example.org
Authorization: authorization string

                        Client
                      │
                 Load balancer
                      │
 IAM ◄─────────── API service ─────────────► Data store
(authn/authz)         │                       Primary data node ──► Secondary
                      ▼                              └─────────────► Secondary
              Metadata service
                      │
                 Metadata DB
    • API service: stateless; calls IAM, metadata store and data store. IAM: authentication + authorization.
    • Data store: stores and fetches bytes by object ID (UUID) only. Metadata store: object metadata.
    • Both stores are logical; Ceph RGW, for example, keeps everything as Rados objects.

    Upload (7 steps):

    1. PUT create bucket bucket-to-share → API service.
    2. IAM checks WRITE permission.
    3. Metadata store creates the bucket entry → success.
    4. PUT object script.txt.
    5. IAM checks WRITE on the bucket.
    6. API service sends the payload to the data store; it stores it and returns a UUID.
    7. Metadata store inserts a row: object_name=script.txt, object_id=<UUID>, bucket_id=<UUID>.

    Download: no real folders, but names like bucket-to-share/script.txt imply a hierarchy. GET /bucket-to-share/script.txt → IAM checks READ → metadata store maps name → UUID → data store returns bytes by UUID → API service returns them.

    Deep dives

    Data store

    API service ◄─► Data routing service ◄─► Placement service ◄─heartbeat─► Data nodes
                       │                                                    │
                       └──────── data traffic ──────► Primary ──replicate──► 2 secondaries
    • Data routing service: stateless (REST/gRPC). Asks placement for the best node, reads and writes data nodes.
    • Placement service: picks primary + replicas. Keeps a virtual cluster map (root → datacenter → host → partition) so replicas are physically apart. Node is "down" after a 15 s missed heartbeat. Critical, so run 5 or 7 nodes with Paxos/Raft; 7 nodes survive 3 failures.
    • Data node: a daemon sends heartbeats (number of disks, data per disk). On first heartbeat, placement assigns an ID and returns the cluster map and where to replicate.

    Persistence flow: API → routing service generates the UUID → placement returns the replication group (deterministic lookup, e.g. consistent hashing) → primary saves and replicates to 2 secondaries → UUID returned.

    Consistency vs latency (when is a write "done"):

    Ack after Consistency Latency
    All 3 nodes Best Highest (wait for slowest)
    Primary + 1 secondary Medium Medium
    Primary only Worst Lowest

    The last two are eventual consistency. The book's flow waits for all secondaries (strong).

    How data is organized

    One file per object breaks with many small files:

    • Wasted blocks: a disk block is ~4 KB; a tiny file still takes a full block.
    • Inode exhaustion: inode count is fixed at format time; the OS handles huge inode counts badly.

    Fix: append small objects into one big read-write file, like a WAL. At a threshold (a few GBs) it becomes read-only and a new read-write file starts. Writes to one file must be serialized, which kills throughput on many cores, so use one read-write file per core.

    Object lookup: object_mapping(object_id, file_name, start_offset, object_size).

    • RocksDB (SSTable): fast writes, slower reads. RDBMS (B+ tree): fast reads, slower writes. Access is write once, read many → relational.
    • Mapping is local to each node, so no shared cluster: run SQLite on each data node.

    Updated write: append "object 4" to /data/c → insert into object_mapping → return UUID.

    Durability

    • Replication: disk annual failure rate ~0.81%. 3 copies → 1 − 0.0081³ ≈ 0.999999 (rough).
    • Failure domains: node, rack (shared switch/power), row/room, availability zone. Spreading replicas across AZs does not raise durability on paper but survives outages, cooling failures and disasters.

    Erasure coding: split data into chunks, compute parities, rebuild lost chunks from survivors.

    • (4+2) example: d1..d4 + p1, p2; lose d3, d4 → rebuild from d1, d2, p1, p2.
    • (8+4): 12 equal pieces in 12 failure domains; survives 4 lost nodes. Reads need at least 8 healthy nodes.
    • Space: 1 GB → 3 GB with 3× replication (200% overhead) vs 1.5 GB with EC (50%).
    Replication Erasure coding
    Durability 6 nines (3 copies) 11 nines (8+4) — EC wins
    Storage overhead 200% 50% — EC wins
    Compute None — replication wins Parity math
    Write Copy to nodes — replication wins Slower: compute parities first
    Read One replica; unaffected by failure — replication wins Reads from many nodes; slower in failure (rebuild)

    Replication suits latency-sensitive systems; EC minimizes cost but complicates the data node. This design focuses on replication.

    Correctness (checksums): in-memory corruption is common at scale. Compare checksums across process boundaries; mismatch = corrupted. Choice: MD5. Append a checksum after each object, and a whole-file checksum before a file turns read-only. On read with (8+4) EC: fetch data + checksum, recompute; on mismatch read from another failure domain; repeat until 8 good pieces, then rebuild.

    Metadata data model

    Queries: (1) object ID by name, (2) insert/delete by name, (3) list objects in a bucket by prefix.

    bucket: bucket_name, bucket_id, owner_id, enable_versioning
object: bucket_name, object_name, object_version, object_id
    • bucket table: 1M customers × 10 buckets × 1 KB = 10 GB. Fits one server; add read replicas for load.
    • object table: too big; shard it.
    Shard key Problem
    bucket_id Hot shards; a bucket can hold billions of objects
    object_id Even load, but queries 1 and 2 are by URI
    hash(bucket_name, object_name) Chosen: most operations are by URI. Listing gets harder

    Listing objects in a bucket

    Path s3://mybucket/abc/d/e/f/file.txt → bucket mybucket, object name abc/d/e/f/file.txt, prefix abc/d/e/f/. Prefixes look like folders but are not.

    Three uses: aws s3 list-buckets; aws s3 ls s3://mybucket/abc/ (deeper names roll up, e.g. CA/ NY/ federal.txt); --recursive (no rollup).

    Single DB:

    SELECT * FROM bucket WHERE owner_id = {id};
SELECT * FROM object WHERE bucket_id = "123" AND object_name LIKE 'a/b/%'
  ORDER BY object_name OFFSET 0 LIMIT 10;

    Rollup is done in app code. Paging: the server returns a cursor with the offset encoded; next page uses OFFSET 10.

    Sharded DB: query every shard and merge. Paging is hard: each shard returns a different count, so the server must track one offset per shard in the cursor (hundreds of shards → hundreds of offsets).

    Choice: listing speed is rarely a priority (all commercial stores are sub-optimal here). Denormalize listing data into a separate table sharded by bucket ID. One DB per listing query; fine even for billions of objects.

    Object versioning

    • Without versioning: the new metadata replaces the old; the old object is marked deleted and the GC reclaims it.
    • With versioning (enabled on the bucket): a PUT inserts a new row with the same bucket_id + object_name, a new object_id, and object_version = TIMEUUID. Current version = largest TIMEUUID.
    • Delete: keep all versions and insert a delete marker as the newest version. GET then returns 404.

    Optimizing uploads of large files (multipart)

    1. Client ─initiate─► Data store       2. ◄─ uploadID
3. Client ─part i + uploadID─►          4. ◄─ ETag i (MD5 of the part)
5. Client ─complete(uploadID, part numbers, ETags)─►
6. Data store reassembles by part number (may take minutes) ─► success

    Example: 1.6 GB file → 8 parts × 200 MB. A failed part is retried alone. Old parts become garbage after reassembly.

    Garbage collection

    Garbage sources: lazy deletion (marked, not removed), orphan data (half or abandoned multipart uploads), corrupted data (failed checksum). It is cleaned later by periodic compaction, on all replicas (or all 12 nodes for (8+4) EC).

    • Compaction: copy live objects from /data/b to /data/d, skipping ones with the delete flag. Then update file_name and start_offset in object_mapping in one transaction (obj_id, object_size stay).
    • Wait for many read-only files and merge them into a few large ones, to avoid many small files.

    Wrap-up

    The book compares block, file and object storage, then covers upload, download, listing and versioning. Object storage = data store + metadata store. Deep dives: data persistence, replication vs erasure coding, multipart upload, schema design, and sharding the metadata store.

    ✓ Key points
    • Separate metadata (name → UUID, mutable) from data (UUID → bytes, immutable).
    • Placement service with a cluster map + Paxos/Raft; primary replicates to secondaries across failure domains.
    • Pack small objects into large append-only files; per-node SQLite for UUID → (file, offset, size).
    • Replication (fast, 200% overhead) vs (8+4) erasure coding (11 nines, 50% overhead, slower). Checksums catch corruption.
    • Shard object metadata by hash(bucket, name); use a bucket-sharded listing table for prefix listing.
    • Versioning via TIMEUUID rows + delete markers; multipart upload; compaction-based GC.
    ⚠ Common trap

    storing each object as its own file on the data node. Many small objects waste disk blocks and run out of inodes. Also: sharding metadata by bucket, which creates hot shards.

    V2·10 Real-time Gaming Leaderboard

    leaderboardrankingRedissorted setZINCRBYZREVRANGEZREVRANKskip listtop KshardingRedis clusterhash slotscatter-gatherDynamoDBwrite shardingpercentileAWS Lambda
    See also SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases · Big-O Cheat Sheet

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 10.

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design a real-time leaderboard for an online mobile game. It shows the top players and where the current user ranks.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    How is score calculated? +1 point per match won; each user has a total score
    All players included? Yes
    Time segment? A new tournament and new leaderboard each month
    Only top 10? Top 10 + a user's rank. Bonus: 4 players above and below a user
    Users? 5M DAU, 25M MAU
    Matches? 10 per player per day on average
    Ties? Same score = same rank. Tie-breaking is a bonus topic
    Real-time? Yes, or as close as possible. No batched results

    Requirements:

    • Functional: top 10 players; a user's rank; 4 places above and below a user (bonus).
    • Non-functional: real-time score updates reflected on the leaderboard; scalable, available, reliable.

    Estimates:

    • Users: 5M / 10^5 s ≈ 50 users/s. Peak 5× → 250 users/s.
    • Score QPS: 50 × 10 = ~500. Peak 5× → 2,500.
    • Top-10 fetch QPS: one game open per user per day → ~50.

    Try it first: pick the data structure that makes "add 1 point" and "what is my rank" both fast with 25M players, and sketch who is allowed to update scores.

    Solution

    High-level design

    APIs:

    API Purpose
    POST /v1/scores Update score after a win. Params: user_id, points. Internal: only game servers call it. 200 OK / 400 Bad Request
    GET /v1/scores Top 10 players
    GET /v1/scores/{:user_id} Rank of one user 
    GET /v1/scores →
{ [ { "user_id": "user_id1", "user_name": "alice", "rank": 1, "score": 976 },
    { "user_id": "user_id2", "user_name": "bob",   "rank": 2, "score": 965 }, ... ],
  "total": 10 }

GET /v1/scores/user5 →
{ "user_info": { "user_id": "user5", "score": 1000, "rank": 6 } }

                   Player (mobile client)
          ① win a game │        │ ④ a. get leaderboard
                       ▼        ▼    b. get player_rank
              Game service ─② update score─► Leaderboard service
                                                   │ ③ update score
                                                   ▼
                                           Leaderboard store
    • Game service validates the win, then calls the leaderboard service.
    • The client reads the leaderboard directly from the leaderboard service.
    • Client must not set the score. A man-in-the-middle proxy could change it. In server-authoritative games (e.g. online poker) the game server sets it without the client.
    • Message queue? Only if other consumers need the scores (analytics, push notifications, turn-based/multiplayer updates). Then: game service → Kafka → leaderboard / analytics / push services. Not required here, so no queue.

    Data model option 1: relational database

    Table per month: leaderboard(user_id varchar, score int).

    INSERT INTO leaderboard (user_id, score) VALUES ('mary1934', 1);
UPDATE leaderboard SET score = score + 1 WHERE user_id = 'mary1934';

SELECT (@rownum := @rownum + 1) AS rank, user_id, score
FROM leaderboard ORDER BY score DESC;          -- add LIMIT 10 for top 10

    Why it fails at scale:

    • Rank needs every player sorted; duplicate scores mean rank is not just row position.
    • Ranking over millions of rows takes 10s of seconds. Data changes constantly, so caching does not help.
    • Batch ranking works but breaks the real-time requirement.
    • Index + LIMIT 10 helps top 10, but a user's rank still needs a table scan; no easy answer for users far from the top.
    • Rank for one user needs a nested query: SELECT *, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leaderboard lb2 WHERE lb2.score >= lb1.score) RANK FROM leaderboard lb1 WHERE lb1.user_id = {:user_id};

    Data model option 2: Redis sorted sets (chosen)

    A sorted set: unique members, each with a score; ordered by score. Built from a hash table (user → score) and a skip list (score → users).

    Skip list: a sorted linked list (O(n) search) plus index levels, each skipping every other node of the level below. Search jumps like binary search. Example with 5 index levels: 11 nodes visited instead of 62. Insert, update and find are O(log n), and elements stay in order on every write.

    Command Use Cost
    ZADD Insert user or set score O(log n)
    ZINCRBY Add to score (starts at 0 if new) O(log n)
    ZRANGE / ZREVRANGE Range by rank, asc / desc O(log n + m)
    ZRANK / ZREVRANK Position of a user, asc / desc O(log n)

    Workflow (one sorted set per month; old months move to historical storage):

    ZINCRBY  leaderboard_feb_2021 1 'mary1934'        # user wins a match
ZREVRANGE leaderboard_feb_2021 0 9 WITHSCORES     # top 10 with scores
ZREVRANK leaderboard_feb_2021 'mary1934'          # user's rank
ZREVRANGE leaderboard_feb_2021 357 365            # Mallow007 at rank 361: 4 above, 4 below

    Storage: worst case all 25M MAU have an entry. 24-char id + 2-byte score = 26 B → ~650 MB. Double it for skip list + hash overhead; one Redis server is enough. 2,500 updates/s is easy for one node.

    Persistence: Redis can persist, but restarting a big instance from disk is slow. Use a read replica; promote it on failure and attach a new replica.

    MySQL alongside Redis: user (id, display name) and point (user_id, score, timestamp of each win). Used for play history and to rebuild Redis after a failure. Optionally cache user details for the top 10.

    Deep dives

    Cloud or own services

    Own services:

    Client ─► Load balancer ─► Web servers ─┬─► Redis: leaderboard sorted set
                                        ├─► MySQL: user profile + user points
                                        └─► Redis: user profile cache (top 10)

    The API servers read the sorted set, then fetch names and profile images from MySQL (or the top-10 cache).

    On AWS: API Gateway maps REST endpoints to Lambda functions.

    API Lambda
    GET /v1/scores LeaderboardFetchTop10
    GET /v1/scores/{:user_id} LeaderboardFetchPlayerRank
    POST /v1/scores LeaderboardUpdateScore

    (The book's table swaps the two GET rows; the mapping above follows the function names.)

    • Score a point: leaderboard service → API Gateway → Lambda → ZINCRBY in Redis + insert into MySQL point table.
    • Get leaderboard: API Gateway → Lambda → ① ZREVRANGE in Redis → ② user details from MySQL.

    Choice: serverless if building from scratch. Lambda auto-scales; no servers to set up or maintain.

    Scaling Redis

    At 500M DAU (100×): 65 GB and 250,000 QPS. Needs sharding.

    Fixed partition (by score range): e.g. scores 1–1000 in 10 shards: [1,100], [101,200], …, [901,1000]. Each shard is a sorted set; sharding is done in app code.

    • Ranges must give an even spread; adjust them if not.
    • To find a user's shard: read the score from MySQL, or better, a secondary cache user_id → score. When a score crosses a range, remove the user from the old shard and update the cache.
    • Top 10: read the top of the highest shard ([901, 1000]).
    • User rank = local rank in the shard + count of players in all higher shards. A shard's size comes from info keyspace in O(1).

    Hash partition (Redis cluster): good if scores are clumped. 16,384 hash slots; slot = CRC16(key) % 16384. Not consistent hashing, but nodes can still be added or removed without moving all keys. Example: node 1 = [0, 5500], node 2 = [5501, 11000], node 3 = [11001, 16383].

    • Update: just the user's shard.
    • Top 10: scatter-gather — top 10 from every shard (in parallel), app merges and sorts.
    • Limits: large top-K is slow (many entries to sort); many partitions → wait for the slowest; no simple way to get a user's rank.

    Choice: fixed partition.

    Sizing a node: write-heavy apps need extra memory for snapshots during failure; allocate 2× memory. Benchmark with redis-benchmark.

    Alternative: NoSQL (DynamoDB)

    Want: optimized for writes, and efficient sorting by score inside a partition. DynamoDB, Cassandra or MongoDB fit. Design: leaderboard service → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB (replaces Redis + MySQL).

    1. Denormalized table (user_id PK; score, email, profile_pic, leaderboard_name like chess#2020-02). Works, but top scores need a full scan.
    2. Global secondary index: partition key game_name#{year-month}, sort key score. Works, but the current month is one hot partition (DynamoDB places items by consistent hashing on the partition key).
    3. Write sharding: partition key game_name#{year-month}#p{user_id % N}, sort key score. Each partition is locally sorted. Top 10 = scatter-gather over N partitions.

    Trade-off: more partitions = less load each but more read fan-out. Pick N by write volume or DAU, and benchmark.

    Exact rank is still hard. Offer a percentile instead ("top 10–20%" beats "rank 1,200,001"). Assume shards share a score distribution; a cron job computes and caches cut-offs, e.g. 10th percentile = score < 100, 20th = < 500, …, 90th = < 6500.

    Wrap-up

    • MySQL rejected: does not scale to millions of users in real time. Redis sorted sets chosen; sharded for 500M DAU; DynamoDB as an alternative.
    • Faster retrieval: a Redis hash of user_id → user object avoids DB lookups for display.
    • Break ties: also store user_id → timestamp of the latest win; on equal score, the older timestamp ranks higher.
    • Failure recovery: replay the MySQL point table (one row per win, with timestamp) and call ZINCRBY per entry to rebuild the leaderboard offline.
    ✓ Key points
    • One Redis sorted set per month; ZINCRBY / ZREVRANGE / ZREVRANK are all O(log n).
    • Skip list + hash table is why rank queries are fast; SQL must sort the whole table.
    • ~650 MB and 2,500 QPS fit one Redis node plus a replica; MySQL keeps the durable win log.
    • Only the game service updates scores; add Kafka only if other consumers need them.
    • At 100× scale, range-partition by score so top 10 and rank stay cheap; hash slots need scatter-gather and lose rank.
    ⚠ Common trap

    ranking with ORDER BY in SQL and hoping a cache fixes it. Scores change constantly, so the cache is always stale. Also: letting the client post its own score.

    V2·11 Payment System

    payment systempay-inpay-outPSPStripehosted payment pageidempotency keyexactly-oncereconciliationsettlement filedouble-entry ledgerretry queuedead letter queuewebhookPCI DSS
    See also Transactions & Isolation Levels · Kafka vs RabbitMQ

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 11. · Your write-up: Wallet and Ledger

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design the payment backend for an e-commerce site like Amazon. It handles everything related to money movement when a customer places an order.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    What kind of payment system? A payment backend for an e-commerce app like Amazon.com
    Payment options? All in real life. Use credit cards as the example
    Do we process cards ourselves? No. Use third-party processors (Stripe, Braintree, Square)
    Do we store card data? No. Security and compliance rules are too strict. The PSP holds it
    Global? Many currencies? Global, but assume one currency
    How many transactions? 1 million per day
    Pay sellers too (pay-out)? Yes
    Anything else? Many internal and external services can drift apart. Reconciliation is required

    Requirements:

    • Functional: pay-in (receive money from customers on behalf of sellers) and pay-out (send money to sellers around the world).
    • Non-functional: reliability and fault tolerance (handle failed payments carefully). An async reconciliation process between internal services (payment, accounting) and external ones (PSPs).

    Estimates: 1,000,000 tx / 10^5 s = 10 TPS. Any database handles that. The focus is correct handling of each payment, not throughput.

    Try it first: sketch the services between "place order" and the card network, and the tables you would keep. Then explain how you stop a double charge when the user clicks "pay" twice or the PSP response is lost.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Money flow: Buyer credit card ─pay-in─► e-commerce bank account ─pay-out─► seller bank account. The site is only a custodian of the seller's money, for a fee. Pay-out happens later, e.g. when the product is delivered.

    Pay-in flow (Figure 2):

    user ─(1) payment event─► Payment Service ─(3) payment order─► Payment Executor ─(5)─► PSP ─► Card schemes
                             │(2) DB            │(4) DB          (internal │ external)  (PayPal,    (Visa,
                         (8) │   (6)                                                  Stripe,     MasterCard)
                             ▼    ▼                                                   Adyen)
                          Ledger  Wallet
                           │(9)    │(7)
                           DB      DB
    1. "Place order" creates a payment event. The payment service stores it (after a risk check for AML/CFT, usually by a third party).
    2. One event can hold several payment orders (one per seller). The service calls the payment executor for each.
    3. The executor stores the order and calls the PSP to charge the card.
    4. On success, the service updates the wallet (seller balance), then the ledger (append-only financial record).

    APIs:

    POST /v1/payments        execute a payment event
  buyer_info        json
  checkout_id       string   globally unique per checkout
  credit_card_info  json     encrypted card info or a PSP token
  payment_orders    list of { seller_account string, amount string,
                              currency string (ISO 4217), payment_order_id string }
GET  /v1/payments/{:id}  status of one payment order
    • payment_order_id is globally unique. The PSP uses it as the idempotency key.
    • amount is a string, not a double. Precision differs across protocols and hardware, which causes rounding errors. Numbers can be huge (Japan's GDP ≈ 5×10^14 yen) or tiny (1 satoshi = 10^-8). Parse only for display or math.

    Data model. Choose storage for proven stability (5+ years at big financial firms), tooling, and a mature DBA job market, not speed. So: a relational DB with ACID transactions over NoSQL/NewSQL.

    payment_event:  checkout_id string PK, buyer_info, seller_info, credit_card_info, is_payment_done bool
payment_order:  payment_order_id string PK, buyer_account, amount string, currency,
                checkout_id string FK, payment_order_status, ledger_updated bool, wallet_updated bool
    • payment_order_status: NOT_STARTED → EXECUTING → SUCCESS | FAILED.
    • On SUCCESS: update the wallet, set wallet_updated; then update the ledger, set ledger_updated. When all orders of a checkout succeed, set is_payment_done.
    • A scheduled job watches in-flight orders and alerts if one does not finish within a threshold.

    Double-entry ledger. Record every transaction in two accounts with the same amount: buyer debit $1, seller credit $1. The sum of all entries must be 0. One cent lost means someone else gained a cent. This gives end-to-end traceability.

    Hosted payment page. To avoid PCI DSS, the PSP's widget, iframe or SDK page collects the card. Card data never touches our system.

    Pay-out works like pay-in, but a third-party accounts-payable provider (e.g. Tipalti) moves money from the site's bank to the seller's.

    Deep dives

    PSP integration

    • Direct links to banks or card schemes are rare. Only very large companies justify them.
    • Option 1: PSP API. We build the payment pages and store card data ourselves.
    • Option 2: PSP hosted page. The PSP collects and stores card data. Most companies choose this.

    Hosted payment flow (Figure 4):

    Checkout page ─(1)─► Payment Service ─(2) register payment + nonce─► PSP
                     Payment Service ◄─(3) token────────────────────  PSP
                     (4) store token in DB
Browser shows PSP hosted page with token (5) ─(6) start payment─► PSP ─(7) result─► page
page ─(8) redirect to completion page (status in URL)
PSP ─(9) webhook with final status─► Payment Service → update payment_order_status
    • The nonce (usually the payment order ID) makes registration exactly-once. The token is the PSP's ID for that registration.
    • The hosted page needs the token (to look up the amount) and a redirect URL. The redirect URL is not the webhook URL.

    Reconciliation

    • Async messages may never arrive, and responses may be lost. Reconciliation periodically compares states between services. It is the last line of defense.
    • Each night the PSP or bank sends a settlement file (balance + the day's transactions). We parse it and compare with the ledger. We also compare ledger vs wallet internally.
    • Mismatches go to three buckets:
    Case Handling
    Classifiable, fix can be automated Program classifies and adjusts automatically
    Classifiable, automation too costly Job queue; finance team fixes manually
    Unclassifiable Special job queue; finance team investigates

    Handling payment processing delays

    • Some payments take hours or days: high-risk manual review, or 3D Secure needing more card-holder details.
    • The PSP returns pending. The client shows it and offers a status page.
    • The PSP tracks it and notifies us by webhook (or we poll it). Then we update and ship.
    • Three parties are involved, so every call must be idempotent, and reconciliation keeps them eventually consistent.

    Communication among internal services

    Synchronous (HTTP) Asynchronous
    Performance One slow service slows the whole chain Decoupled
    Failure isolation PSP down → client gets no response Queue buffers it
    Coupling Sender must know the receiver Loose
    Scaling No buffer for spikes Queue absorbs spikes
    • Single receiver: a shared message queue. One consumer processes a message, then it is removed.
    • Multiple receivers: Kafka. Messages stay, so the payment, analytics and billing services all read the same payment event.
    • Choice: async. It trades design simplicity and consistency for scalability and resilience. That fits a large system with many third-party dependencies.

    Handling failed payments

    • Track payment state in an append-only table. After a failure, the state tells you whether to retry or refund.
    • Retry queue + dead letter queue (Figure 10):
    failure ─► retryable? ─no─► DB (e.g. invalid input)
              │yes
              ▼
         retry queue ─► payment system ─► fails again ─► retries left? ─yes─► retry queue
                                                              │no
                                                              ▼
                                                      dead letter queue (inspect)

    Exactly-once delivery

    Double charging is among the worst bugs. Exactly-once = at-least-once + at-most-once.

    Retry (at-least-once). Strategies: immediate, fixed interval, incremental interval, exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s…), or cancel. Use exponential backoff when the issue will not clear soon. Too aggressive a retry wastes resources and overloads services. Return an error code with a Retry-After header.

    Idempotency (at-most-once). The client sends a UUID in the header idempotency-key: <value> (Stripe and PayPal do this). It expires after a while.

    • Scenario 1: user clicks "pay" twice. The key is the shopping cart ID right before checkout. The second request is seen as a retry, and we return the latest status of the first. Concurrent requests with the same key: process one, return 429 Too Many Requests to the rest.
    • Implementation: use the key as the table's primary key. Insert succeeds → new request. Insert fails on a duplicate key → seen before, do not process.
    • Scenario 2: PSP charged the card, but the response was lost, and the user clicks again. The nonce maps to the payment order, and the token maps to the nonce. The retry carries the same token. The PSP uses the token as its idempotency key and returns the earlier result.

    Consistency

    • Stateful parts: payment service (nonce, token, order, status), ledger, wallet, PSP, and DB replicas.
    • Between internal services: exactly-once processing.
    • Internal vs PSP: idempotency (reuse the same key on retry) plus reconciliation, because the external system is not always right.
    • Replica lag: (1) read and write from the primary only. Simple, but replicas waste resources. Or (2) keep replicas in sync with Paxos/Raft, or use a consensus DB like YugabyteDB or CockroachDB.

    Payment security

    Problem Solution
    Eavesdropping HTTPS
    Data tampering Encryption and integrity monitoring
    Man-in-the-middle SSL with certificate pinning
    Storing passwords Salted hashing
    Data loss Replicate across regions, take snapshots
    DDoS Rate limiting and a firewall
    Card theft Tokenization: store and use tokens, not real card numbers
    PCI compliance Follow PCI DSS
    Fraud Address verification, CVV, user behavior analysis

    Wrap-up

    • Covered: pay-in, pay-out, retry, idempotency, consistency, error handling, security.
    • More to discuss: monitoring (e.g. acceptance rate per payment method), alerting, debugging tools for "why did this payment fail?", currency exchange, regional payment methods, cash payments (India, Brazil), and Google/Apple Pay integration.
    ✓ Key points
    • Say early that 10 TPS is tiny. The hard part is correctness under failure.
    • Split a checkout into a payment event and per-seller payment orders, each with a status enum.
    • Use a hosted payment page so card data never touches you (avoids PCI DSS scope).
    • Exactly-once = retry with backoff + idempotency key (DB unique key; payment_order_id/token at the PSP).
    • Prefer async messaging (Kafka) with a retry queue and a DLQ.
    • Reconcile against the PSP settlement file every night, and between ledger and wallet.
    ⚠ Common trap

    assuming a retry is safe, or that the PSP is always right. Without an idempotency key a retry can double charge. Without reconciliation, lost webhooks and silent mismatches are never found.

    Chapter 4 · System Design › 4.2 Case Studies › 4.2.2 Volume 2

    V2·12 Digital Wallet

    digital walletbalance transferdistributed transactiontwo-phase commit2PCTC/Ctry-confirm-cancelsagacompensating transactionevent sourcingCQRSreproducibilityRaftsnapshotRocksDBmmap
    See also Transactions & Isolation Levels · Locking & Concurrency Control

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 12. · Your write-up: Wallet and Ledger

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design the backend of a digital wallet (like PayPal) that supports balance transfers between two wallets on the same platform.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Which features? Balance transfer between two wallets only
    Throughput? 1,000,000 TPS
    Are transactional guarantees enough for correctness? Yes
    Must we prove correctness? Reconciliation only shows that a difference exists, not how it happened. We want reproducibility: rebuild any historical balance by replaying data from the start
    Availability? 99.99%
    Foreign exchange? Out of scope

    Requirements:

    • Functional: transfer balance between two wallets.
    • Non-functional: 1M TPS, 99.99% reliability, transactional guarantees, reproducibility.

    Estimates: a relational DB node does a few thousand TPS; assume 1,000. Each transfer is two operations (debit and credit), so we need 2M TPS → 2,000 nodes. Higher per-node TPS means fewer nodes and lower cost:

    Per-node TPS Nodes
    100 20,000
    1,000 2,000
    10,000 200

    Try it first: start with sharded balances and show where a transfer between two shards breaks. Then pick a way to make it atomic, and a way to answer an auditor's "what was A's balance last Tuesday, and prove it".

    Solution

    High-level design

    API:

    POST /v1/wallet/balance_transfer
  from_account    string   debit account
  to_account      string   credit account
  amount          string   (string, not double: see the payment chapter)
  currency        string   ISO 4217
  transaction_id  uuid     for deduplication
→ { "Status": "success", "Transaction_id": "01589980-2664-11ec-9621-0242ac130002" }

    The book discusses three designs, each fixing the previous one's flaw.

    1. In-memory sharding (Redis)

    Wallet service (stateless) ──► Redis 1 (A)   Redis 2 (B)   Redis 3 (C)
   │  partition = accountID.hashCode() % partitionNumber
   └─ Zookeeper: partition count + Redis node addresses
    • The wallet service receives the command, validates it, and updates two balances, usually on two Redis nodes.
    • Flaw: no atomicity. If the service crashes after "A −$1" but before "C +$1", the transfer is incomplete. Also, data is not durable.

    2. Distributed transactions on sharded relational DBs

    Replace each Redis node with a transactional DB. Each local update is now safe, but the two updates still live on two databases. We need a distributed transaction.

    Two-phase commit (2PC), low-level (in the DB):

    1. The coordinator (wallet service) reads and writes on both DBs. Both rows are locked.
    2. Phase 1: the coordinator asks every DB to prepare.
    3. Phase 2: all say yes → commit. Any says no → abort.
    • Needs special DB support (X/Open XA).
    • Slow: locks are held while waiting for other nodes. The coordinator is a single point of failure; if it crashes, the DBs wait.

    Try-Confirm/Cancel (TC/C), high-level (in the app). A compensating transaction. Each phase is its own local transaction. Transfer $1 from A to C:

    Phase Operation Account A Account C
    1 Try −$1 do nothing (NOP)
    2 Confirm do nothing +$1
    2 Cancel +$1 (undo) do nothing
    First phase Second phase: success Second phase: fail
    2PC Local transactions not done yet (locked) Commit all Abort all
    TC/C Local transactions done (unlocked) Run new local transactions if needed Reverse the committed effect ("undo")
    • Pro: database-agnostic; any DB with transactions works. Con: the app owns all the complexity.
    • Phase status table: survives a wallet-service restart. It stores the tx ID and content, the Try status per DB (not sent / sent / response received), the second phase name (Confirm or Cancel), its status, and an out-of-order flag. Keep it in the DB of the account being debited.
    • Unbalanced state: after Try, A lost $1 and C has not gained it, so the sum is short by $1. That is fine. The app sees intermediate state that a DB-level transaction would hide.
    • Valid order: only deduct first works. Add-first (NOP on A, +$1 on C) can fail: someone may spend the $1 from C before Cancel takes it back. Doing both at once creates messy partial failures.
    • Out-of-order execution: C's DB may get Cancel before Try (network delay). Allow Cancel without Try: it leaves a flag. Try checks the flag and fails if it is set.

    Saga. The de facto standard in microservices.

    Start ─► A−$1 ─► C+$1 ─► success
          │error   │error
          ▼        ▼
         A+$1     C−$1 ─► A+$1 ─► error
    • Operations run in linear order, each a local transaction. On failure, run compensations in reverse order. So n operations need 2n definitions.
    • Choreography: services react to each other's events. Fully decentralized, but each service needs its own state machine. Hard with many services.
    • Orchestration: one coordinator drives the order. Preferred for a wallet.
    TC/C Saga
    Compensating action In Cancel phase In rollback phase
    Central coordination Yes Yes (orchestration)
    Execution order Any Linear
    Parallel execution Yes No
    Partial inconsistent state visible Yes Yes
    Logic lives in Application Application
    • Choice: few services and no latency need → either; go with Saga to follow the microservice trend. Latency-sensitive with many operations → TC/C.
    • Remaining flaw: no audit trail. If a user enters a wrong operation, we cannot trace the root cause, and old balances are overwritten.

    3. Event sourcing

    Auditors ask: what was the balance at any time? Are past and current balances correct? Is the logic still correct after a code change? Event sourcing (from DDD) answers all three.

    • Command: an intended action from outside ("transfer $1 A→C"). It may be invalid. Commands go in a FIFO queue (e.g. Kafka).
    • Event: a validated fact, in past tense ("transferred $1"). It must be applied. One command makes zero or more events. Event generation may use randomness or I/O, but applying an event must be deterministic.
    • State: the balances, a map account → balance (KV store or relational DB).
    • State machine: validates commands into events and applies events to state. It must have no randomness.
    Command queue: [A−$1→C] [A−$1→B] [A−$1→D]
   (1) read command → (2) read state (A's balance) → (3) validate → events
Event queue:   [A:−$1][C:+$1] [A:−$1][B:+$1] [A:−$1][D:+$1]
   (4) read event → (5) update state
    • Reproducibility: the event list is immutable and the logic is deterministic, so replaying from the start always gives the same states. Answers: replay up to a time; recompute balances from events; rerun events with the new code and compare.
    • CQRS: do not publish state. Publish the events. One write state machine, many read-only state machines that build their own views: a balance DB for queries, or a per-hour view to investigate double charges. Read side is eventually consistent.
    Client ─► Write path: command queue → state machine → event queue → state
              │ publish events
              ▼
          Read path: rebuild state → historical state ◄── query service ◄── client

    Deep dives

    High-performance event sourcing

    • File-based command and event lists on local disk instead of remote Kafka. No network hop. Append-only means sequential writes, which are fast even on HDDs; sequential disk can beat random memory access.
    • Cache recent commands and events in memory. Use mmap: the file is mapped to memory, the OS caches it, and appends almost always stay in memory.
    • File-based state: a local store instead of a networked DB. SQLite or RocksDB; the book picks RocksDB because its LSM tree is write-optimized, with recent data cached for reads.
    • Snapshots: periodically save the state to a file, so replay starts from the last snapshot, not the beginning. Finance often wants one at 00:00 each day. Snapshots are large binaries; store them in object storage like HDFS.
    memory: Command list ─► state machine ─► Event list ─replicate─► read-only state machine ◄─ query
             ▲ mmap        │ RocksDB cache    ▲ mmap                     ▲ load snapshot
disk:   command file    RocksDB file ─take snapshot─► object store (daily snapshots)
                                         event file

    Reliable high-performance event sourcing

    Local files make the node stateful and a single point of failure.

    • Computation can rerun anywhere. Only data needs protection.
    • State and snapshots can be rebuilt from events. Commands cannot rebuild events, because event generation may be non-deterministic. So only the event list needs strong reliability.
    • Replicate it with consensus (Raft): no data loss and the same order on every node. Works while a majority is up: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2.
    • Roles: one leader, the rest followers (and candidates during elections). The leader accepts commands, makes events, and Raft replicates them. Every node applies events, so all states match.
    • Leader crash: Raft elects a new leader. If the crash happened before the command became an event, the client sees a timeout or error and resends to the new leader.
    • Follower crash: Raft retries until it is restarted or replaced.

    Distributed event sourcing

    Two limits remain: CQRS clients do not know when their transfer finished, and one Raft group has limited capacity.

    Pull vs push:

    • Pull: the client polls the read side. Not real-time, and frequent polling can overload the service.
    • Reverse proxy + pull: the proxy forwards commands and polls for the client. Simpler client, still not real-time.
    • Reverse proxy + push: the read-only state machine pushes status to the proxy as soon as it gets the event. Feels real-time. This makes the async framework look synchronous.

    Distributed transaction across partitions. Shard accounts (book example: hash % 2), one Raft group per partition, and reuse TC/C or Saga.

    user ◄──► TC/C or Saga coordinator ── Phase status table (DB)
              │ command            ▲ response (pushed)
              ▼                    │
   Partition 1 (A): reverse proxy → Raft leader [commands → events] ⇄ followers → read path
   Partition 2 (C): reverse proxy → Raft leader [commands → events] ⇄ followers → read path

    Saga happy path for A→C $1:

    1. User sends the tx (A−$1, C+$1) to the Saga coordinator. It writes a record in the phase status table.
    2. Deduct first: send A−$1 to partition 1. Its Raft leader stores the command, validates it, makes an event, replicates it with Raft, then applies it.
    3. CQRS syncs to partition 1's read path, which pushes the status back to the coordinator. The coordinator records success.
    4. Send C+$1 to partition 2. The same steps run. The coordinator records success.
    5. All steps succeeded. The coordinator replies to the caller.

    Wrap-up

    • About 2,000 nodes are needed at 1,000 TPS each, so per-node throughput matters.
    • Redis: not durable or atomic. Transactional DBs + 2PC, TC/C or Saga: atomic, but hard to audit.
    • Event sourcing with external Kafka and a DB: auditable but slow. Local files (mmap, RocksDB, snapshots): fast.
    • One node is a SPOF, so replicate the event list with Raft.
    • CQRS + a pushing reverse proxy make it feel synchronous. TC/C or Saga coordinates across Raft groups.
    ✓ Key points
    • Do the node math out loud: one transfer = two writes, so 2M ops/s.
    • Explain why a non-atomic cross-shard update loses money, then compare 2PC, TC/C and Saga with their trade-offs.
    • Always deduct before you add, and handle Cancel-before-Try with a flag.
    • Use event sourcing for reproducibility and audits: an immutable event log plus a deterministic state machine.
    • Only the event log needs consensus replication. State and snapshots can be rebuilt.
    ⚠ Common trap

    saying "use a DB transaction" for a transfer between shards. A local transaction cannot span two databases. Another trap: replicating commands instead of events. Event generation may be non-deterministic, so only events give reproducibility.

    V2·13 Stock Exchange

    stock exchangematching engineorder booklimit ordersequencerorder managermarket datacandlestickFIXevent sourcingmmapCPU pinningapplication loophot-warmRaftp99 latencymulticast
    See also Concurrency Models (GIL, Threads, Processes, asyncio) · Big-O Cheat Sheet

    Source: System Design Interview Vol 2, Ch 13. · Your write-up: Order Book and Matching Engine

    ↑ top

    Problem

    Design an electronic stock exchange that matches buyers and sellers. Clients place and cancel orders, receive matched trades in real time, and view the live order book.

    Clarifying questions → answers:

    Question Answer
    Which securities? Stocks only
    Which operations and order types? Place and cancel. Limit orders only
    After-hours trading? No, normal hours only
    Scale? Tens of thousands of concurrent users, at least 100 symbols, billions of orders per day
    Risk checks? Simple ones, e.g. max 1M shares of Apple per user per day
    Wallet? Yes. Check funds when an order is placed, and withhold funds while the order waits in the book

    Requirements:

    • Functional: place and cancel limit orders; real-time fills; real-time order book; risk checks; fund checks.
    • Non-functional: availability ≥ 99.99% (seconds of downtime hurt reputation); fault tolerance with fast recovery; millisecond round-trip latency, focus on p99; security (KYC before opening an account, DDoS protection for public market data). Small-to-medium scale, but it must be extensible.

    Estimates: 100 symbols, 1B orders/day. NYSE is open 9:30–16:00, 6.5 hours. QPS = 1B / 6.5 / 3600 ≈ 43,000. Peak = 5 × QPS ≈ 215,000 (volume spikes at open and close).

    Try it first: draw the order's path from the broker to the matching engine and back. Then design the order book so place, match and cancel are O(1), and explain how a crashed matching engine recovers with exactly the same state.

    Solution

    High-level design

    Business basics: retail clients trade through brokers (Schwab, Robinhood). Institutional clients need order splitting or very low latency. A limit order has a fixed price and may fill partly or not at all. A market order has no price and fills at once. Market data: L1 = best bid/ask and quantities; L2 = more price levels; L3 = price levels plus the queued quantity at each level. Candlestick = open, close, high, low per interval (1 min to 1 month). FIX = a vendor-neutral protocol for securities transactions (1991).

    client ─1─► Broker ─2─► Client gateway ─3─► Order manager ─7─► Sequencer ─8─► Matching engine
       ◄14─        ◄13─                ◄12─  │ (6) Wallet     ◄11─          ◄10─  (9) Order book
                                             │ 4/5 ⇄ Aggregated risk check           │ M1
                                             │ R1                                    ▼
                                          Reporter ─R2─► DB (orders, executions)   Market data publisher
Broker ◄─M3── Data service ◄─M2 (candlesticks, order books)─────────────────────────┘
    • Trading flow (critical path, steps 1–14). The gateway validates, rate-limits, authenticates and normalizes. The order manager runs risk checks and the wallet check. The sequencer stamps the order. The matching engine matches it and emits two executions (fills), one for each side. Fills flow back the same way.
    • Market data flow (M1–M3). The publisher builds candlesticks and order books from the fill stream and sends them to the data service. Brokers read from it.
    • Reporting flow (R1–R2). The reporter merges fields from orders and executions (client_id, price, quantity, filled/remaining) and writes them to a DB.
    • Only the trading flow has strict latency needs.

    Matching engine (cross engine): keeps an order book per symbol, matches buy and sell orders, and publishes the fill stream. It must be deterministic: the same input sequence must give the same fill sequence on replay. That is the base of high availability.

    Sequencer: an inbound one stamps every order and an outbound one stamps every pair of fills. IDs are consecutive, so gaps are easy to spot. Reasons: timeliness and fairness, fast recovery and replay, and exactly-once. It is also a message queue and an event store, like two Kafka streams. Kafka would work if its latency were lower and more predictable.

    Order manager: sends orders to the risk check and the wallet check, then to the sequencer, with only the attributes the engine needs (smaller messages). It gets fills back and returns them to brokers. Managing order state transitions is its main complexity; event sourcing fits it well.

    Client gateway: auth, validation, rate limit, normalization, FIXT support. Keep it light because it sits on the critical path; push complex logic to the matching engine and risk check. Different gateways serve retail and institutions. Colocation: a broker's engine on rented servers in the exchange's data center; latency is about light travel time.

    APIs (broker ↔ gateway, REST; institutions may need a faster protocol):

    POST /v1/order                 symbol, side, price (long), orderType, quantity (long)
  → id, creationTime, filledQuantity, remainingQuantity, status (new/canceled/filled)
GET /execution?symbol=&orderId=&startTime=&endTime=
  → executions[]: id, orderId, symbol, side, price, orderType, quantity
GET /marketdata/orderBook/L2?symbol=&depth=          → bids[], asks[] (price, size)
GET /marketdata/candles?symbol=&resolution=&startTime=&endTime=
  → candles[]: open, close, high, low

    Data models:

    • Product: type, symbol, lot size, tick size, currencies. Static and highly cacheable.
    • Order (inbound) and execution/fill (outbound): an order has 0..n executions.
    • On the critical path, orders and executions are not stored in a DB. They live in memory and in the sequencer, and are archived after market close. The reporter writes them to a DB. The market data processor uses them to rebuild order books and candlesticks.
    • Market data goes to an in-memory columnar DB (e.g. KDB) for real-time analytics, then to a historical DB after the close.

    Deep dives

    Order book

    Needs: constant-time lookup of volume at a price; O(1) add, cancel and execute; fast update; best bid/ask query; iterate price levels.

    Example: a market buy for 2,700 Apple shares takes the whole best-ask queue at 100.10 (200 + 400 + 1100 + 100) and the first order at 100.11 (900). Best ask moves up to 100.11 and the spread widens.

    class PriceLevel { Price limitPrice; long totalVolume; List<Order> orders; }
class Book<Side>  { Side side; Map<Price, PriceLevel> limitMap; }
class OrderBook   { Book<Buy> buyBook; Book<Sell> sellBook;
                    PriceLevel bestBid; PriceLevel bestOffer;
                    Map<OrderID, Order> orderMap; }

    A plain list is not O(1) for removal. Use a doubly linked list for orders:

    • Place: append to the tail of the PriceLevel. O(1).
    • Match: remove from the head. O(1).
    • Cancel: find the order with orderMap, then unlink it. O(1).

    The market data processor uses the same structure to rebuild L1/L2/L3 from fills.

    Candlesticks: a new Candlestick is added to the chart's linked list each interval. Many symbols × intervals use a lot of memory. Fixes: pre-allocated ring buffers (fewer allocations) and keeping only recent sticks in memory, the rest on disk.

    Performance: latency

    • Latency = Σ execution time along the critical path. Reduce the number of tasks, or shorten each one (less network and disk, faster code). Even logging is off the critical path.
    • With separate servers, each network round trip is about 500 µs, so the hops add up to single-digit ms. The sequencer's disk writes add tens of ms. Total: tens of ms. Modern exchanges target tens of µs.
    • Put everything on one server:
    One server:  [Order manager: app loop]  [Matching engine: app loop]  [Market data publisher: app loop]
                          ▲                        ▲                         ▲
                          └────────────── mmap message bus ─────────────────┘
                          ▼               ▼                 ▼                ▼
                     Reporter         Logging     Aggregated risk check   Position keeper
    • Application loop: a while loop that polls for tasks. It is single-threaded and pinned to one CPU core. Gains: no context switches and no locks, so a low p99. Cost: harder code; no task may hog the loop.
    • mmap over a file in /dev/shm (memory-backed) gives shared memory with no disk access. A message on this bus takes under 1 µs.

    Event sourcing

    • Instead of storing current state (Order V1 New → V2 Filled), store an immutable log of events (seq 100 NewOrderEvent, seq 101 OrderFilledEvent). Replay to recover any state.
    FIX ─► Gateway (FIX → SBE) ─NewOrderEvent─► Event store (mmap) ─► Matching engine
                                            entry = [sequence | event type | SBE payload]
                                              │       (embedded order manager validates,
                                              │        updates state, sends to matching core)
                                              │  ◄── OrderFilledEvent
                                              ├─► Market data publisher
                                              └─► Reporter (embedded order manager)
    • The gateway converts FIX to FIX over SBE (Simple Binary Encoding) for fast, compact messages.
    • The order manager becomes a library embedded in each component. A central service would add latency for everyone. Event sourcing keeps each copy identical and replayable.
    • The sequencer becomes a single writer. It pulls events from each component's local ring buffer, stamps a sequence ID, and writes to the event store. Multiple sequencers would fight over the write lock. Keep backup sequencers for HA.
    • This looks like Kafka pub-sub. Without strict latency needs, Kafka could be used.

    High availability

    • 99.99% means 8.64 s of downtime per day, so recovery must be almost instant.
    • Stateless parts (gateway) scale horizontally. Stateful parts (order manager, matching engine) need replicated state.
    • Hot-warm matching engine: the warm one reads the same events but publishes nothing. On primary failure it takes over at once. A restarted warm engine recovers from the event store. Detect failure with monitoring and heartbeats from the engine.
    • Across servers or data centers, the whole server is hot or warm, and the event store is replicated, e.g. over reliable UDP (see Aeron).

    Fault tolerance

    • What if the warm instances die too? Replicate core data to data centers in several cities.
    • When to fail over: false alarms cause needless failovers, and the same bug can kill the backup too. Start with manual failover; automate after you gain operational confidence. Use chaos engineering.
    • Who takes over: Raft. In a 5-server cluster each server has its own mmap event store. The leader replicates events over RPC; quorum is N/2 + 1 = 3. Empty AppendEntries are heartbeats. A follower that times out becomes a candidate and sends RequestVote; a majority makes it leader. A split vote times out and restarts the election. Terms divide time.
    • RTO (allowed downtime): seconds, so failover must be automatic. Rank services by priority and define degraded modes.
    • RPO (allowed data loss): near zero. Raft keeps many consistent copies, so the new leader works immediately.

    Matching algorithm

    handleOrder(book, event):
  if event.sequenceId != nextSequence → ERROR(OUT_OF_ORDER)
  if !validateOrder(symbol, price, quantity) → ERROR(INVALID_ORDER)
  NEW    → handleNew: BUY matches sellBook, SELL matches buyBook
  CANCEL → if orderId not in orderMap → ERROR(CANNOT_CANCEL_ALREADY_MATCHED)
           else remove, set CANCELED
match(book, order):
  walk orders at limitMap[order.price] while leavesQuantity > 0:
    matched = min(...); update matchedQuantity; remove; generateMatchedFill()
    • This is FIFO: the first order at a price level fills first. Other algorithms exist, e.g. FIFO with LMM (a Lead Market Maker gets a negotiated share ahead of the queue), mostly in futures. Dark pools also use matching algorithms.

    Determinism

    • Functional determinism: the sequencer and event sourcing give the same results on replay. Only event order matters, not wall-clock time, so replay can squeeze out idle gaps and run fast.
    • Latency determinism: almost the same latency for every trade. Measure p99 or p99.99 (e.g. with HdrHistogram). Investigate spikes; in Java, safe points (Stop-the-World GC, deoptimization, stack dumps) pause all threads.

    Market data publisher

    • Detailed L2/L3 data is valuable; hedge funds record it themselves. Tiers: retail sees 5 levels of L2 by default and pays for 10.
    • Candlesticks for 1 min, 1 hour and 1 day each live in a ring buffer holding the recent 100 ticks, then go to persistence and the data service.
    • Ring buffer: fixed size, pre-allocated, no object creation, lock-free. Padding keeps the sequence number alone in its cache line.

    Fairness, multicast, colocation

    • Lower latency is like seeing the future. If the first subscriber always gets data first, clients race to connect first. Fixes: multicast over reliable UDP (one source to a group of hosts, all at about the same time), or a random subscriber order.
    • Unicast = one to one; broadcast = one to a whole subnet; multicast = one to a group across subnets. UDP can drop datagrams, so add retransmission.
    • Colocation is a paid VIP service. It does not break fairness.

    Network security (DDoS)

    1. Isolate public services from private ones; serve read-only copies.
    2. Cache data that rarely changes.
    3. Harden URLs: /data/recent instead of /data?from=123&to=456, which attackers can vary endlessly; it also caches at the CDN.
    4. Safelists and blocklists at the network gateway.
    5. Rate limiting.

    Wrap-up

    • Some big exchanges really run everything on one huge server, or even one process.
    • Many crypto exchanges run on the cloud. Some DeFi projects use AMM (automatic market making) and need no order book.
    ✓ Key points
    • Do the QPS math, and note the open and close peaks (5×).
    • Separate the critical trading path from market data and reporting.
    • Sequencer + deterministic matching engine + event log = replay, recovery and exactly-once.
    • O(1) order book: price → doubly linked list of orders, plus an orderId index for cancels.
    • For µs latency: one server, an mmap bus, single-threaded loops pinned to cores, nothing extra on the path.
    • HA: hot-warm engine first, then Raft across servers; RPO ≈ 0, RTO in seconds.
    ⚠ Common trap

    a typical microservice design with Kafka and a DB on the critical path. Each network hop costs ~500 µs and disk costs ms, so p99 never reaches exchange levels. Another trap: a list-based price level, which makes cancel O(n).
