    Chapter 8 · Django

    Django Overview

    6 pages. Each card says what the page covers and its key lines; open the page for the full depth.

    Django Interview Questions

    quick-fire Django questions with short answers, grouped by topic. Each links to the deep page.

    • Count queries: lazy QuerySet, cache per object, FK in a loop = N+1, .filter() on a prefetched manager = new query.
    • update() / bulk_* skip save() and save-signals; on_commit for Celery; F() for counters.
    • select_related = JOIN (FK), prefetch_related = extra IN query (M2M / reverse FK).
    • DRF: scope in get_queryset(), object permissions don't run on list, cursor pagination for big lists.
    • Async ORM = thread wrapper; no atomic() in async code.
    Read the full page →

    Django ORM in Depth

    the ORM turns Python method chains into SQL. A QuerySet is a description of a query that runs only when you need the rows.

    • A QuerySet is lazy: it hits the DB only when evaluated (iterate, list(), len(), bool(), step-slice, repr). Its results are cached on that object.
    • select_related = SQL JOIN (FK / one-to-one, 1 query). prefetch_related = separate query + Python join (M2M / reverse FK, 1 + 1 per relation).
    • N+1 shows up in loops and serializers. Catch it with assertNumQueries / debug-toolbar.
    • F() = do the math in the DB (no lost update). Q() = OR / NOT / complex filters.
    • update(), bulk_create(), bulk_update() skip save() and pre/post_save signals.
    • get_or_create is only race-safe with a unique constraint in the DB.
    Read the full page →

    Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals

    how an HTTP request travels through Django, and the hooks (middleware, signals) you can plug into that path.

    • Flow: server (gunicorn/uvicorn) → WSGI/ASGI handler → middleware (top→down) → URL resolver → process_view → view → response → middleware (bottom→up).
    • Middleware is an onion: order in MIDDLEWARE matters (Session before Auth, Security first).
    • CBV: as_view() creates a new instance per request, dispatch() picks the method handler.
    • Signals are synchronous, run in the same transaction, and are not fired by update() / bulk_*.
    • Prefer explicit service functions over signals for business logic; use transaction.on_commit for side effects.
    Read the full page →

    Transactions & Migrations

    how Django manages DB transactions and row locks, and how schema changes (migrations) are created and deployed safely.

    • Default is autocommit: every query commits alone. atomic() groups them; nested atomic() = savepoint.
    • select_for_update() locks rows until the transaction ends; only works inside atomic(). skip_locked=True for job queues.
    • Start Celery tasks with transaction.on_commit(...), never directly inside a transaction.
    • Migrations: Django diffs models vs the state built from migration files, not the DB. django_migrations records what ran.
    • Zero-downtime = expand / contract: add nullable (or db_default), backfill, then constrain; rename/drop over several deploys; AddIndexConcurrently with atomic = False.
    Read the full page →

    Django REST Framework

    DRF is the standard toolkit for JSON APIs on Django: serializers (validation + conversion), views/viewsets, routers, and plug-in policies for auth, permissions, throttling, pagination, filtering and versioning.

    • Validation order: each field (to_internal_value + field validators) → validate_<field> → Meta/class validators → validate(attrs).
    • ModelSerializer does not write nested data; override create() / update().
    • SerializerMethodField that queries = N+1. Fix in get_queryset() with select_related / prefetch_related / annotate.
    • Authentication = who are you (sets request.user). Permission = are you allowed. has_object_permission runs only via get_object(), not on list.
    • Offset pagination = slow on deep pages + COUNT(*); cursor pagination = stable and fast, no page numbers.
    • Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key + unique constraint.
    Read the full page →

    Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async

    the things that decide whether a Django app survives real traffic: caching, DB connections, process model, static files, security settings, async limits, background jobs, observability and tests.

    • Cache layers: per-view (cache_page), template fragment ({% cache %}), low-level (cache.get_or_set). Hard part = invalidation (versioned keys, delete in on_commit).
    • CONN_MAX_AGE=0 (default) = new DB connection per request. Use CONN_MAX_AGE=60 + CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS, or pgbouncer / Django 5.1 "pool". Total connections = instances × workers × threads.
    • Security: DEBUG=False, ALLOWED_HOSTS, secrets from env, HTTPS settings, never f-strings in raw(), |safe only on trusted HTML. Run check --deploy.
    • Async ORM methods (aget, async for) still run the sync driver in a thread; atomic() doesn't work in async code → wrap in sync_to_async.
    • TestCase = rollback per test (fast, on_commit never fires); TransactionTestCase = real commits (slow, needed for locking / on_commit).
    Read the full page →

    Django Interview Questions

    Django interview questionsDjango quizhow many querieswhat's wrong with this codeORM questionsDRF questionsmiddleware questionstransaction questionsDjango security questionsDjango async questionsDjango deployment questions
    See also Django ORM in Depth · Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals · Transactions & Migrations · Django REST Framework · Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async

    What: quick-fire Django questions with short answers, grouped by topic. Each links to the deep page.

    ℹ Why it matters

    Iranian backend interviews (Digikala, Snapp, Divar, Cafe Bazaar, fintechs) usually start with fast "do you know X?" questions before going deep. Answer in 1–3 sentences, then offer detail.

    ↑ top

    ORM

    1. When does a QuerySet hit the database? Only when it's evaluated: iteration, list(), len(), bool(), step-slicing, repr(). Then the result is cached on that QuerySet object. count(), exists(), first() run their own queries. more

    2. select_related vs prefetch_related? select_related follows FK/one-to-one with a SQL JOIN (one query). prefetch_related runs a separate query per relation (WHERE id IN (...)) and joins in Python; use it for M2M and reverse FK. more

    3. How many queries?

    books = Book.objects.all()          # Book has FK author
for b in books:
    print(b.title, b.author.name)

    1 + N (one for books, one per book for its author). With .select_related("author") → 1.

    4. How many queries?

    authors = Author.objects.prefetch_related("books")
for a in authors:
    print(a.books.filter(published=True).count())

    1 + 1 + N. The prefetch runs (2 queries), but .filter() on the related manager ignores the prefetch cache and runs a new query per author. Fix: Prefetch("books", queryset=Book.objects.filter(published=True), to_attr="pub") then len(a.pub) → 2, or annotate(Count(...)) → 1.

    5. How many queries?

    qs = Order.objects.filter(status="paid")
if qs:
    total = len(qs)
    first = qs[0]
print(qs.count())

    1. if qs evaluates and caches all rows; len(), qs[0] and count() use the cache. Correct but wasteful if you only need a check: exists() loads no rows.

    6. What are F() and Q()? F("field") refers to a column inside SQL, so update(stock=F("stock") - 1) is atomic in the DB (no lost update). Q() builds OR/NOT/dynamic conditions: Q(a=1) | ~Q(b=2). more

    7. annotate vs aggregate? aggregate returns one dict for the whole queryset; annotate adds a computed value to each row (with GROUP BY). Two Counts over different joins multiply rows → use distinct=True or Subquery. more

    8. only() / defer() vs values()? only/defer still return model instances but skip columns; touching a skipped field = an extra query per object. values()/values_list() return dicts/tuples, no model overhead.

    9. Is get_or_create safe under concurrency? Only if there's a unique constraint on the lookup fields. It does SELECT → INSERT → on IntegrityError, SELECT again. Without the constraint, two requests can both insert duplicates. more

    10. How do you process 10 million rows? .iterator(chunk_size=...) (no cache, server-side cursor on Postgres), or loop over PK ranges in batches with update()/bulk_update() per batch in short transactions. Never list(Model.objects.all()). more

    ↑ top

    Models and signals

    11. Does QuerySet.update() call save() or send post_save? No. update(), bulk_create() and bulk_update() run SQL directly: no save(), no pre/post_save, no auto_now update. (qs.delete() does send pre/post_delete.) more

    12. Why can signals be dangerous? They hide side effects, run synchronously in the same transaction (before commit), slow down every save, and are skipped by bulk operations. Prefer explicit service functions for business logic. more

    13. What's wrong with this code?

    @receiver(post_save, sender=Order)
def notify(sender, instance, created, **kw):
    if created:
        send_invoice.delay(instance.id)

    If the order is created inside atomic(), the task can start before commit → DoesNotExist in the worker, or run after a rollback. Use transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_invoice.delay(instance.id)).

    ↑ top

    Request lifecycle and middleware

    14. Describe the request lifecycle. Web server (gunicorn/uvicorn) → WSGI/ASGI handler → middleware top-down → URL resolver → process_view → view → response → middleware bottom-up → request_finished (closes old DB connections). more

    15. Why does middleware order matter? Give an example. It's an onion: each layer sees what outer layers already did. AuthenticationMiddleware needs request.session, so it must come after SessionMiddleware; SecurityMiddleware goes first to redirect to HTTPS early.

    16. WSGI vs ASGI? WSGI is synchronous, one request per worker thread. ASGI is async and supports websockets and long-lived connections. Under ASGI, sync views run in a thread pool, so it only helps if your code is really async. more

    ↑ top

    Transactions

    17. What does nested atomic() do? The outer block is a transaction; each inner block is a savepoint. An exception leaving the inner block rolls back only to that savepoint. Catch it outside the inner atomic, never inside. more

    18. When do you use select_for_update? What are skip_locked and nowait? To lock rows you read and then change based on logic (balances, seats). Must be inside atomic(). skip_locked skips locked rows (job queues), nowait fails immediately instead of waiting. more

    19. What's wrong with this code?

    def withdraw(account_id, amount):
    acc = Account.objects.get(pk=account_id)
    if acc.balance >= amount:
        acc.balance -= amount
        acc.save()

    Race condition: two requests read the same balance and both withdraw (lost update, negative balance). Fix: Account.objects.filter(pk=account_id, balance__gte=amount).update(balance=F("balance") - amount) and check the returned row count, or select_for_update() inside atomic().

    20. What is ATOMIC_REQUESTS and why do many teams avoid it? It wraps every view in a transaction. Simple, but transactions last the whole request (including slow API calls), holding locks and connections longer. Explicit atomic() around the critical part is better.

    ↑ top

    Migrations

    21. How does makemigrations know what changed? It replays all existing migration files to build an in-memory model state and diffs it against your current models. It never reads the real DB. migrate checks django_migrations for what's applied. more

    22. How do you add a NOT NULL column to a big table with zero downtime? Add it nullable (or with db_default in Django 5.0+), deploy code that writes it, backfill in batches, then add NOT NULL (on Postgres via a NOT VALID check constraint + validate). Indexes with AddIndexConcurrently and atomic = False. more

    23. Why not RenameField in production? During a rolling deploy, old code still uses the old column name and crashes. Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one in a later deploy.

    ↑ top

    DRF

    24. What's the serializer validation order? Each field's parsing and validators → validate_<field>() → serializer-level validators (e.g. unique together) → validate(attrs). more

    25. What's wrong with this serializer?

    class PostSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    comments_count = serializers.SerializerMethodField()
    def get_comments_count(self, obj):
        return obj.comments.count()

    One COUNT query per post (N+1). Annotate in the view: Post.objects.annotate(comments_count=Count("comments")) and use IntegerField(read_only=True).

    26. Authentication vs permission? 401 vs 403? Authentication identifies the user (sets request.user); permissions decide access. 401 = not authenticated (with a WWW-Authenticate header, e.g. token/JWT), 403 = authenticated but not allowed (or session auth). more

    27. Why isn't has_object_permission enough to protect a list endpoint? DRF calls it only from get_object() (detail routes). list() never calls it, so filter the queryset by user in get_queryset().

    28. Offset vs cursor pagination? Offset needs COUNT(*) and scans skipped rows, so deep pages are slow and inserts cause duplicates/skips. Cursor uses WHERE key < cursor on an indexed, unique ordering: fast and stable, but no total or jump-to-page. more

    29. How do you make a "create payment" POST safe to retry? Client sends an Idempotency-Key; store it with a unique constraint and the first response; on a repeat, return the stored response instead of creating again. more

    ↑ top

    Performance and deployment

    30. Your endpoint is slow. What do you check first? Query count and time (debug-toolbar / Sentry / assertNumQueries) → N+1 and missing indexes (EXPLAIN ANALYZE) → payload size and serializer cost → caching → external calls that should be async (Celery). more

    31. What do CONN_MAX_AGE and pgbouncer solve? CONN_MAX_AGE=0 opens a new DB connection per request. A positive value reuses connections per thread (add CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS). Pgbouncer (transaction mode) or Django 5.1's "pool" option limits real Postgres connections when you have many workers; with pgbouncer set DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS. more

    ↑ top

    Security

    32. How does Django prevent CSRF, XSS and SQL injection? CSRF: middleware checks a secret token on unsafe methods for cookie-based auth. XSS: templates auto-escape (broken by mark_safe/safe). SQL injection: ORM and params are parameterized (broken by f-strings in raw()/extra()/cursor.execute()). more

    33. Production settings checklist? DEBUG=False, real ALLOWED_HOSTS, SECRET_KEY from env, SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, secure cookies, HSTS, SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER behind a proxy, and manage.py check --deploy in CI.

    ↑ top

    Async and testing

    34. Can you use the ORM in an async view? Transactions? Yes via the async API (aget, acreate, async for), but it still runs the sync driver in a thread. atomic() doesn't work in async code: put that logic in a sync function and call it with sync_to_async. Calling the sync ORM directly raises SynchronousOnlyOperation. more

    35. TestCase vs TransactionTestCase? TestCase wraps each test in a transaction and rolls back (fast), so on_commit callbacks never run (use captureOnCommitCallbacks). TransactionTestCase really commits and truncates tables (slow); use it for locking, on_commit and multi-connection tests.

    ✓ Key points
    • Lead with the one-line answer, then the "why", then offer a code example.
    • For "how many queries" questions: find every place a lazy relation is touched in a loop.
    • For "what's wrong" questions: look for N+1, read-modify-write races, side effects before commit, and missing user scoping.
    ❝ Interview line

    "Most Django problems I've fixed in production were N+1 queries, races from read-modify-write, and Celery tasks started before commit, so I check for exactly those three in every code review."

    ⚠ Common trap

    answering only with API names ("use select_related"). Interviewers want the mechanism: what SQL runs, how many queries, and what happens under concurrency.

    Django ORM in Depth

    QuerySetlazy evaluationqueryset cacheselect_relatedprefetch_relatedPrefetchto_attrN+1assertNumQueriesdjango-debug-toolbarF expressionQ objectannotateaggregateSubqueryOuterRefExistsvaluesvalues_listonlydeferbulk_createbulk_updateupdate vs saveiteratorchunk_sizeget_or_createupdate_or_createMeta indexesUniqueConstraintraw SQLRawSQLconnection.cursor
    See also Transactions & Migrations · Django REST Framework · Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async · Indexes · Locking & Concurrency Control · Django Interview Questions · Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals

    2. select_related vs prefetch_related
    3. Detecting N+1

    6. Loading less: values, values_list, only, defer

    What: the ORM turns Python method chains into SQL. A QuerySet is a description of a query that runs only when you need the rows.

    ℹ Why it matters

    most Django performance bugs are ORM bugs: N+1 queries, loading whole rows you don't need, read-modify-write races. Interviewers love "how many queries does this run?".

    ↑ top

    Laziness and evaluation

    qs = Book.objects.filter(published=True)   # 0 queries: nothing runs
qs = qs.exclude(price=0).order_by("-id")   # 0 queries: still building SQL
for b in qs: ...                           # 1 query: evaluated, results cached in qs
for b in qs: ...                           # 0 queries: uses qs's cache

    What evaluates a QuerySet (runs the query and fills the cache): iteration, list(qs), len(qs), bool(qs) / if qs:, slicing with a step (qs[::2]), repr(qs) (shell), pickling.

    What does NOT fill the cache (runs its own query every time):

    Call SQL Note
    qs.count() SELECT COUNT(*) uses cache if qs already evaluated
    qs.exists() SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1 cheapest "is there any?"
    qs[0], qs.first() LIMIT 1 on an unevaluated qs, a new query every call
    qs[10:20] LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 returns a new lazy QuerySet
    qs.get(...) WHERE ... raises DoesNotExist / MultipleObjectsReturned 
    # How many queries?
qs = Book.objects.all()
if qs:                 # 1: loads ALL rows into memory just to check
    print(qs[0])       # 0: qs is already evaluated, uses cache
# Better: if qs.exists() when you don't need the rows.

print(Book.objects.all()[0])  # 1
print(Book.objects.all()[0])  # 1 again: a new QuerySet every time → 2 total

    Calling .filter() / .all() on a QuerySet returns a new QuerySet without the cache.

    ↑ top

    select_related vs prefetch_related

    select_related prefetch_related
    Relation ForeignKey, OneToOne (forward; reverse one-to-one too) ManyToMany, reverse FK (author.book_set), also FK
    SQL one query with JOIN one extra query per relation: WHERE id IN (...)
    Join done in the database Python
    Risk wide rows, big joins big IN lists, memory 
    # N+1: 1 query for books + 1 per book for author
for b in Book.objects.all():
    print(b.author.name)

# 1 query (JOIN)
for b in Book.objects.select_related("author", "author__country"):
    print(b.author.name)

# 2 queries: authors, then all their books with WHERE author_id IN (...)
for a in Author.objects.prefetch_related("books"):
    print([b.title for b in a.books.all()])

    Prefetch objects let you filter, order or select_related the inner query, and store the result in a list:

    from django.db.models import Prefetch

authors = Author.objects.prefetch_related(
    Prefetch(
        "books",
        queryset=Book.objects.filter(published=True).select_related("publisher"),
        to_attr="published_books",          # a plain list attribute
    )
)
for a in authors:                           # 2 queries total
    for b in a.published_books:
        print(b.publisher.name)

    Trap: a.books.filter(published=True) inside the loop ignores the prefetch cache and runs a new query per author. Only .all() uses the cache. Filter in the Prefetch instead.

    ↑ top

    Detecting N+1

    • django-debug-toolbar: SQL panel shows count, duplicates ("similar queries") and time per page.
    • Tests: lock the query count so a regression fails CI.
    def test_book_list_queries(self):
    with self.assertNumQueries(2):
        self.client.get("/api/books/")
# pytest-django: django_assert_num_queries(2) fixture
    • Production: Sentry performance ("N+1 query" detection), nplusone, or django-silk in staging. connection.queries works only with DEBUG=True.
    ↑ top

    F() and Q()

    F("field") refers to a column value inside SQL, so the DB does the math atomically.

    # ❌ read-modify-write: two requests both read 10 and both write 9 (lost update)
p = Product.objects.get(pk=1)
p.stock -= 1
p.save()

# ✅ one atomic UPDATE: SET stock = stock - 1
Product.objects.filter(pk=1, stock__gt=0).update(stock=F("stock") - 1)  # returns rows changed

# F also compares columns
Order.objects.filter(paid_amount__lt=F("total"))

    Q() builds OR, NOT and dynamic filters:

    from django.db.models import Q
Book.objects.filter(Q(title__icontains=s) | Q(author__name__icontains=s), ~Q(status="draft"))
    ↑ top

    annotate, aggregate, Subquery, Exists

    • aggregate() → one dict for the whole queryset ({"avg": 12.5}). It ends the chain.
    • annotate() → adds a computed column per row (GROUP BY when used with aggregates).
    from django.db.models import Count, Avg, Sum, Exists, OuterRef, Subquery

Book.objects.aggregate(avg=Avg("price"))                       # {'avg': Decimal('12.50')}
Author.objects.annotate(n=Count("books")).filter(n__gt=5)      # HAVING COUNT(...) > 5

    Trap: two Counts on different relations multiply rows (JOIN fan-out):

    # ❌ wrong numbers: books × reviews
Author.objects.annotate(b=Count("books"), r=Count("reviews"))
# ✅ distinct=True (ok for counts) or Subquery (always correct, also for Sum)
Author.objects.annotate(b=Count("books", distinct=True), r=Count("reviews", distinct=True))

    Subquery + OuterRef = a correlated subquery, e.g. "latest order date per customer":

    latest = Order.objects.filter(customer=OuterRef("pk")).order_by("-created")
Customer.objects.annotate(
    last_order_at=Subquery(latest.values("created")[:1]),
    has_open=Exists(Order.objects.filter(customer=OuterRef("pk"), status="open")),
).filter(has_open=True)

    Exists is usually faster than Count(...) > 0 or __in with a big list, because the DB can stop at the first match. In Django 3.0+ you can pass Exists(...) straight into .filter().

    ↑ top

    Loading less: values, values_list, only, defer

    Call Returns Use
    values("id", "title") dicts reports, JSON, grouping (values(...).annotate(...) = GROUP BY)
    values_list("id", flat=True) tuples / flat values lists of IDs
    only("id", "title") model instances, other fields deferred need methods but few columns
    defer("body") model instances without body skip big text/JSON columns

    Trap: accessing a deferred field later runs one extra query per object (a new N+1).

    ↑ top

    Bulk writes and update() vs save()

    Operation Queries save() called? pre/post_save signals?
    obj.save() in a loop N yes yes
    qs.update(x=...) 1 no no (also no auto_now update)
    bulk_create(objs, batch_size=1000) ~N/batch no no
    bulk_update(objs, ["x"], batch_size=1000) ~N/batch no no
    qs.delete() 1+ Model.delete() not called yes, pre/post_delete are sent (Django loads the objects to send them and handle cascades)
    • bulk_create sets PKs on the objects on PostgreSQL (uses RETURNING). Options: ignore_conflicts=True, or update_conflicts=True, unique_fields=[...], update_fields=[...] for upsert.
    • bulk_update builds a big CASE WHEN statement; it is slower than people think on large sets. For one value on many rows, update() is best.
    • If a field has auto_now=True, update() won't touch it; set it yourself: update(status="x", updated_at=timezone.now()).
    ↑ top

    Big tables: iterator()

    for row in Event.objects.filter(day=today).iterator(chunk_size=2000):
    process(row)
    • Streams rows without filling the queryset cache, so memory stays flat. On PostgreSQL it uses a server-side cursor.
    • With prefetch_related, you must pass chunk_size (prefetch runs per chunk).
    • Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, server-side cursors break → set DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS: True in the DB settings.
    • For updates over millions of rows, process by PK ranges (filter(pk__gt=last_id).order_by("pk")[:1000]) in small transactions.
    ↑ top

    get_or_create / update_or_create races

    obj, created = Tag.objects.get_or_create(name="python", defaults={"color": "blue"})

    How it works: SELECT → if missing, INSERT inside a savepoint → on IntegrityError it SELECTs again. So:

    • With a unique constraint on name: two parallel calls are safe; one inserts, the other gets the IntegrityError, catches it, and reads the row.
    • Without a unique constraint: both SELECTs miss, both INSERT → duplicates, and later get() raises MultipleObjectsReturned.

    update_or_create locks the row with select_for_update() inside a transaction, then updates or creates (same unique-constraint rule for the create path). Django 5.0 added create_defaults= for values used only on create.

    ↑ top

    Indexes and constraints in Meta

    class Order(models.Model):
    customer = models.ForeignKey(Customer, on_delete=models.CASCADE)  # FK gets an index automatically
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20)
    created = models.DateTimeField(db_index=True)

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            models.Index(fields=["customer", "-created"], name="order_cust_created_idx"),
            models.Index(fields=["created"], name="order_open_idx",
                         condition=Q(status="open")),           # partial index (Postgres)
        ]
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(fields=["customer", "external_id"], name="uniq_ext_id"),
            models.CheckConstraint(condition=Q(total__gte=0), name="total_non_negative"),
        ]

    Composite index column order matters (leftmost prefix). See indexes. Note: CheckConstraint(condition=...) is the Django 5.1+ name; older versions use check=.

    ↑ top

    Raw SQL when the ORM is not enough

    Use it for window functions you can't express, CTEs, DISTINCT ON edge cases, or tuned reporting queries.

    # Model instances from raw SQL: always pass params, never f-strings
Book.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM shop_book WHERE price > %s", [min_price])

from django.db import connection
with connection.cursor() as cur:
    cur.execute("SELECT status, count(*) FROM shop_order WHERE created > %s GROUP BY 1", [since])
    rows = cur.fetchall()

    Also available: RawSQL("...", params) inside annotate, and Func / Window expressions (Django has Window, RowNumber, Rank, Lag). Check generated SQL with print(qs.query) or qs.explain(analyze=True).

    ✓ Key points
    • QuerySets are lazy and cached per object; exists()/count() for checks, not if qs.
    • FK → select_related; M2M / reverse FK → prefetch_related (+ Prefetch to filter). Filtering a prefetched manager breaks the cache.
    • Use F() for counters and balances; it's an atomic UPDATE, not read-modify-write.
    • Bulk operations and update() skip save() and save-signals; qs.delete() still sends delete signals.
    • Multiple Counts across joins give wrong numbers; use distinct=True or Subquery.
    • Race safety comes from DB constraints, not from Python checks.
    ❝ Interview line

    "QuerySets are lazy; they hit the DB only on evaluation and cache the result. To avoid N+1 I use select_related for foreign keys, which is a JOIN, and prefetch_related for many-to-many or reverse relations, which is one extra IN query, and I lock the query count with assertNumQueries. For counters I use F() so the update is atomic in the database."

    ⚠ Common trap

    obj.counter = F("counter") + 1; obj.save() is atomic, but obj.counter now holds an expression, not a number. Saving the object again applies +1 again. Call obj.refresh_from_db() after it.

    5. Signals

    What: how an HTTP request travels through Django, and the hooks (middleware, signals) you can plug into that path.

    ℹ Why it matters

    questions like "where do you put auth / logging / request-id?", "why didn't my signal fire?" and "WSGI or ASGI?" test whether you understand the framework or just use it.

    ↑ top

    WSGI vs ASGI

    WSGI ASGI
    Model sync, one request per worker thread async, event loop; many connections per worker
    Protocols HTTP only HTTP, WebSocket, long-polling, HTTP/2 via server
    Servers gunicorn, uWSGI uvicorn, daphne, hypercorn (or gunicorn + uvicorn worker)
    Entry wsgi.py → application asgi.py → application
    Async views work, but run in their own event loop per request: no benefit real benefit for I/O-heavy views

    Under ASGI, sync views and sync middleware run in a thread pool (via sync_to_async). Each sync/async switch costs a bit, so a mostly-sync app gets nothing from ASGI. See async-await and concurrency-models.

    ↑ top

    The request path

    client
  │
  ▼
nginx / LB ──► gunicorn worker ──► WSGIHandler (signal: request_started)
                                     │  builds HttpRequest
                                     ▼
              ┌─── SecurityMiddleware ─────────────────────┐
              │ ┌─ SessionMiddleware ─────────────────────┐│
              │ │ ┌─ CsrfViewMiddleware / AuthMiddleware ─┐││
              │ │ │  URL resolver (ROOT_URLCONF or        │││
              │ │ │    request.urlconf) → view + kwargs   │││
              │ │ │  process_view() hooks (top→down)      │││
              │ │ │  view(request, **kwargs) → response   │││
              │ │ │  (process_exception() if it raised)   │││
              │ │ │  TemplateResponse rendered here       │││
              │ │ └───────────────────────────────────────┘││
              │ └─────────────────────────────────────────┘│
              └────────── response goes back up ──────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
                       response sent (signal: request_finished
                       → closes DB connections older than CONN_MAX_AGE)
    1. The server calls the handler; Django sends request_started.
    2. Middleware __call__ "before" code runs top → down.
    3. The URL resolver matches urlpatterns in order (first match wins; path converters like <int:pk>). No match → 404.
    4. process_view(request, view_func, args, kwargs) hooks run (CSRF check lives here).
    5. The view runs and returns an HttpResponse. If it raises, process_exception hooks run bottom → up.
    6. If the response is a TemplateResponse, process_template_response runs, then it is rendered.
    7. Middleware "after" code runs bottom → up.
    ↑ top

    Writing middleware

    import uuid, time, logging
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class RequestIdMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):          # once, at startup
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):               # every request
        request.id = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID") or uuid.uuid4().hex
        start = time.monotonic()
        response = self.get_response(request)  # calls the next layer (or the view)
        response["X-Request-ID"] = request.id
        logger.info("req %s %s %s %.0fms", request.id, request.path,
                    response.status_code, (time.monotonic() - start) * 1000)
        return response
    • Return a response early (without calling get_response) to short-circuit, e.g. maintenance mode or IP block. Inner layers and the view don't run.
    • Middleware runs for every request: keep it cheap, no DB queries if you can avoid them.
    • request.user is a lazy object set by AuthenticationMiddleware; it hits the DB only when touched.
    • DRF authenticates in the view, not in middleware. So in a custom middleware request.user is AnonymousUser for JWT/token requests.

    Order matters (default order):

    MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",          # HTTPS redirect, HSTS: first
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",   # must come before auth
    "django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",# needs the session
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware",
]

    GZipMiddleware goes near the top (it must see the final response body). CorsMiddleware (django-cors-headers) goes as high as possible, before CommonMiddleware.

    ↑ top

    Function-based vs class-based views

    # FBV: explicit, easy to read
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def order_list(request): ...

# CBV
class OrderDetail(LoginRequiredMixin, DetailView):
    model = Order
    def get_queryset(self):
        return super().get_queryset().filter(customer=self.request.user)

path("orders/<int:pk>/", OrderDetail.as_view())
    • as_view() returns a function. Each request creates a new instance, so storing state on self is safe per request.
    • dispatch() maps the HTTP method to get()/post()/...; unknown method → 405.
    • Mixin order follows the MRO: put LoginRequiredMixin left of the base view.
    • Trade-off: CBVs/generic views remove boilerplate but hide control flow; FBVs are clearer for unusual logic. DRF's APIView/viewsets are CBVs.
    ↑ top

    Signals

    # apps.py
class OrdersConfig(AppConfig):
    name = "orders"
    def ready(self):
        from . import signals      # import here so receivers get registered once

# signals.py
@receiver(post_save, sender=Order, dispatch_uid="order_created_notify")
def on_order_saved(sender, instance, created, **kwargs):
    if created:
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(instance.pk))

    Common built-ins: pre_save/post_save, pre_delete/post_delete, m2m_changed, request_started/request_finished, user_logged_in.

    How they really run: Signal.send() calls every receiver synchronously, in the same thread, inside the same DB transaction as the caller. A receiver exception propagates to the caller (use send_robust() to collect errors instead). Django 5.0 added asend() / asend_robust() for async receivers.

    Pitfalls:

    Pitfall Detail
    Hidden coupling Reading order.save() gives no hint that an email, a cache purge and a webhook happen. Hard to debug and to test.
    Not fired on bulk ops qs.update(), bulk_create(), bulk_update() skip pre/post_save. Raw SQL skips everything.
    Transaction timing post_save runs before commit. A Celery task started there may run before the row is visible, or after a rollback for a row that never exists. Fix: transaction.on_commit.
    Slow saves Every receiver adds latency to every save, including in admin and scripts.
    Double registration Importing the module twice or bad ready() → receiver runs twice. Use dispatch_uid.
    Ordering Receiver order = registration order; don't depend on it.

    Signals vs explicit service calls:

    # services.py: business logic is visible and testable
def place_order(user, cart) -> Order:
    with transaction.atomic():
        order = Order.objects.create(user=user, total=cart.total)
        OrderItem.objects.bulk_create([...])
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(order.pk))
    return order

    Use signals for decoupling across apps you don't own (e.g. reacting to user_logged_in, or a reusable app that shouldn't import yours), and for cross-cutting things like cache invalidation or audit logs. Use explicit service functions for business workflows in your own code.

    ✓ Key points
    • Middleware = onion around the view; order is part of correctness.
    • URL resolution happens after request middleware, so middleware can change request.urlconf.
    • request_finished is where Django closes old DB connections.
    • Signals are sync, same-transaction, and skipped by bulk operations.
    • Side effects from signals or services → transaction.on_commit.
    ❝ Interview line

    "A request goes from gunicorn or uvicorn into Django's handler, through the middleware stack top to bottom, then the URL resolver picks the view, and the response goes back through middleware in reverse. I avoid signals for business logic because they're synchronous, hidden, run before commit and are skipped by bulk updates; I prefer an explicit service function with transaction.on_commit for side effects."

    ⚠ Common trap

    thinking a post_save signal runs "after the data is saved" in the sense of committed. Inside atomic() it runs before commit, so a Celery task triggered there can read stale data or get DoesNotExist.

    Transactions & Migrations

    autocommitATOMIC_REQUESTStransaction.atomicsavepointnested atomicTransactionManagementErrorselect_for_updateskip_lockednowaitofno_keytransaction.on_commitdelay_on_commitcaptureOnCommitCallbacksF expression racemakemigrationsmigratedjango_migrationsmigration dependenciesRunPythonapps.get_modeldata migrationsquashmigrationszero-downtime migrationexpand and contractdb_defaultSeparateDatabaseAndStateAddIndexConcurrentlyatomic = Falselock_timeoutAddConstraintNotValid
    See also Django ORM in Depth · Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals · Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async · Transactions & Isolation Levels · Locking & Concurrency Control · Celery with Redis as Broker · Django Interview Questions
    On this page
    1. Transaction basics
    2. select_for_update
    3. transaction.on_commit
    4. Migrations: how they work
    5. Data migrations
    6. Squashing
    7. Zero-downtime migration rules

    What: how Django manages DB transactions and row locks, and how schema changes (migrations) are created and deployed safely.

    ℹ Why it matters

    money, stock and counters break under concurrency; a bad migration can lock a production table for minutes. Senior interviews always touch one of these.

    ↑ top

    Transaction basics

    • Autocommit (default): each query is its own transaction.
    • ATOMIC_REQUESTS = True (per database): wraps each view in one transaction; commits if the view returns, rolls back if it raises. Middleware and streaming response generators run outside it. Cost: transactions as long as the request, including slow external API calls → locks held longer. Opt out with @transaction.non_atomic_requests. Most teams prefer explicit atomic() where needed.
    • transaction.atomic(): decorator or context manager.
    from django.db import transaction, IntegrityError

with transaction.atomic():                 # BEGIN
    order = Order.objects.create(...)
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():         # SAVEPOINT
            Coupon.objects.create(code=code, order=order)   # may raise IntegrityError
    except IntegrityError:                 # ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT: outer tx still OK
        order.note = "coupon already used"
    order.save()
                                           # COMMIT

    Rule: catch the exception outside an atomic block. If you catch a DB error inside the same block and keep querying, PostgreSQL's transaction is broken and Django raises TransactionManagementError: An error occurred in the current transaction.... The inner atomic() is what makes recovery possible.

    • Savepoints cost a round trip each; atomic(savepoint=False) skips them when you don't need partial rollback.
    • Isolation level is the DB default (Postgres: READ COMMITTED). You can change it in OPTIONS. See transactions-isolation.
    ↑ top

    select_for_update

    with transaction.atomic():
    acc = Account.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=acc_id)   # SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    if acc.balance < amount:
        raise InsufficientFunds
    acc.balance -= amount
    acc.save(update_fields=["balance"])
# lock released at COMMIT
    • Must be inside atomic(); evaluating it in autocommit raises TransactionManagementError. Note it's lazy: the lock is taken when the queryset is evaluated.
    • nowait=True → error immediately if locked (DatabaseError), instead of waiting.
    • skip_locked=True → skip locked rows. Perfect for DB-backed job queues: many workers each take different rows.
    • of=("self",) → with select_related, lock only the main table's rows.
    • no_key=True (Postgres FOR NO KEY UPDATE) → weaker lock that doesn't block inserts of rows referencing this one by FK.
    • Lock rows in a consistent order (e.g. by PK) to avoid deadlocks when locking several.
    # job queue: each worker takes up to 10 unclaimed jobs
with transaction.atomic():
    jobs = list(Job.objects.select_for_update(skip_locked=True)
                .filter(status="pending").order_by("id")[:10])
    Job.objects.filter(id__in=[j.id for j in jobs]).update(status="running")

    F() vs select_for_update: for a single counter, a conditional UPDATE with F() is simpler and faster (no lock wait):

    updated = Product.objects.filter(pk=pid, stock__gte=qty).update(stock=F("stock") - qty)
if not updated:
    raise OutOfStock          # 0 rows changed = not enough stock, no race

    Use select_for_update when the decision needs several reads or business logic in Python. See locking-concurrency.

    ↑ top

    transaction.on_commit

    with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(...)
    send_receipt.delay(order.pk)          # ❌ worker may run before COMMIT → DoesNotExist
                                          #    or after ROLLBACK → email for a ghost order
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(order.pk))   # ✅ runs after COMMIT
    • If the transaction rolls back, the callback is dropped. Outside a transaction, it runs immediately.
    • Callbacks run in order; robust=True (Django 4.2+) keeps one failing callback from stopping the others.
    • Celery 5.4+ has task.delay_on_commit(...) as a shortcut.
    • In TestCase nothing really commits, so callbacks never run. Use with self.captureOnCommitCallbacks(execute=True):.
    • on_commit gives "after commit" but not "exactly once": if the process dies between COMMIT and delay(), the task is lost. For strong guarantees use a transactional outbox table. See celery-redis-broker.
    ↑ top

    Migrations: how they work

    • makemigrations loads all migration files, replays them in memory to build the "project state", diffs it against your current models, and writes new operations (AddField, AlterField...). It never looks at the real DB.
    • migrate builds a dependency graph (dependencies = [("orders", "0007_..."), ("users", "0003_...")]), checks the django_migrations table for applied ones, and runs the rest in order. On PostgreSQL each migration runs in one transaction by default (DDL is transactional there; not on MySQL).
    • Useful commands: showmigrations, migrate --plan, sqlmigrate app 0008 (see the real SQL), makemigrations --check --dry-run (CI: fail if models changed without migrations), migrate app 0007 (roll back), --fake (mark as applied without running).
    • Two branches creating 0008_* in the same app → conflict; fix with makemigrations --merge or by renumbering before merge.
    ↑ top

    Data migrations

    from django.db import migrations

def forwards(apps, schema_editor):
    User = apps.get_model("users", "User")        # historical model, NOT `from users.models import User`
    for u in User.objects.filter(full_name="").iterator(chunk_size=2000):
        u.full_name = f"{u.first_name} {u.last_name}".strip()
        u.save(update_fields=["full_name"])

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [("users", "0012_user_full_name")]
    operations = [migrations.RunPython(forwards, migrations.RunPython.noop)]
    • Use apps.get_model: it gives the model as it was at that migration. Importing the real model breaks when the model changes later.
    • Historical models have no custom methods and no custom save(); custom managers only if use_in_migrations = True. Signals still fire for them, but receivers expecting the real class may not match the historical one.
    • Always give a reverse (RunPython.noop if nothing to undo), or the migration can't be rolled back.
    • Large backfills inside a migration = one long transaction + long deploy. For big tables, run the backfill as a separate batched job/management command (or set atomic = False and batch).
    ↑ top

    Squashing

    squashmigrations app 0001 0040 creates one migration with replaces = [...]. New DBs run the squashed one; existing DBs that already applied the old ones keep working. After every environment has migrated past it, delete the old files and remove replaces. RunPython operations without elidable=True are kept, so squashes can stay big.

    ↑ top

    Zero-downtime migration rules

    During a rolling deploy, old code and new code run at the same time against the same schema. Every migration must work with both.

    Change Unsafe one-step way Safe way
    Add NOT NULL column AddField(null=False, default=x): Django sets the default only to fill existing rows and then drops it from the DB, so old code's INSERTs (without the column) fail add null=True (or Django 5.0 db_default=, which stays in the DB) → deploy code that writes it → backfill in batches → then make NOT NULL
    Rename column/table RenameField → old code queries the old name → errors add new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, drop old (several deploys); or db_column= to keep the DB name
    Drop column drop in the same deploy as the code change → old code still SELECTs it deploy 1: remove field from code (make it nullable first if NOT NULL); deploy 2: drop column. SeparateDatabaseAndState helps split state vs DB change
    Add index on big table AddIndex → CREATE INDEX locks writes for the whole build AddIndexConcurrently + atomic = False
    Add NOT NULL / CHECK / FK on big table full scan under a strong lock Postgres: add constraint NOT VALID, then validate separately (AddConstraintNotValid + ValidateConstraint in django.contrib.postgres.operations)
    Change column type table rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock new column + backfill + switch 
    from django.contrib.postgres.operations import AddIndexConcurrently

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    atomic = False      # CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can't run inside a transaction
    dependencies = [("orders", "0020_...")]
    operations = [
        AddIndexConcurrently("order", models.Index(fields=["created"], name="order_created_idx")),
    ]

    Extra safety:

    • Set a short lock_timeout (e.g. SET lock_timeout = '5s') for migrations. Even a fast ALTER TABLE waits behind a long-running query for its lock, and every other query queues behind it → outage. Better to fail and retry.
    • Run migrations before the new code rolls out (as a release step), so the new code always finds its columns.
    • Tools: django-pg-zero-downtime-migrations, or a linter like django-migration-linter in CI.
    ✓ Key points
    • Nested atomic = savepoints; catch errors outside the inner block.
    • select_for_update needs a transaction; skip_locked for queues; nowait to fail fast.
    • Single-row counters: conditional update() with F().
    • Side effects (Celery, email, webhooks) → on_commit.
    • Migrations come from replayed migration state; data migrations use apps.get_model.
    • Every migration must be compatible with the previous code version.
    ❝ Interview line

    "I keep transactions short with explicit atomic() blocks, lock rows with select_for_update when the logic needs it, and trigger Celery tasks with on_commit so workers never see uncommitted data. For migrations I follow expand and contract: add nullable columns or use db_default, backfill in batches, add constraints later, create indexes concurrently, and never rename or drop in the same deploy as the code change."

    ⚠ Common trap

    AddField(..., default=0) on a NOT NULL column looks safe, but Django doesn't keep the default in the database. Old code still running during the deploy inserts rows without that column and gets NOT NULL constraint errors. Use db_default (Django 5.0+) or add it as nullable first.

    Django REST Framework

    What: DRF is the standard toolkit for JSON APIs on Django: serializers (validation + conversion), views/viewsets, routers, and plug-in policies for auth, permissions, throttling, pagination, filtering and versioning.

    ℹ Why it matters

    most Django jobs in Iran are API backends behind a mobile/web app. Interviewers check if you can keep DRF endpoints correct and fast.

    ↑ top

    Request flow inside an APIView

    dispatch()
  initialize_request()   → wraps HttpRequest in DRF Request (parsers, authenticators)
  initial()
    perform_authentication()   → request.user (lazy, but forced here)
    check_permissions()        → has_permission() for each permission class
    check_throttles()          → 429 if over the rate
    (version determined here)
  handler: list() / create() / retrieve() ...
    get_object() → check_object_permissions() → has_object_permission()
  finalize_response()    → renderer (JSON), content negotiation
  handle_exception()     → APIException → proper status code
    ↑ top

    Serializers

    class OrderSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    customer_name = serializers.CharField(source="customer.name", read_only=True)
    items = OrderItemSerializer(many=True)

    class Meta:
        model = Order
        fields = ["id", "customer_name", "status", "total", "items"]
        read_only_fields = ["status"]

    def validate_total(self, value):               # field-level
        if value <= 0:
            raise serializers.ValidationError("must be positive")
        return value

    def validate(self, attrs):                     # object-level, after all fields
        if attrs["total"] > 10_000 and not self.context["request"].user.is_staff:
            raise serializers.ValidationError("limit exceeded")
        return attrs

    Validation order for serializer.is_valid():

    1. For each field: to_internal_value() (type parsing) + field validators=[...] (e.g. UniqueValidator), then validate_<field_name>().
    2. Serializer-level validators (e.g. UniqueTogetherValidator, auto-added from unique_together/UniqueConstraint).
    3. validate(self, attrs).

    Errors are collected per field; is_valid(raise_exception=True) returns a 400 with them.

    Writing: serializer.save() calls create() (no instance) or update() (instance given). Pass server-side values: serializer.save(owner=request.user).

    Nested writes: ModelSerializer.create() raises an error if writable nested data is present. You write it yourself:

        def create(self, validated_data):
        items = validated_data.pop("items")
        with transaction.atomic():
            order = Order.objects.create(**validated_data)
            OrderItem.objects.bulk_create([OrderItem(order=order, **i) for i in items])
        return order

    For updates of nested lists you must decide: replace all, or match by id and diff. Often simpler: a separate endpoint for items.

    SerializerMethodField N+1 trap:

    class AuthorSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    book_count = serializers.SerializerMethodField()
    def get_book_count(self, obj):
        return obj.books.count()          # ❌ 1 COUNT query per author: page of 50 = 51 queries

# ✅ compute it in the queryset and read the attribute
class AuthorViewSet(viewsets.ReadOnlyModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = AuthorSerializer
    def get_queryset(self):
        return Author.objects.annotate(book_count=Count("books"))
# serializer: book_count = serializers.IntegerField(read_only=True)

    Same for nested serializers: OrderSerializer with items and customer needs .select_related("customer").prefetch_related("items__product").

    Other notes: to_representation() customizes output; serializers are slow for big payloads (pure-Python per field), so for huge read-only lists use .values() or a lighter serializer.

    ↑ top

    Views, viewsets and routers

    Class Gives you
    APIView get/post/... methods + DRF policies
    GenericAPIView + mixins get_queryset, get_object, pagination, filtering
    ListCreateAPIView etc. ready combinations
    ModelViewSet list, create, retrieve, update, partial_update, destroy
    ReadOnlyModelViewSet / GenericViewSet + mixins pick only what you expose 
    class OrderViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = OrderSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated, IsOwner]

    def get_queryset(self):                       # per request, scoped to user, no N+1
        return (Order.objects.filter(customer=self.request.user)
                .select_related("customer").prefetch_related("items__product"))

    @action(detail=True, methods=["post"])
    def cancel(self, request, pk=None):           # POST /orders/{pk}/cancel/
        order = self.get_object()                 # runs object permissions
        order.cancel()
        return Response(status=204)

router = DefaultRouter()                          # DefaultRouter adds an API root view
router.register("orders", OrderViewSet, basename="order")
urlpatterns = router.urls

    Use get_queryset(), not a class-level queryset = Order.objects.filter(customer=...): the class attribute is built once at import and can't see request.user. Filtering by user in get_queryset() also makes other users' objects return 404 instead of 403 (no data leak).

    ↑ top

    Authentication vs permissions

    • Authentication classes (SessionAuthentication, TokenAuthentication, JWT via djangorestframework-simplejwt) set request.user and request.auth. Failing all → AnonymousUser, not an error.
    • Permissions (IsAuthenticated, IsAdminUser, DjangoModelPermissions, custom) decide access.
    • 401 vs 403: not authenticated → 401 if the first auth class sends a WWW-Authenticate header (Token/JWT do), otherwise 403 (Session). Authenticated but not allowed → 403.
    • SessionAuthentication enforces CSRF for unsafe methods; token/JWT auth doesn't need CSRF.
    class IsOwner(BasePermission):
    def has_permission(self, request, view):          # every request, incl. list
        return request.user.is_authenticated
    def has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj):  # only via get_object()
        return obj.customer_id == request.user.id

    Trap: has_object_permission is not called for list() or for objects you fetch manually. Scope the list in get_queryset().

    ↑ top

    Throttling

    AnonRateThrottle, UserRateThrottle, ScopedRateThrottle (throttle_scope = "login" + "login": "5/min"). State is kept in the Django cache, so use a shared cache (Redis), not local memory, with several workers. It's a soft limit (race between read and write), fine for abuse protection, not for billing. Behind a proxy set NUM_PROXIES so the client IP is read correctly from X-Forwarded-For. Real DoS protection belongs in nginx / the gateway.

    ↑ top

    Pagination

    Style SQL Pros Cons
    PageNumberPagination (?page=3) LIMIT/OFFSET + COUNT(*) page numbers, total slow deep pages, COUNT(*) on big tables, duplicates/skips when rows are inserted
    LimitOffsetPagination same flexible same
    CursorPagination WHERE created < :cursor ORDER BY created DESC LIMIT n O(1) per page with an index, stable under inserts no total, no jump to page N; needs a unique, fixed ordering (default -created)

    Use cursor pagination for feeds, timelines and infinite scroll. Always set a default PAGE_SIZE and max_page_size so nobody can request 1M rows.

    ↑ top

    Filtering and ordering

    filter_backends = [DjangoFilterBackend, SearchFilter, OrderingFilter]
filterset_fields = ["status", "customer"]       # ?status=paid
search_fields = ["number", "customer__email"]   # ?search=... → ILIKE '%x%' (no index! use full-text/trigram for big tables)
ordering_fields = ["created", "total"]          # whitelist; never allow ordering by any field

    Each filtered/ordered field should match an index.

    ↑ top

    Versioning

    URLPathVersioning (/api/v1/..., most common), NamespaceVersioning, AcceptHeaderVersioning (Accept: application/json; version=2), QueryParameterVersioning. Read request.version and pick a serializer in get_serializer_class(). Keep old versions working until clients (old mobile app builds!) are gone.

    ↑ top

    Idempotency for POST

    GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not. Mobile networks retry, users double-click → duplicate orders or payments.

    def create(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
    key = request.headers.get("Idempotency-Key")
    if not key:
        return Response({"detail": "Idempotency-Key required"}, status=400)
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():
            rec = IdempotencyRecord.objects.create(user=request.user, key=key)  # unique (user, key)
            response = super().create(request, *args, **kwargs)
            rec.status_code, rec.body = response.status_code, response.data
            rec.save()
            return response
    except IntegrityError:
        rec = IdempotencyRecord.objects.get(user=request.user, key=key)
        if rec.status_code is None:
            return Response({"detail": "in progress"}, status=409)
        return Response(rec.body, status=rec.status_code)      # replay the first result

    The unique constraint is what makes it race-safe. Also store a hash of the request body to reject the same key with a different payload, and expire old keys. A natural unique key (e.g. (user, client_order_id)) works too.

    ✓ Key points
    • Validation: fields → validate_<field> → validators → validate().
    • Nested writes are manual; wrap them in atomic().
    • Performance lives in get_queryset(): select_related, prefetch_related, annotate; test with assertNumQueries.
    • Scope data in get_queryset(); object permissions don't protect lists.
    • Cursor pagination for big or live lists.
    • Throttles need a shared cache.
    ❝ Interview line

    "In DRF I keep views thin: get_queryset() scopes data to the user and fixes N+1 with select_related/prefetch_related or annotations, serializers only validate and shape data, and business logic goes to a service function. For big lists I use cursor pagination, and for create endpoints that clients retry I require an idempotency key backed by a unique constraint."

    ⚠ Common trap

    relying on has_object_permission for security on a list endpoint. It's never called there, so GET /orders/ returns everyone's orders unless get_queryset() filters by user.

    On this page
    1. Caching

    What: the things that decide whether a Django app survives real traffic: caching, DB connections, process model, static files, security settings, async limits, background jobs, observability and tests.

    ℹ Why it matters

    senior interviews ask "your endpoint is slow / your DB has too many connections / how do you deploy Django?". These answers show production experience.

    ↑ top

    Caching

    CACHES = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django.core.cache.backends.redis.RedisCache",   # built in since Django 4.0
        "LOCATION": "redis://redis:6379/1",
        "TIMEOUT": 300,
        "KEY_PREFIX": "shop",
    }
}

    django-redis is the popular third-party backend (extra features: delete_pattern, locks, compression). LocMemCache is per process: useless for shared state with many workers.

    Level Example Good for
    Per-view @cache_page(60) (+ @vary_on_headers("Accept-Language")) public pages, same for everyone
    Template fragment {% cache 300 sidebar request.user.id %}...{% endcache %} expensive parts of a page
    Low-level cache.get_or_set(key, fn, 300), get_many, incr query results, computed values, counters
    HTTP Cache-Control, ETag (@condition), CDN static and public API responses 
    def product_detail_data(pid):
    key = f"product:v2:{pid}"                      # version in the key → bump to invalidate all
    return cache.get_or_set(key, lambda: build_product(pid), timeout=600)

def update_product(p, **changes):
    with transaction.atomic():
        ...
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: cache.delete(f"product:v2:{p.pk}"))  # after commit, not before

    Invalidation strategies: short TTLs (accept staleness), delete on write (in on_commit, or the next read may cache old data), versioned keys / generation counters for groups (products:gen incremented on any change). Watch for stampede (many requests rebuild an expired hot key at once): use a lock (cache.add(lock_key, 1, 10)), random TTL jitter, or early refresh in the background.

    Trap: cache_page on a view that depends on the user → one user's page served to others. Per-view cache is for anonymous/public content.

    ↑ top

    Database connections

    • CONN_MAX_AGE = 0 (default): open and close a connection every request (TCP + TLS + Postgres auth ≈ several ms, and a Postgres backend process fork).
    • CONN_MAX_AGE = 60 (or None = forever): reuse per thread; closed at request_finished when too old. Add CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS = True (4.1+) so a dead connection is detected before reuse.
    • Django 5.1+ with psycopg 3: built-in pool via "OPTIONS": {"pool": True} (or a dict of pool options). Don't combine with CONN_MAX_AGE.
    • Under ASGI, Django docs say to disable persistent connections (CONN_MAX_AGE = 0) and use a pool (backend pool or pgbouncer), because async code runs ORM calls in different threads.
    • PgBouncer in transaction mode: many app connections share few Postgres connections. Limits: no session state across transactions (session SET, advisory session locks, LISTEN), and server-side cursors break → DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS = True. Prepared statements need care (newer PgBouncer 1.21+ can handle protocol-level ones).

    Sizing math: max DB connections = instances × gunicorn workers × threads (+ Celery workers × concurrency + cron). Example: 6 pods × 5 workers × 4 threads = 120, plus Celery 40 → 160, above Postgres' default max_connections = 100 → "too many connections". Fix with a pooler, not by raising max_connections forever (each Postgres connection is a process with memory).

    ↑ top

    Gunicorn / uvicorn sizing

    Setup When Rule of thumb
    gunicorn --workers N (sync) CPU-light, simple N ≈ 2 × CPU + 1
    gunicorn --worker-class gthread --threads T I/O-heavy sync views (DB, HTTP calls) fewer workers, 2–8 threads each; the GIL is released during I/O
    gunicorn -k uvicorn_worker.UvicornWorker / uvicorn --workers N ASGI, async views, websockets ~1 worker per CPU
    • Set --timeout (default 30s), --max-requests 1000 --max-requests-jitter 100 (recycle workers to contain memory leaks), and --graceful-timeout for clean deploys.
    • In Kubernetes, prefer fewer workers per pod and scale pods; the CPU limit (not the node CPU count) is what matters.
    • Slow external API calls inside a sync view block a whole worker/thread: move them to Celery or use timeouts.
    ↑ top

    Static and media files

    • Static (your CSS/JS): collectstatic copies them to STATIC_ROOT; serve with nginx, a CDN, or WhiteNoise (middleware, simple for containers). Use hashed filenames (ManifestStaticFilesStorage / CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage) for long cache headers. Since 4.2, configure with the STORAGES setting.
    • Media (user uploads): never on the container disk in multi-instance setups. Use object storage (S3 / MinIO / ArvanCloud) via django-storages, ideally with pre-signed URLs so uploads bypass Django. Validate size and type; never serve uploads from the same domain as HTML without care (stored XSS via SVG/HTML).
    ↑ top

    Security

    Threat Django protection How it breaks
    CSRF CsrfViewMiddleware + {% csrf_token %}; DRF SessionAuthentication enforces it @csrf_exempt on cookie-authenticated endpoints; CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS too wide
    XSS templates auto-escape {{ var }} mark_safe(user_input), the safe filter on user data, {% autoescape off %}, building HTML in JS from API data
    SQL injection ORM and params are parameterized f-strings/% in raw(), cursor.execute(), extra(), RawSQL(); user input as order_by() field without whitelist
    Clickjacking XFrameOptionsMiddleware, X_FRAME_OPTIONS = "DENY" (default) removing the middleware
    Host header attacks ALLOWED_HOSTS ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["*"] → poisoned password-reset links
    Info leak DEBUG = False DEBUG=True in prod shows settings, SQL, stack traces 
    # ❌ SQL injection
User.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE username = '{name}'")
# ✅ parameterized
User.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE username = %s", [name])

    HTTPS settings (behind a TLS-terminating proxy):

    SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")   # only if the proxy sets/overwrites it
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000          # start small; HSTS is hard to undo
SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = True
SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF = True      # default True

    Secrets: SECRET_KEY, DB passwords and API keys come from env vars / a secret manager, never git. SECRET_KEY signs sessions, password reset tokens and signing data; leaking it lets attackers forge them (SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS allows rotation). Use Argon2 or the default PBKDF2 for passwords. Run python manage.py check --deploy in CI. Rate-limit login (throttles / django-axes).

    ↑ top

    Async views and the async ORM

    async def dashboard(request):
    user = await User.objects.aget(pk=request.user_id)
    orders = [o async for o in Order.objects.filter(user=user)[:20]]
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=3) as client:
        r1, r2 = await asyncio.gather(client.get(URL1), client.get(URL2))   # real concurrency here
    return JsonResponse({...})

    Limits to know (Django 5.x):

    • Async ORM methods (aget, acreate, acount, aupdate, async for) exist, but DB drivers are still used synchronously: Django runs them through sync_to_async in a thread. You save threads for waiting on other I/O, not DB time.
    • Transactions don't work in async mode. transaction.atomic() and select_for_update must run in a sync function: await sync_to_async(place_order)(...).
    • Calling the sync ORM directly in async code raises SynchronousOnlyOperation.
    • Lazy relations: order.customer in async code triggers a sync query → error. Use select_related first or await Customer.objects.aget(...).
    • sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=True) (default) runs all such calls on one shared thread per request context, which serializes them. thread_sensitive=False is parallel but unsafe for DB connections.
    • Any sync middleware in the stack forces a switch per request; check that your middleware is async-capable.
    • Async pays off for I/O fan-out (calling several external APIs, websockets, SSE, long-polling); not for typical CRUD.
    ↑ top

    Celery integration best practices

    • Pass IDs, not model instances (data goes stale; pickling is unsafe).
    • Enqueue with transaction.on_commit (or delay_on_commit).
    • Tasks must be idempotent; use acks_late=True for important work.
    • autoretry_for=(RequestException,), retry_backoff=True, retry_jitter=True, max_retries=5.
    • Set soft_time_limit / time_limit; separate queues for slow vs fast tasks so a backlog doesn't block emails.
    • Never call result.get() inside a task (deadlock risk); chain instead.
    • Celery workers hold DB connections too; close or reuse them correctly (Celery's Django fixup handles per-task cleanup).

    See celery-redis-broker.

    ↑ top

    Logging and monitoring

    • LOGGING dictConfig → JSON logs to stdout (container standard), with a request ID (middleware) and user ID in every line.
    • Sentry (sentry_sdk.init(integrations=[DjangoIntegration(), CeleryIntegration()], traces_sample_rate=0.1)): exceptions with request context, performance traces, N+1 and slow-DB detection. Scrub PII (send_default_pii=False).
    • Metrics: request latency p95/p99, error rate, DB query count/time per endpoint, Celery queue length (Prometheus via django-prometheus). Postgres side: pg_stat_statements, slow-query log.
    • The django.db.backends logger prints SQL only when DEBUG=True.
    ↑ top

    Testing

    Class DB How it isolates Use for
    SimpleTestCase no DB access — pure logic, forms, URL tests
    TestCase yes wraps each test in a transaction and rolls back almost everything (fast)
    TransactionTestCase yes truncates tables after each test real commits: on_commit behavior, select_for_update with threads, multiple connections
    LiveServerTestCase yes runs a real server Selenium/Playwright
    • setUpTestData() (class-level, created once per class) is much faster than setUp() per test.
    • In TestCase, on_commit callbacks don't run → self.captureOnCommitCallbacks(execute=True).
    • factory_boy factories instead of fixtures (OrderFactory(customer__name="x")), readable and keep up with model changes.
    • pytest-django: @pytest.mark.django_db (like TestCase), @pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True) (like TransactionTestCase), fixtures client, django_assert_num_queries, settings.
    • Mock external services at the boundary (responses, respx); run Celery tasks eagerly in tests or call the task function directly.
    • Speed: --reuse-db, pytest-xdist (-n auto), fast password hasher (MD5PasswordHasher) in test settings.
    ✓ Key points
    • Cache close to the data that's expensive; invalidate after commit; protect hot keys from stampede.
    • Persistent connections or a pool; size total connections against Postgres max_connections.
    • Threads (gthread) for I/O-heavy sync Django; ASGI only if you really use async.
    • DEBUG=False, ALLOWED_HOSTS, HTTPS settings, parameterized SQL, check --deploy.
    • Async ORM is a thread wrapper; transactions need sync code.
    • TestCase for speed, TransactionTestCase for commit/locking behavior.
    ❝ Interview line

    "In production I run gunicorn with threads or a few workers per pod, keep DB connections persistent with health checks or behind pgbouncer, and count the total connections against Postgres' limit. I cache expensive reads in Redis with versioned keys and invalidate them in on_commit, monitor with Sentry and per-endpoint query counts, and I only use async views for I/O fan-out, because Django's async ORM still runs the DB driver in a thread and doesn't support transactions."

    ⚠ Common trap

    switching a CRUD app to ASGI + async views expecting a big speedup. The DB calls still run through sync_to_async threads, and sync middleware adds context switches, so it can be slower. The bottleneck is usually queries, not the server model.

    Chapter 9 · Hr

    Hr Overview

    3 pages. Each card says what the page covers and its key lines; open the page for the full depth.

    HR Interview Fundamentals

    the HR/behavioral round is a different game than the technical round — it's short (usually 30–90 minutes), low-signal per question, and graded on tone and judgment as much as content.

    • Answer what was actually asked, then stop. Don't volunteer a justification nobody asked for.
    • Internal employer details (budgets, manager conversations, team politics, headcount changes) never belong in an answer, no matter how relevant they feel to the real story.
    • Keep "why are you leaving" to one forward-looking sentence. If pressed, one more sentence, still with no specifics.
    • If you notice yourself adding a third or fourth clause to an answer, that's the cue to stop talking.
    • HR is pattern-matching for red flags and culture fit in a short conversation, not investigating the full truth.
    Read the full page →

    STAR Method for Behavioral Questions

    a structure for answering any "tell me about a time..." question without rambling or forgetting the point.

    • STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result. Give each part one or two sentences; the whole answer should run 45–90 seconds spoken.
    • A good weakness names a real, specific pattern plus what you're actively doing about it — not a humblebrag ("I work too hard") and not a technical skill gap you're "fixing with AI".
    • "Why should we hire you" works best as a direct map from your concrete skills to their stated needs, not a self-description ("I'm smart", "I'm capable").
    • Keep one go-to story (your strongest project) and adapt which angle of it you tell per question — achievement, pressure, conflict, failure can often all draw from the same project.
    Read the full page →

    Salary, Notice Period & Logistics Questions

    the practical, logistics-flavored questions that usually come near the end of an HR round.

    • Let the company name a number first when you can; give a range only if pressed, and frame your current number as context, not an anchor.
    • State your notice period plainly — it needs no justification.
    • "Are you interviewing elsewhere?" gets a brief, honest answer with no names or details.
    • Administrative questions (military service status, marital status, address) just need a direct factual answer — don't over-explain them either.
    Read the full page →

    Chapter 9 · Hr

    HR Interview Fundamentals

    HR interviewbehavioral interviewsoft skillsinterview etiquetteoversharing
    See also STAR Method for Behavioral Questions · Salary, Notice Period & Logistics Questions
    On this page
    1. The core skill: answer, then stop
    2. What never belongs in an answer
    3. "Why are you leaving / looking to leave?"
    4. Structure of a typical round

    What: the HR/behavioral round is a different game than the technical round — it's short (usually 30–90 minutes), low-signal per question, and graded on tone and judgment as much as content.

    ℹ Why it matters

    a technically strong candidate can still get screened out here by sounding unstable, indiscreet, or hard to work with — usually from oversharing, not from a bad underlying story.

    ↑ top

    The core skill: answer, then stop

    Most HR questions have a short, clean answer. The risk isn't giving too little — interviewers ask follow-ups when they want more — it's giving too much:

    • You answer the question.
    • Then you add "...and the reason for that is..." nobody asked for.
    • Then you add context to the context, to make sure they don't misunderstand.

    Each added clause is a chance to reveal something that reads worse out of context than it felt while explaining it. A good rule: before adding a detail, ask "does this answer what was actually asked, or am I justifying myself preemptively?"

    ❝ Interview line

    keep it to one or two sentences, then stop and let the silence sit. If they want more, they'll ask.

    ↑ top

    What never belongs in an answer

    Regardless of how directly relevant it feels to the real story, leave out:

    • Specific numbers or internal decisions from your current employer (budgets, headcount, project cancellations).
    • Verbatim things a manager said to you privately.
    • Team politics, who-said-what, or disagreements above your level.
    • Speculation about your current employer's future.

    These details don't make your answer more convincing — they make you look indiscreet about this employer too, which is itself the red flag.

    ↑ top

    "Why are you leaving / looking to leave?"

    This is the question most likely to trigger oversharing, because the honest answer is often complicated. The fix isn't to lie — it's to compress the honest reason into a forward-looking, neutral sentence:

    "The scope of my current project is shifting, and I'm looking for a place where I can take on longer-term, more stable ownership and keep growing technically."

    If pushed for more specifics, one more neutral layer is enough:

    "The project's direction and resourcing are being reassessed."

    Nothing about why beyond that. This is true in spirit even when the underlying situation (reorg, funding, a role winding down) is more specific — the interviewer doesn't need the specifics to evaluate you, and volunteering them only invites doubt about your discretion.

    ⚠ Common trap

    treating a visible signal (being open to work, a public job search) as something that needs explaining. It doesn't. Plenty of people look for new roles proactively; you don't owe anyone the backstory just because the search is visible.

    ↑ top

    Structure of a typical round

    Phase What's being tested Typical length
    Warm-up / "tell me about yourself" Can you give a clear, structured narrative 3–5 min
    Motivation ("why us", "why this role") Genuine interest vs. generic answer 5 min
    Behavioral / STAR questions Judgment, self-awareness, how you work with others 20–40 min
    Logistics (salary, notice period, location) Practical fit 5–10 min
    Your questions for them Genuine engagement, not just politeness 5–10 min

    See STAR Method for Behavioral Questions and Salary, Notice Period & Logistics Questions for the next two phases.

    ✓ Key points
    • Compress the honest reason for leaving into one neutral, forward-looking sentence — never the full internal story.
    • Treat every answer as a draft you're editing for length, not a chance to be fully understood.
    • A visible job search doesn't need justifying.
