    Chapter 9 · Hr

    STAR Method for Behavioral Questions

    STAR methodbehavioral questionsstrengthsweaknessesconflictachievementfailurefive year plan
    See also HR Interview Fundamentals · Salary, Notice Period & Logistics Questions
    On this page
    1. The structure
    2. One story, several angles
    3. Specific questions

    What: a structure for answering any "tell me about a time..." question without rambling or forgetting the point.

    ℹ Why it matters

    behavioral questions reward a clear shape more than a dramatic story. An unstructured answer — even about a genuinely impressive project — reads as unfocused; a structured answer about a modest situation reads as competent.

    ↑ top

    The structure

    Part Content Length
    Situation One sentence of context — what was going on 1 sentence
    Task What you specifically were responsible for 1 sentence
    Action What you actually did — the part interviewers care about most 2–4 sentences
    Result What happened, ideally with a number or concrete outcome 1 sentence

    Say the Action part in first person ("I delegated...", "I set up...") even in a team project — the question is about your judgment, not the team's.

    ↑ top

    One story, several angles

    Most people have one or two projects strong enough to answer several different questions. The same project can usually supply:

    • Greatest achievement — lead with the Result.
    • Challenging project / pressure — lead with the constraint (deadline, scale, ambiguity) and how you broke it down.
    • Conflict with a teammate — if the project had any friction, lead with the disagreement and how it resolved, ideally ending on what you'd do differently now (shows growth, not just "I was right").

    Reusing one story is efficient and consistent — interviewers rarely mind hearing about the same project from different angles, as long as each answer actually addresses its own question.

    ↑ top

    Specific questions

    Tell me about yourself. Not a full biography — a short, chronological line through your career (2–4 sentences) ending at today, plus one line on education/credentials if relevant. Resist the urge to justify any gaps or changes here; save that for if it's asked directly.

    What are your strengths? Pick one or two, each with a one-sentence example, not a list of adjectives. "I take ownership end-to-end" means little without a concrete instance attached.

    What's a weakness you're working on? Why it matters: this question screens for self-awareness, not for an actual disqualifying flaw. Both failure modes are visible to interviewers:

    • The fake weakness: "I work too hard" or "I'm a perfectionist" — reads as evasive.
    • The disqualifying weakness: naming something core to the role as broken, with no mitigation.

    The answer that works is a real, specific, non-core pattern, stated plainly, with what you're doing about it:

    "Sometimes I don't fully trust the first solution I come up with, so I double-check it or consult others before committing — which can take more time than necessary. I'm working on setting a time limit for myself and moving forward with reasonable confidence after that."

    Where do you see yourself in 5 years? A short three-part shape works well: deepen technical expertise → take on more scope (mentoring, architecture-level ownership) → broaden into an adjacent skill if you have one (product collaboration, cross-functional work). Keep it to what's plausible from where you are now — a jump to "founder" or "VP" from an IC role reads as disconnected from reality.

    Why should we hire you? Map concrete skills to their stated needs directly:

    "I think my experience with [specific stack/domain] lines up closely with what you need for [specific thing in their posting]. Given the opportunity, I can show that quickly in practice."

    Avoid closing on a vague self-assessment ("I'm smart", "I'm a hard worker") — it's the weakest form of evidence available and undercuts an otherwise concrete answer.

    How do you handle mistakes or failure? Three beats: own it immediately, fix the immediate problem, then do a short root-cause pass so it doesn't repeat (a test, a process tweak, a monitoring gap closed). Ending on "I'd rather surface a mistake early than let it compound" signals maturity without needing a dramatic failure story.

    ✓ Key points
    • STAR keeps any behavioral answer to a predictable, scannable shape.
    • One well-chosen story usually answers several different questions from different angles.
    • A weakness answer needs to be real and non-core, paired with a concrete mitigation — not a disguised strength and not a core-skill admission.
    ❝ Interview line

    "Let me give you a quick example..." is a good way to transition from a general claim into the STAR structure without announcing "I'm now going to use the STAR method."

    ↑ Back to top⌂ Home
    ← PreviousHR Interview FundamentalsNext →Salary, Notice Period & Logistics Questions

    Chapter 9 · Hr

    Salary, Notice Period & Logistics Questions

    salary negotiationnotice periodlogisticsavailabilitycounteroffermilitary servicebackground questions
    See also HR Interview Fundamentals · STAR Method for Behavioral Questions
    On this page
    1. Salary expectations
    2. Notice period / availability
    3. Are you interviewing elsewhere / open to work?
    4. If your current employer made a counteroffer?
    5. Explaining a resume with shorter stints
    6. Administrative / background questions

    What: the practical, logistics-flavored questions that usually come near the end of an HR round.

    ℹ Why it matters

    these feel more "objective" than behavioral questions, which tempts people into over-explaining them the same way — the oversharing rule from HR Interview Fundamentals still applies.

    ↑ top

    Salary expectations

    Two competing instincts to balance: don't anchor low, but don't make the number the center of the conversation either.

    A working default:

    "I'd rather the company propose a number based on the level they see me at, and I'd expect a fair offer matching that level."

    If pressed for a specific figure, state your current compensation as context, then a preference, then (optionally) soften it if the role itself is compelling:

    "If it helps, I'm currently around [your number]. I'd want something in that range or a bit higher — though if the opportunity itself is a strong fit, the exact number matters less to me."

    Decide before the interview whether you're comfortable stating an exact figure or would rather give a range — don't decide live in the room.

    ↑ top

    Notice period / availability

    State the real number without justifying it:

    "My current contract has a one-month notice period, but I'll try to start sooner, or at least begin onboarding early, if possible."

    No need to explain why the notice period is what it is.

    ↑ top

    Are you interviewing elsewhere / open to work?

    Both a yes and a no are fine answers here — what matters is keeping it brief:

    "Yes, I'm exploring a few opportunities, but this one is a priority for me."

    No names of other companies, no stage-of-process details, no comparison of offers.

    ↑ top

    If your current employer made a counteroffer?

    Answer in terms of what you're optimizing for, not loyalty or disloyalty:

    "I'd weigh it against the long-term fit and growth I'm looking for, not just a retention offer — the reasons I'm looking to move usually aren't solved by a counteroffer alone."

    ↑ top

    Explaining a resume with shorter stints

    If your history includes a short role next to longer ones, lead with the long, stable one and frame the short one around genuine interest rather than circumstance:

    "My time at [long role] was a stable, multi-year run where I grew from [X] to [Y]. My most recent move was driven by genuine interest in [specific technical domain], and now I'm looking for the next place to build something long-term."

    ↑ top

    Administrative / background questions

    Depending on the country and company, HR may ask things like military service status, marital status, or where you live relative to the office. These aren't trick questions — answer them directly and briefly, the same oversharing discipline applies: a factual answer, not an explanation of the factual answer.

    ✓ Key points
    • Let the company anchor the salary number when possible; share your own number as context, not as the start of a negotiation.
    • Every logistics question still benefits from "answer, then stop."
    • A counteroffer question is really asking whether you're loyal to the job or to what the job gives you — answer in terms of fit and growth.
    ⚠ Common trap

    treating "are you interviewing elsewhere" as a question that needs a defensive non-answer. A brief, honest yes is a completely normal and expected answer — vagueness or visible discomfort reads worse than the plain truth.

    Design Problems

    Design Problems Overview

    7 pages. Each card says what the page covers and its key lines; open the page for the full depth.

    Chat System

    • Separate the stateful gateway (WebSockets) from stateless chat logic; estimate connections per server.
    • Store the message before acking "sent"; real-time push is best-effort and backed by sync from last seq.
    • Per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering, not client clocks; no need for global order.
    • Explain cross-server fan-out: session registry (user → gateway) + Redis Pub/Sub per gateway (or a broker), with the trade-off.
    Read the full page →

    Connection Pool (Nobitex round 2)

    Read the full page →

    Notification System

    • Accept with 202 and process async; make the idempotency key required for callers.
    • Queue per channel and per priority so OTPs never wait behind a campaign.
    • Retries with exponential backoff + jitter, separate retryable vs non-retryable errors, DLQ with replay.
    • Explain the three sources of duplicates and how each is handled; admit exactly-once to an external provider isn't possible.
    Read the full page →

    Order Book and Matching Engine

    • Define price-time priority and trade at the maker's price.
    • Data structures: sorted price levels + FIFO doubly linked list per level + order_id hash map (O(1) cancel); give complexities.
    • Single-threaded engine per market fed by one ordered log (sequencer) → no locks, deterministic.
    • Hold funds before matching; release/adjust after fills or cancel.
    Read the full page →

    Rate Limiter

    • Compare all five algorithms in one table and name the fixed-window edge burst problem.
    • Pick token bucket (bursts OK, 2 fields per key) and say why not sliding log (memory).
    • Show the race condition and solve it with an atomic Lua script; mention EVALSHA and single-slot keys in Redis Cluster.
    • Use one clock (Redis TIME) to avoid skew between servers.
    Read the full page →

    URL Shortener

    • Do the math: 7 base62 chars ≈ 3.5 trillion codes; 100:1 read:write; hot set fits in RAM.
    • Compare ID strategies (hash / random / counter / Snowflake) and explain why counter ranges + shuffle avoid both collisions and guessable codes.
    • Explain 301 vs 302 and connect it to the analytics requirement.
    • Cache-aside on the redirect path, plus negative caching for unknown codes and an in-process cache for hot links.
    Read the full page →

    Wallet and Ledger (Crypto Exchange)

    • Double-entry: every transfer sums to zero; balances are a cache of entries and can be rebuilt.
    • Never use float; integer smallest units or NUMERIC.
    • Prevent double spend with atomic conditional UPDATE (or SELECT FOR UPDATE in fixed order) + CHECK (amount >= 0).
    • Idempotency key UNIQUE in the same transaction as the entries.
    Read the full page →

    Design Problems

    Chat System

    On this page
    1. 1. Requirements
    2. 2. Estimates
    3. 3. API
    4. 4. Data model
    5. 5. High-level design
    6. 6. Deep dives
    7. 7. Wrap-up
    8. Interview checklist

    Design a chat app like WhatsApp/Telegram: 1:1 and small group chats, online/offline delivery, receipts and presence. Follows the 7-step framework.

    ↑ top

    1. Requirements

    Functional:

    • 1:1 chat and group chat (up to ~500 members).
    • Real-time delivery when the receiver is online; stored and delivered later when offline (+ mobile push).
    • Message history (scroll back), multi-device per user.
    • Sent / delivered / read receipts.
    • Presence: online / last seen.

    Non-functional:

    • Low latency: < 200 ms end to end within a region.
    • Ordering: messages in one conversation appear in the same order for everyone.
    • Durability: a message that got "sent ✓" is never lost.
    • High availability; eventual consistency is fine for presence and receipts.
    • Scale: 50M DAU.

    Out of scope: end-to-end encryption details (mention it), voice/video calls, media processing (upload to object storage, send a link), search.

    ↑ top

    2. Estimates

    • 50M DAU × 40 messages/day = 2B messages/day → 2×10⁹ / 10⁵ s ≈ 20k msg/s avg, peak ~60k/s.
    • Fan-out: average 1:1, groups bigger → deliveries ≈ 2–3× messages → ~150k deliveries/s at peak.
    • Concurrent connections: ~30% of DAU online at peak = 15M WebSockets. One tuned gateway server holds ~100k–500k idle connections (memory ~10–20 KB each); with 100k each → ~150 gateway servers.
    • Storage: 2B × ~200 B (text + metadata) = 400 GB/day → ~150 TB/year (before replication ×3). Media goes to object storage, not here.
    • Reads: users open a chat → load the last 50 messages; read-heavy on recent data.

    Conclusion: write-heavy, append-only, huge data → a wide-column store; connections need a separate stateful tier.

    ↑ top

    3. API

    Real-time over WebSocket (wss://chat.example.com/ws, authenticated with a token on connect):

    client → server
  send_message   {client_msg_id, conversation_id, body, sent_at}
  ack            {conversation_id, seq}          (delivered up to seq)
  read           {conversation_id, seq}          (read up to seq)
  typing         {conversation_id}
server → client
  message        {conversation_id, seq, message_id, sender_id, body, created_at}
  send_ack       {client_msg_id, message_id, seq}   ← this is the "sent ✓"
  receipt        {conversation_id, user_id, type: delivered|read, seq}
  presence       {user_id, status, last_seen}

    REST for the rest:

    GET  /conversations?cursor=                      → list with last message + unread count
GET  /conversations/{id}/messages?before_seq=&limit=50   → history page
POST /conversations  {member_ids}                → create group

    client_msg_id (UUID made on the device) is the idempotency key: if the client retries after a network drop, we don't store the message twice.

    ↑ top

    4. Data model

    messages (ScyllaDB / Cassandra):

    Column Note
    conversation_id partition key (with a time bucket, see below)
    bucket e.g. month — keeps partitions < ~100 MB
    seq clustering key DESC — per-conversation sequence number
    message_id, sender_id, body, created_at, client_msg_id

    Query "last 50 messages of conversation X" = one partition, already sorted → very fast.

    conversations / members (Postgres): conversations(id, type, created_at), members(conversation_id, user_id, role, last_read_seq, last_delivered_seq), index on (user_id) for "my chats".

    inbox (ScyllaDB): user_conversations(user_id, last_activity DESC, conversation_id) for the chat list.

    Presence / sessions (Redis): session:{user_id} → set of {device_id → gateway_id}, TTL refreshed by heartbeat.

    DB choice:

    • ScyllaDB/Cassandra for messages: LSM-tree, very high write throughput, linear scaling, partitioning by conversation matches the main query. ScyllaDB is the C++ rewrite with lower tail latency (Discord moved to it). Trade-off: no joins, no multi-row transactions, must design tables per query.
    • Postgres alternative: works up to a few billion rows with partitioning by time + index (conversation_id, seq), and sharding by conversation_id later (Citus). Simpler for a smaller company; harder at 400 GB/day.
    • Postgres for membership: small, relational, needs consistency.
    ↑ top

    5. High-level design

     mobile/web ──wss──► L4 LB ──► Gateway servers (stateful, hold WebSockets)
                                   │   ▲
                       send_message│   │ deliver
                                   ▼   │
                             Chat service (stateless)
                     ┌────────────┼──────────────┬─────────────────┐
                     ▼            ▼              ▼                 ▼
               Sequencer     ScyllaDB      Redis: sessions    Kafka "messages"
              (Redis INCR    (messages)    (user → gateway)        │
               per conv)                                           ▼
                                                     fan-out workers ──► gateway (via Redis Pub/Sub
                                                           │              channel per gateway)
                                                           └──► push service (APNs / FCM) if offline

    Send flow (A → B):

    1. A's gateway receives send_message, forwards to the chat service.
    2. Chat service checks membership, dedups by client_msg_id, gets seq = INCR seq:{conversation_id}.
    3. Writes the message to ScyllaDB (quorum write). Only now sends send_ack → A sees "sent ✓".
    4. Publishes to Kafka topic messages (key = conversation_id, so per-conversation order is kept).
    5. Fan-out worker reads members, looks up each member's sessions in Redis, publishes to the channel of each gateway that holds a member's connection.
    6. B's gateway pushes message to B's devices. B's client sends ack(seq) → "delivered ✓✓" goes back to A.
    7. Members with no live session → push notification via APNs/FCM.

    Reconnect / sync: client sends its last known seq per conversation; server returns everything after it from ScyllaDB. This makes delivery reliable even if a real-time push was lost.

    ↑ top

    6. Deep dives

    6.1 Connection gateway and cross-server fan-out

    Problem: 15M connections on ~150 servers. B is connected to gateway 87; the message was processed somewhere else. How does it reach gateway 87?

    Options:

    • Redis Pub/Sub, one channel per gateway (gw:87): fan-out worker looks up session:B → gw:87 → PUBLISH. Fast (sub-ms), simple. It is fire-and-forget: if the gateway is down, the message is dropped — OK because the message is already stored and the client re-syncs by seq. (Redis Pub/Sub notes)
    • Kafka/broker per gateway: durable, but thousands of consumers and higher latency for a "best-effort push" that is already backed by storage.
    • Direct gRPC from worker to gateway (service discovery by gateway ID): fewest hops; more connection management.

    Choice: Kafka for the durable "message accepted" stream (ordering, replay, multiple consumers: fan-out, push, search indexing, analytics), and Redis Pub/Sub per gateway for the last hop. Trade-off: two systems to run, but each does what it's good at — durable log vs low-latency fire-and-forget.

    Gateway notes: keep them thin (auth, heartbeats, forward); use a L4 load balancer (long-lived TCP); on deploy, drain connections gradually so 100k clients don't reconnect at once (add jitter to client reconnect).

    6.2 Ordering per conversation

    Problem: two users in a group send at the same moment; clocks on phones are wrong; messages must show in one order for all.

    Choice: a server-assigned, per-conversation sequence number (INCR seq:{conv} in Redis, or a counter column updated in the DB). The sequence is the order of truth; client timestamps are only for display. Kafka key = conversation_id keeps the order through fan-out. Clients sort by seq and detect gaps (got 41, 43 → fetch 42).

    Trade-off: the per-conversation counter is a tiny serialization point — fine, since a single conversation rarely exceeds a few msg/s. If Redis loses the counter, recover from max(seq) in ScyllaDB (persist with AOF to reduce risk). We don't need global ordering, only per conversation — saying that is a key point.

    6.3 Delivery and read receipts

    • Sent ✓: server stored it (step 3).
    • Delivered ✓✓: recipient device acked seq. Store last_delivered_seq per (member, conversation) — one number, not one row per message.
    • Read (blue): client sends read(seq); store last_read_seq. Unread count = latest_seq − last_read_seq.
    • In large groups, receipts are many (500 members × each message). Batch them (send at most every ~1 s), and show "read by N" lazily on request.
    • Delivery semantics: at-least-once with client dedup by message_id — retries and re-sync may send a message twice; the client ignores duplicates.

    6.4 Presence

    • Gateway sets presence:{user} = online with TTL 60 s, refreshed by heartbeats every 30 s. Disconnect or missing heartbeat → key expires → "last seen = t".
    • Fan-out of presence changes is expensive (a user with 500 contacts). So: push presence only to users who have that chat open (subscribe on open), others fetch on demand. Debounce flapping (bad mobile network) by waiting a few seconds before showing "offline".
    • Trade-off: presence is eventually consistent and slightly delayed — users accept that.
    ↑ top

    7. Wrap-up

    • Bottlenecks: gateway count (memory per connection), ScyllaDB write throughput (add nodes), huge groups (fan-out cost → switch to "pull" for channels with 10k+ members).
    • Failures:
    • Gateway dies → clients reconnect to another one and re-sync by seq; nothing lost.
    • Redis Pub/Sub message lost → client sync covers it.
    • ScyllaDB node down → RF=3 + quorum keeps working.
    • Push provider down → retry with backoff; messages are still in history.
    • Monitoring: connected sockets per gateway, send→deliver latency p99, Kafka consumer lag, push failure rate, reconnect storms.
    • Next: E2E encryption (Signal protocol: server stores only ciphertext), multi-region with users homed to a region, media pipeline.
    ↑ top

    Interview checklist

    • Separate the stateful gateway (WebSockets) from stateless chat logic; estimate connections per server.
    • Store the message before acking "sent"; real-time push is best-effort and backed by sync from last seq.
    • Per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering, not client clocks; no need for global order.
    • Explain cross-server fan-out: session registry (user → gateway) + Redis Pub/Sub per gateway (or a broker), with the trade-off.
    • Pick ScyllaDB/Cassandra with partition = conversation (+ time bucket), clustering = seq DESC; mention the Postgres partitioning alternative.
    • Receipts as last_delivered_seq / last_read_seq per member, not per message.
    • Offline users → APNs/FCM push; presence with heartbeats + TTL and limited fan-out.
    • Idempotency with client_msg_id for client retries.

    Design Problems

    Connection Pool (Nobitex round 2)

    On this page
    1. 1. Diagnosis (part 1, went well)
    2. 2. Requirements
    3. 3. Design
    4. 4. What I drew on the board
    5. 5. What to improve (design level, not syntax)

    A service runs at ~50 RPS. One day load goes to 5–6× and response time jumps to 20–30 s. Investigation shows getting a DB connection is slow. Root cause: connection handling (no pool / bad pool). Task: design and code a connection pool from scratch.

    ↑ top

    1. Diagnosis (part 1, went well)

    Questions I asked: API or worker? Read/write or CPU-heavy? Is there a cache? Where is the lag? Fixes I proposed: cache, connection pool, PgBouncer. The answer was the pool.

    Why load × 6 → latency × 1000: each request opened a new connection (TCP + TLS + auth + Postgres forks a process). At 300 RPS the DB spends its CPU on connection setup, hits max_connections, and new requests queue on connect. Latency grows with the queue, not linearly with load.

    ↑ top

    2. Requirements

    • Cap open connections at max_size.
    • Reuse idle connections; create new ones lazily up to the cap.
    • When all are busy, callers wait in order with a timeout.
    • A transaction must use one connection from BEGIN to COMMIT.
    • Never hand out a broken or dirty (mid-transaction) connection.
    • Recover from DB restart (health check, max lifetime).
    • Safe under concurrency (asyncio coroutines or threads).
    ↑ top

    3. Design

    caller ──acquire()──► [semaphore: max_size slots] ──► idle deque (LIFO) ──empty──► connect()
   ▲                                                                                  │
   └──────────── release() in finally: rollback if dirty / close if broken ◄──────────┘

    Code + table of why each line exists: Connection Pool from Scratch.

    ↑ top

    4. What I drew on the board

    Pseudocode, explained verbally; syntax details didn't matter.

    ConnectionPool (singleton):
  init(num_worker, conn_url)
  workers: queue<QueryWorker>; created_workers_count = 0
  def run_sql(query, atomic=False):
      worker = await first_worker()
      try: worker.run_query(...)
      except: ...
      workers.push(worker)
QueryWorker:  __enter__ / __exit__ (wanted a context manager)   run_query(q, timeout=30)   ping()
async first_worker():
      take an idle worker if any
      else if created_count < num_worker: create one (created_count += 1)
      else wait for one to be returned (channel)
    ↑ top

    5. What to improve (design level, not syntax)

    On the board Gap Better
    run_sql(query, atomic=False) on the pool each call can get a different conn, so begin / q1 / q2 / commit doesn't fit (I noticed this at the end) pool lends conns: async with pool.acquire() as conn, caller runs the txn
    context manager on QueryWorker I noticed during the interview it didn't fit, because callers never held the worker the context manager belongs on acquire(): enter = borrow, exit = return (conn stays open)
    created_count < max then create, then += 1 if creating awaits, many callers pass the check together → over the cap reserve the slot first (semaphore), give it back if connect fails
    waiting on a channel (added late) needs a timeout, otherwise requests pile up acquire timeout → PoolTimeout, fail fast
    return after except return must happen on every path; a broken or mid-txn conn shouldn't go back as-is return in finally; close if broken, rollback if in txn
    singleton it's per process; many workers/pods each have one total = procs × max_size < max_connections → PgBouncer

    Design Problems

    Notification System

    On this page
    1. 1. Requirements
    2. 2. Estimates
    3. 3. API
    4. 4. Data model
    5. 5. High-level design
    6. 6. Deep dives
    7. 7. Wrap-up
    8. Interview checklist

    Design a service that other teams call to send notifications by push (mobile), SMS and email — for example "deposit confirmed", "order filled", OTP codes, marketing campaigns. Follows the 7-step framework.

    ↑ top

    1. Requirements

    Functional:

    • Internal services send a notification: user_id, type (template), params, channels (or "use user preferences").
    • Channels: push (APNs/FCM), SMS (e.g. Kavenegar / a local SMS gateway), email (SMTP provider / SES).
    • Templates with variables and languages (fa/en).
    • User preferences: opt out per category/channel (marketing off, security always on), quiet hours.
    • Bulk campaigns: send to millions of users.
    • Status tracking: queued / sent / delivered / failed.

    Non-functional:

    • Reliability: transactional messages (OTP, withdrawal alerts) must not be lost; at-least-once delivery with deduplication → effectively once.
    • Priority: an OTP must not wait behind a 5M-user marketing campaign. OTP p99 < 5 s end to end.
    • Respect provider limits (SMS gateway may allow ~100–500 msg/s) and protect users from spam.
    • Scalable and horizontally extendable with new channels.

    Out of scope: in-app notification feed UI (mention it), A/B testing, building our own SMS/push infrastructure.

    ↑ top

    2. Estimates

    • 10M users. Transactional: ~10 notifications/user/day across channels → 100M/day ≈ 1,200/s avg, peak ~4k/s (market crash = many order fills).
    • Campaigns: 5M users in one campaign, to be sent within ~1 hour → ~1,400/s extra.
    • By channel (rough): push 80%, email 15%, SMS 5% → SMS ≈ 5M/day ≈ 60/s avg, but cost matters more than load (SMS costs money per message).
    • Storage: notification log row ~500 B × 100M/day = 50 GB/day; keep 90 days hot ≈ 4.5 TB → partition by day, archive older.

    Conclusion: load is moderate; the hard parts are reliability, priority, provider limits and dedup, not raw throughput.

    ↑ top

    3. API

    POST /v1/notifications
Header: Idempotency-Key: deposit-confirmed:tx_9f3a     (required)
{
  "user_id": 42,
  "template": "deposit_confirmed",
  "params": {"amount": "0.5", "asset": "BTC"},
  "channels": ["push", "sms"],          // optional; default = from preferences
  "priority": "high"                    // high | normal | low(bulk)
}
→ 202 Accepted {notification_id, status: "queued"}

GET  /v1/notifications/{id}               → status per channel
POST /v1/campaigns {template, segment_id, schedule_at}   → {campaign_id}
PUT  /v1/users/{id}/preferences {category, channel, enabled}
POST /v1/webhooks/{provider}              ← delivery reports from SMS/email/push providers

    202 because sending is async. The idempotency key is required — the caller (e.g. deposit service) may retry.

    ↑ top

    4. Data model

    Postgres (moderate write rate, needs uniqueness + transactions):

    Table Key columns Notes
    notifications id PK, idempotency_key UNIQUE, user_id, template, params JSONB, priority, created_at partitioned by day
    deliveries id PK, notification_id, channel, status, provider, provider_msg_id, attempts, last_error, updated_at index (provider_msg_id) for webhooks
    templates (name, channel, locale, version) PK, body, subject cached in memory
    preferences (user_id, category, channel) PK, enabled, quiet_hours cached in Redis
    devices (user_id, device_token) PK, platform, last_seen remove token when APNs/FCM says invalid

    Why Postgres: the unique constraint on idempotency_key gives dedup for free, and status updates are transactional. Trade-off: at much higher volume the log table could move to Cassandra/ClickHouse, but 1–4k/s writes is fine for Postgres with partitioning.

    ↑ top

    5. High-level design

     internal services ──► Notification API ──► Postgres (notification + deliveries, outbox)
                             │
                             ▼
                      router / fan-out  (prefs, quiet hours, template render, user rate limit)
                             │
        ┌────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
        ▼                    ▼                     ▼
  queue push.high       queue sms.high         queue email.high
  queue push.low        queue sms.low          queue email.low
        │                    │                     │
  push workers         SMS workers            email workers   (token bucket per provider)
        │                    │                     │
     APNs / FCM       SMS provider A / B      email provider
        └──────── delivery webhooks ───────► status updater ──► Postgres
                    failed after N retries ──► DLQ ──► alert / manual replay

    Flow:

    1. API validates, inserts notifications row (unique idempotency_key; duplicate → return the existing ID). In the same transaction, writes an outbox row.
    2. Outbox relay publishes to the router queue (no lost message if the API crashes after commit).
    3. Router loads preferences (Redis cache), drops channels the user disabled (except mandatory security types), applies quiet hours (delay low priority), checks per-user frequency limits, renders the template, and enqueues one job per channel into the right priority queue.
    4. Channel workers send via the provider, store provider_msg_id, mark sent.
    5. Provider webhook → mark delivered / failed.
    ↑ top

    6. Deep dives

    6.1 Queue per channel and priority

    Problem: one shared queue → a slow SMS provider or a 5M campaign blocks OTPs and push.

    Choice: separate queues per channel and per priority (sms.high, sms.low, ...). Each channel has its own worker pool, so a broken email provider never delays push. Workers always drain high first (or use more workers for high).

    Broker: RabbitMQ — this is a classic task queue: per-message ack, retries with TTL, dead-letter exchanges, priority queues are built in (why). Kafka would work for the event intake, but per-message retry/delay is harder there. Trade-off: RabbitMQ has lower max throughput than Kafka — fine at ~5k/s. (A Celery + Redis setup is also reasonable for a smaller team.)

    6.2 Retries, DLQ and provider failover

    • Retryable errors (timeout, 5xx, 429 from provider): retry with exponential backoff + jitter (e.g. 10 s, 30 s, 2 min, 10 min) using a delay/retry queue (RabbitMQ TTL queue → dead-letters back into the main queue).
    • Non-retryable (invalid phone, unregistered device token): mark failed, clean the token, no retry.
    • After N attempts → DLQ + alert. An admin tool can replay DLQ messages after a fix.
    • Provider failover for SMS: keep two providers; a circuit breaker per provider. If provider A's error rate passes 20%, route to B. Important for OTP.
    • Expiry: OTPs and price alerts become useless after a few minutes → set a TTL; don't send stale messages after an outage.

    6.3 Idempotency (no double SMS)

    Duplicates can come from three places:

    1. Caller retries → unique idempotency_key in notifications returns the existing row.
    2. Queue redelivery (worker crashed after sending, before ack) → before sending, the worker does an atomic state change: UPDATE deliveries SET status='sending' WHERE id=? AND status IN ('queued','retry') — 0 rows updated means someone else handled it. Optionally SET NX a Redis key sent:{delivery_id} with TTL.
    3. Provider ambiguity (timeout, did it send?) → pass our delivery_id as the provider's idempotency/reference ID when supported.

    Trade-off: there is still a small window (sent, then crash before marking sent) where one duplicate is possible — true exactly-once to an external provider is impossible. We minimize it and accept it, and say so.

    6.4 User preferences and rate limiting

    • Categories: security (OTP, login, withdrawal — cannot opt out), transactional (fills, deposits), marketing (opt-out, quiet hours 22:00–08:00 local time).
    • Preferences cached in Redis (prefs:{user}), invalidated on update; DB is the source of truth.
    • Per-user limit (e.g. max 3 marketing pushes/day, max 5 SMS/hour) with a Redis counter — protects users and SMS cost (rate limiter).
    • Per-provider limit: a token bucket in workers matching the provider's contract (e.g. 200 SMS/s). Excess waits in the queue — that's what queues are for.
    • Campaigns: don't enqueue 5M jobs at once; a campaign scheduler pages through the segment and enqueues in batches at a controlled rate, into low queues only.
    ↑ top

    7. Wrap-up

    • Bottlenecks: provider throughput and cost (SMS), not our servers. Postgres log table growth → daily partitions, drop/archive old ones.
    • Failures: provider down → circuit breaker + failover; RabbitMQ node down → quorum queues; worker crash → message redelivered, dedup protects user; router down → outbox keeps messages until it's back.
    • Monitoring: queue depth and age per queue (alert if sms.high oldest message > 10 s), send success rate per provider, delivery rate from webhooks, DLQ size, cost per day per channel, opt-out rate after campaigns.
    • Next: in-app inbox (store and show in the app), smart channel fallback (push not opened in 10 min → SMS for important messages), analytics on opens/clicks.
    ↑ top

    Interview checklist

    • Accept with 202 and process async; make the idempotency key required for callers.
    • Queue per channel and per priority so OTPs never wait behind a campaign.
    • Retries with exponential backoff + jitter, separate retryable vs non-retryable errors, DLQ with replay.
    • Explain the three sources of duplicates and how each is handled; admit exactly-once to an external provider isn't possible.
    • Preferences with mandatory security category, quiet hours, per-user frequency caps.
    • Respect provider rate limits with a token bucket; circuit breaker + second SMS provider.
    • Outbox pattern between the API's DB write and the queue.
    • Track delivery status via provider webhooks.
    ↑ Back to top⌂ Home

    Design Problems

    Order Book and Matching Engine

    On this page
    1. 1. Requirements
    2. 2. Estimates
    3. 3. API
    4. 4. Data model
    5. 5. High-level design
    6. 6. Deep dives
    7. 7. Wrap-up
    8. Interview checklist

    Design the core of a crypto exchange (like Nobitex): users place limit/market orders on markets like BTC-USDT or USDT-IRT; the engine matches them by price-time priority, produces trades, and streams market data. Follows the 7-step framework.

    ↑ top

    1. Requirements

    Functional:

    • Place limit and market orders (buy/sell); cancel orders.
    • Match by price-time priority: best price first; at the same price, earlier order first.
    • Partial fills; order status (open, partially filled, filled, cancelled).
    • Funds must be held before an order enters the book (no selling coins you don't have).
    • Publish trades and order-book updates (market data) to clients in real time.

    Non-functional:

    • Deterministic and correct: same input sequence → same trades, always. No lost or duplicated fills.
    • Low latency: matching in microseconds; order accept → ack p99 < 50 ms end to end (retail exchange, not HFT).
    • Throughput: ~50k orders/s peak across all markets; one hot market (USDT-IRT, BTC-USDT) can get ~10k/s.
    • Recoverable: after a crash, rebuild the exact book state with no data loss.
    • Fairness: strict ordering, no one jumps the queue.

    Out of scope: stop/OCO orders (they are a trigger layer on top), margin/futures, KYC, the full ledger (wallet design).

    ↑ top

    2. Estimates

    • 300 markets, 2M active traders. Normal: ~5k orders+cancels/s total; volatile peak 50k/s (bots cancel/replace a lot — cancels are often > 50% of messages).
    • Order message ≈ 200 B → 50k/s × 200 B = 10 MB/s into the log → Kafka handles this easily (~hundreds of MB/s per broker).
    • Trades: ~10% of orders match → ~5k trades/s peak → ~100M+ trades/day at peak days.
    • Book size in memory: a hot market may have ~100k open orders × ~100 B ≈ 10 MB. All markets ≪ 1 GB → the whole state fits in RAM on one machine.
    • Market data: 100k WebSocket clients; each update fanned out → must batch/throttle (e.g. depth snapshot every 100 ms) or it's millions of messages/s.

    Conclusion: matching itself is cheap CPU work in memory; the design is about ordering, determinism, durability and fan-out.

    ↑ top

    3. API

    POST   /v1/orders   Header: Idempotency-Key (client_order_id)
       {market: "BTC-USDT", side: "buy", type: "limit", price: "65000.00", qty: "0.25", tif: "GTC"}
       → 202 {order_id, status: "accepted"}        (final status comes via events)
DELETE /v1/orders/{order_id}                        → 202 {status: "cancel_requested"}
GET    /v1/orders?market=&status=open              → my orders
GET    /v1/markets/{m}/depth?limit=50              → {bids: [[price, qty]], asks: [...], seq}
GET    /v1/markets/{m}/trades?limit=100            → recent trades

WebSocket /ws
  subscribe {channel: "depth" | "trades" | "orders" (private), market}
  ← depth_update {market, seq, bids: [[p, q]], asks: [[p, q]]}   (q = 0 means remove level)
  ← trade {market, trade_id, price, qty, taker_side, ts}
  ← order_update {order_id, status, filled_qty, avg_price}

    seq on market data lets clients detect gaps and re-fetch a snapshot.

    ↑ top

    4. Data model

    In memory (engine, per market):

    OrderBook
  bids: sorted map price → PriceLevel   (highest first)
  asks: sorted map price → PriceLevel   (lowest first)
  orders: hash map order_id → *Order     (O(1) cancel)
PriceLevel
  price, total_qty
  queue: doubly linked list of Orders   (FIFO = time priority)
Order
  id, user_id, side, price, remaining_qty, seq, prev/next pointers

    Durable:

    Store Content Why
    Kafka orders.{market} (input log) every accepted command (new/cancel), in sequence source of truth for replay; ordered per partition
    Kafka events.{market} (output log) trades, order updates, book deltas many consumers: ledger, market data, history
    Postgres orders, trades queryable history for users/API written by consumers, not by the engine
    Snapshots (object storage / disk) full book state at seq N fast recovery

    Prices and quantities as fixed-point integers (price in 1e-8 units), never floats — determinism and exact money.

    ↑ top

    5. High-level design

     clients ──► API gateway ──► Order service ──(1) hold funds──► Ledger/Wallet (Postgres)
                                │
                                │ (2) append command
                                ▼
                    Kafka "orders" (1 partition per market = sequencer)
                                │
                                ▼
                     Matching engine (1 thread per market, in-memory book)
                                │ (3) events: trades, fills, cancels, book deltas
                                ▼
                    Kafka "events" (partition per market)
          ┌─────────────┬───────┴──────────┬─────────────────┐
          ▼             ▼                  ▼                 ▼
   settlement →    order/trade        market data        snapshotter
   ledger          history (PG)       service ──► Redis Pub/Sub ──► WS gateways ──► clients

    Place order flow:

    1. Order service validates (tick size, min qty, market open), checks idempotency (client_order_id).
    2. Holds funds in the ledger: buy 0.25 BTC @ 65,000 → hold 16,250 USDT (+ max fee). Insufficient → reject immediately.
    3. Appends NewOrder to Kafka partition of that market. The partition offset is the sequence number.
    4. Engine consumes in order, matches against the opposite side, emits Trade and OrderUpdate events, rests any remainder in the book.
    5. Settlement consumer applies trades to the ledger (move held quote → seller, base → buyer, fees; release unused hold), idempotent by trade_id.
    6. Market data service builds depth/trades streams and fans out.

    Cancel: same path (CancelOrder command in the same partition), so a cancel and a fill can never race — whichever is first in the log wins.

    ↑ top

    6. Deep dives

    6.1 Matching algorithm and data structures

    Incoming buy limit at price P, qty Q:

    while Q > 0 and asks not empty and best_ask.price <= P:
    level = best_ask
    while Q > 0 and level.queue not empty:
        maker = level.queue.head
        fill = min(Q, maker.remaining)
        emit Trade(price = level.price, qty = fill, maker, taker)   # trade at the MAKER's price
        Q -= fill; maker.remaining -= fill
        if maker.remaining == 0: remove maker (pop head, delete from orders map)
    if level empty: remove level
if Q > 0: rest order at P in bids (append to tail of level P)   # GTC; IOC → cancel rest

    Market order = same loop without the price check (with a protection limit to avoid sweeping the whole book in a thin market).

    Complexity:

    Operation Structure Cost
    Best bid/ask sorted map (red-black tree / skip list) min/max, or cached pointer O(1)–O(log L)
    Add at existing level hash map price → level, append to list tail O(1)
    New price level tree insert O(log L), L = number of levels
    Cancel orders[id] → unlink from doubly linked list O(1)
    Match one fill pop list head O(1)

    Why these structures: matching only ever touches the best level, and cancels (most messages) need O(1) lookup. An array indexed by price ticks is even faster for markets with a narrow price range, but wastes memory for wide ranges. Trade-off: tree = general and compact; array = fastest for hot markets. In Go: a B-tree/skip list for levels + container/list-style intrusive linked list; avoid allocations on the hot path (object pools).

    6.2 Single-threaded matching per market (sequencer)

    Problem: if two threads match the same book, we need locks, and results depend on thread timing → non-deterministic and slower under contention.

    Choice: one single-threaded engine per market, consuming a single ordered input (the Kafka partition = the sequencer). Like the LMAX architecture: no locks, CPU-cache friendly, millions of simple ops/s per core. Different markets are independent → run many markets in parallel (one goroutine/thread each, or spread across machines). Shard key = market.

    Trade-off: one market's throughput is capped by one core (~100k–1M+ orders/s with a careful implementation — far above our 10k/s). A hot market can't be split, but none needs to be at this scale.

    Determinism rules: no wall-clock reads in matching logic (timestamps come from the command), no randomness, no map iteration order dependence. Then replaying the same log yields the same book and the same trades.

    6.3 Balance holds before matching

    Problem: the engine must not check balances itself (that would need a DB call per order → slow and breaks determinism). But it must never match an order the user can't pay for.

    Choice: hold first, then match. The order service moves funds from available → held in the ledger (atomic conditional update) before the order goes into the log. The engine assumes every order is funded. After fills, settlement moves held funds to the counterparty; on cancel/expiry, the remainder is released.

    Trade-off: an extra synchronous DB write before each order (~a few ms). Bigger exchanges keep balances in the engine's memory (risk engine in the same sequenced pipeline) to avoid it — much faster but much more complex. For a retail exchange, the ledger hold is the right default.

    Edge case: a buy limit that fills at a better price → hold was larger than needed → release the difference at settlement.

    6.4 Persistence, recovery and market data

    Recovery via replay:

    • Input log (Kafka, replication factor 3, acks=all) is the source of truth.
    • The engine writes a snapshot of each book every N seconds (e.g. every 1M messages) with the last processed offset.
    • On crash: load the latest snapshot → replay commands from offset+1 → identical state. Recovery takes seconds.
    • Hot standby: a second engine consumes the same partition and stays in sync (deterministic), ready to take over. Output events carry the input offset; consumers dedup by (market, seq) so a takeover that re-emits events is harmless.

    Idempotent downstream: settlement uses trade_id (derived from market + input offset + fill index) as the ledger idempotency key → re-processed events never double-settle.

    Market data fan-out:

    • Engine emits per-level deltas (price, new_total_qty) with a sequence number.
    • Market data service keeps a copy of the book, publishes throttled depth updates (e.g. every 100 ms, top 50 levels) and every trade.
    • Fan-out to 100k WebSocket clients via gateways subscribed to Redis Pub/Sub channels per market. Client gets a REST snapshot with seq, then applies deltas; on a gap, re-fetch the snapshot.
    • Trade-off: throttling hides some intermediate states (fine for retail UIs); professional clients can get a raw full-depth feed.
    ↑ top

    7. Wrap-up

    • Bottlenecks: the ledger hold before each order (DB write rate), market-data fan-out (batch + throttle), one core per hot market (far from the limit).
    • Failures:
    • Engine crash → standby takes over / snapshot + replay; no order lost because the input was durable before ack.
    • Kafka broker down → RF=3, leader election; order intake pauses for seconds.
    • Settlement lag → balances update late but correctly; alert on consumer lag.
    • Bad input (bug) → halt the market (circuit breaker), fix, replay; exchanges prefer halting to wrong trades.
    • Monitoring: order → ack latency p99, engine processing time per message, Kafka lag per market, trades/s, settlement lag, reconciliation (sum of held funds = sum of open order values), WebSocket gap/resubscribe rate.
    • Next: stop orders, self-trade prevention, per-user rate limits for bots (rate limiter), co-located low-latency API for market makers.
    ↑ top

    Interview checklist

    • Define price-time priority and trade at the maker's price.
    • Data structures: sorted price levels + FIFO doubly linked list per level + order_id hash map (O(1) cancel); give complexities.
    • Single-threaded engine per market fed by one ordered log (sequencer) → no locks, deterministic.
    • Hold funds before matching; release/adjust after fills or cancel.
    • Input log as source of truth; snapshot + replay for recovery; hot standby.
    • Trades and events via Kafka; downstream idempotent by trade_id.
    • Market data: deltas with seq numbers, snapshot + delta protocol, throttling, Redis Pub/Sub fan-out.
    • Fixed-point integers, no floats; no wall-clock or randomness in matching.

    Rate Limiter

    On this page
    1. 1. Requirements
    2. 2. Estimates
    3. 3. API
    4. 4. Data model
    5. 5. High-level design
    6. 6. Deep dives
    7. 7. Wrap-up
    8. Interview checklist

    Design a distributed rate limiter that protects an API (for example an exchange's public and trading APIs) from abuse and overload. Follows the 7-step framework.

    ↑ top

    1. Requirements

    Functional:

    • Limit requests per key (user ID, API key, or IP) per rule (e.g. POST /orders: 10/s per user; public market data: 1,200/min per IP).
    • Rules are configurable without a deploy.
    • Rejected requests get HTTP 429 with headers telling the client when to retry.

    Non-functional:

    • Low overhead: < 1–2 ms added latency per request.
    • Distributed: the limit is global across all API servers, not per server.
    • Highly available: if the limiter fails, the API must keep working (fail open for most routes).
    • Accurate enough: small overshoot (a few %) is acceptable; big bursts at window edges are not.

    Out of scope: DDoS protection at the network layer (that's the CDN/WAF job), billing quotas per month.

    ↑ top

    2. Estimates

    • 10M DAU, peak 50k requests/s hitting the API gateway.
    • Each request = 1 Redis call (one Lua script) → 50k ops/s. One Redis node handles ~100k simple ops/s, but Lua scripts are heavier → use a Redis Cluster with 3–6 shards for headroom and HA.
    • Memory: active keys ≈ 10M users × 2 rules × ~100 B (token bucket = 2 fields) ≈ 2 GB. A sliding-window log would be much bigger: 100 req/min limit × 16 B per entry × 10M = 16 GB+ — one reason to avoid it at scale.
    • Latency budget: Redis round trip in the same DC ≈ 0.5 ms → fits.
    ↑ top

    3. API

    The limiter is a library/middleware in the API gateway, not a public API. Internal interface:

    allow(key="user:42", rule="orders_create") → {allowed: bool, remaining: int, reset_at: ts, retry_after_s: int}

    Responses to the client:

    200 OK
X-RateLimit-Limit: 10
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 3
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1759740000        (unix seconds when the window/bucket is full again)

429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2                        (seconds; standard HTTP header)
X-RateLimit-Limit: 10
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

    (The IETF draft standardizes RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset; many APIs still use the X- names.)

    ↑ top

    4. Data model

    Rules (Postgres or a YAML in a config service, cached in each gateway, reloaded every ~30 s):

    Field Example
    rule_id orders_create
    match POST /api/v1/orders
    key_type user / api_key / ip
    algorithm token_bucket
    capacity / refill_rate 20 tokens, 10 tokens/s
    fail_mode open / closed

    Counters (Redis, ephemeral, with TTL):

    • Token bucket: hash rl:{rule}:{key} → {tokens, ts}, TTL = time to fully refill.
    • Sliding window counter: rl:{rule}:{key}:{window_start} → count, TTL = 2 × window.

    Why Redis: in-memory (sub-ms), atomic Lua scripts, built-in TTL to clean up idle keys. Trade-off: it's another hop and a dependency; we must decide what happens when it's down.

    ↑ top

    5. High-level design

    client ──► CDN/WAF ──► API gateway (rate-limit middleware) ──► backend services
                          │    ▲
                          │    │ rules (cached, refreshed every 30 s)
                          │  config service / Postgres
                          ▼
                    Redis Cluster (counters, Lua scripts)

    Flow:

    1. Request arrives at the gateway; middleware finds matching rules and builds the key (user:42, or IP if unauthenticated).
    2. Calls EVALSHA with the token-bucket script on Redis → gets allowed, remaining, retry_after.
    3. Allowed → forward to backend, add X-RateLimit-* headers. Denied → return 429 + Retry-After immediately (no backend work).
    4. Redis timeout (> 5 ms) or error → apply the rule's fail_mode (open by default), increment a metric.

    Putting it in the gateway (not in each service) means one place for rules and rejected requests never reach the backend.

    ↑ top

    6. Deep dives

    6.1 Choosing the algorithm

    Algorithm How Bursts Memory per key Accuracy Note
    Fixed window counter per minute INCR + EXPIRE 2× burst at the window edge (limit at 0:59 and again at 1:00) 1 int low at edges simplest
    Sliding window log sorted set of timestamps; drop old, count rest none O(limit) — one entry per request exact too much memory at high limits
    Sliding window counter current + previous window counts, weighted: prev × (1 − elapsed/window) + curr small 2 ints ~approximate (assumes even spread) good general default
    Token bucket bucket of N tokens, refills at r/s; each request takes 1 allows controlled bursts up to capacity 2 fields exact for its model used by AWS, Stripe
    Leaky bucket requests enter a queue, processed at a fixed rate smooths output, no bursts queue exact shapes traffic; adds waiting, not a pure reject

    Choice: token bucket for user/API-key limits: it allows short bursts (a trading bot sends 5 orders at once) but enforces the average rate, and needs only 2 fields. Sliding window counter is a fine choice for simple "N per minute" public limits. Trade-off: token bucket has two knobs (capacity, rate) that are a bit harder to explain to API users than "100 per minute".

    6.2 Atomic implementation in Redis (Lua)

    Problem: "read tokens → compute → write tokens" from two gateways at the same time is a race: both read 1 token, both allow. GET + SET is not atomic.

    Options: WATCH/MULTI (optimistic, retries under contention), a distributed lock (slow), or a Lua script (Redis runs it atomically, single-threaded). Choice: Lua.

    -- KEYS[1] = bucket key; ARGV = capacity, refill_per_sec, now_ms, cost
local cap    = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost   = tonumber(ARGV[4])

local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now

-- refill based on elapsed time
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)

local allowed = 0
local retry_ms = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
else
  retry_ms = math.ceil((cost - tokens) / rate * 1000)
end

redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate * 1000))
return {allowed, math.floor(tokens), retry_ms}

    Notes:

    • Load once with SCRIPT LOAD, call with EVALSHA (less bandwidth).
    • Clock: gateways' clocks may differ. Safer: use Redis time inside the script (redis.call('TIME')), so one clock decides. (Allowed since Redis 5 with effect replication.)
    • In Redis Cluster, a script may only touch keys in one slot — fine here (one key). For multi-key scripts, use hash tags rl:{user:42}:....
    • cost lets heavy endpoints consume more tokens (e.g. a batch order = 5).

    6.3 Distributed concerns

    • Per-server local limits (no Redis) are fast but wrong: with 20 gateways, a user can get 20× the limit if the LB spreads requests. Only OK as a coarse first layer.
    • Hot keys: one abusive IP at 20k/s hits one Redis shard. Add a local in-memory pre-limiter in each gateway (e.g. deny an IP locally for 1 s after Redis says it is far over the limit). Cuts Redis load for attackers.
    • Batching / approximate mode: for very high QPS, each gateway can take tokens in chunks (lease 10 tokens at once) and count locally. Fewer Redis calls, small overshoot. Trade-off: accuracy vs load.
    • Multi-region: a global exact limit needs cross-region coordination (~100 ms) — too slow. Use per-region limits (global limit ÷ regions) or async sync between regions; accept some overshoot.
    • Fail open vs fail closed: if Redis is down, fail open for read/public routes (availability first), but for sensitive routes (login, withdrawal, OTP) fail closed or use a strict local limit — abuse there is more costly than a short outage.

    6.4 Client experience

    • Always return Retry-After on 429, so well-behaved clients back off instead of retrying in a tight loop.
    • Different limits per tier (free vs VIP market maker) come from the rule lookup by API key.
    • Log rejections with the key and rule — support needs to answer "why am I blocked?".
    ↑ top

    7. Wrap-up

    • Bottleneck: Redis throughput on hot keys → local pre-limiter + cluster sharding by key.
    • Failures: Redis shard down → replica promotion (seconds); during that time fail_mode decides. Config service down → gateways keep the last cached rules.
    • Monitoring: 429 rate per rule (spikes = attack or a bad client release), limiter latency p99, Redis CPU/ops, fail-open count (alert if > 0 for long).
    • Next: adaptive limits based on backend health (load shedding), per-endpoint cost weights.
    ↑ top

    Interview checklist

    • Compare all five algorithms in one table and name the fixed-window edge burst problem.
    • Pick token bucket (bursts OK, 2 fields per key) and say why not sliding log (memory).
    • Show the race condition and solve it with an atomic Lua script; mention EVALSHA and single-slot keys in Redis Cluster.
    • Use one clock (Redis TIME) to avoid skew between servers.
    • Put the limiter in the gateway; return 429 + Retry-After + X-RateLimit-* headers.
    • Discuss fail open vs fail closed per route (login/withdraw closed, market data open).
    • Mention hot keys, local pre-limiting, and multi-region trade-offs.

    URL Shortener

    On this page
    1. 1. Requirements
    2. 2. Estimates
    3. 3. API
    4. 4. Data model
    5. 5. High-level design
    6. 6. Deep dives
    7. 7. Wrap-up
    8. Interview checklist

    Design a service like bit.ly: turn a long URL into a short link (sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x) and redirect visitors to the long URL. Follows the 7-step framework.

    ↑ top

    1. Requirements

    Functional:

    • Create a short link for a long URL (optional custom alias, optional expiry).
    • Redirect GET /{code} to the long URL.
    • Basic click analytics per link (count, by day, by country/referrer).

    Non-functional:

    • Read-heavy: ~100 redirects per 1 create.
    • Low latency redirect: p99 < 50 ms server-side.
    • High availability for redirects (a dead link breaks every page that uses it). Creation can be slightly less available.
    • Short codes must be unique and not easy to guess in order (no one should scan all links).
    • Durability: a created link must never be lost.

    Out of scope: user accounts/billing, link editing, spam/malware scanning (mention it), custom domains.

    ↑ top

    2. Estimates

    • Writes: 100M new links/month ≈ 3.3M/day → 3.3M / 10⁵ s ≈ ~40 creates/s, peak ~100/s.
    • Reads: 100:1 → ~4,000 redirects/s avg, peak ~10–12k/s.
    • Storage: one row ≈ 500 B (code, long URL ~ 200 B, timestamps, owner). 100M/month × 12 × 5 years = 6B links × 500 B ≈ 3 TB over 5 years.
    • Code length: base62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9). 62⁶ ≈ 57B, 62⁷ ≈ 3.5T. 7 chars is plenty for 6B links (and leaves room for sparse/random IDs).
    • Bandwidth: redirect response is tiny (~500 B) → 12k/s × 0.5 KB ≈ 6 MB/s. Not a problem.
    • Cache: 80/20 rule — 20% of links get most traffic. Hot set of ~10M links × 500 B ≈ 5 GB → fits one Redis node (with a replica).
    • Analytics events: = redirects → ~4k events/s avg, ~350M/day × ~100 B ≈ 35 GB/day raw.

    Conclusion: writes are tiny (one Postgres primary is enough); reads need a cache; analytics needs an async pipeline.

    ↑ top

    3. API

    POST /api/v1/links          {long_url, custom_alias?, expires_at?}
                            Header: Idempotency-Key (optional)
                            → 201 {code, short_url, long_url, expires_at}
GET  /{code}                → 302 Location: <long_url>   (404 if unknown, 410 if expired)
GET  /api/v1/links/{code}/stats?from=&to=  → {total_clicks, by_day[], top_countries[]}
DELETE /api/v1/links/{code} → 204

    Rate-limit POST per API key / IP (see rate limiter) to stop abuse.

    ↑ top

    4. Data model

    links (Postgres):

    Column Type Note
    code varchar(10) PK
    long_url text
    owner_id bigint nullable; index (owner_id, created_at) for "my links"
    created_at timestamptz
    expires_at timestamptz nullable

    click_events (ClickHouse): (code, ts, country, referrer, user_agent_family), ordered by (code, ts), partitioned by month.

    DB choice:

    • Postgres for links: 40 writes/s and a 3 TB table is fine with one primary + read replicas; the access pattern is a single PK lookup. A key-value store (DynamoDB/Cassandra) would also work and scales writes more easily, but we don't need it at this size. Trade-off: if we grow 100×, we shard by code (hash), which is easy because every query is by code.
    • ClickHouse for analytics: columnar, fast GROUP BY over billions of rows, cheap compression. Trade-off: not for point updates, but click events are append-only.
    ↑ top

    5. High-level design

                        ┌───────────── create ─────────────┐
client ──► LB ──► API servers ──► ID allocator (ranges) │
   │                 │   └──► Postgres primary ──► replicas
   │                 │
   └── GET /{code} ──► redirect servers ──► Redis cache ──(miss)──► Postgres replica
                          │
                          └── click event ──► Kafka ──► analytics consumers ──► ClickHouse

    Create flow:

    1. API validates the URL (scheme http/https, length ≤ 2 KB, optional blocklist check).
    2. Gets the next numeric ID from its local ID range (see deep dive), encodes it to base62.
    3. Inserts into Postgres. Custom alias → insert with that code; unique PK violation → 409 Conflict.
    4. Optionally writes the new link into Redis (write-through), returns the short URL.

    Redirect flow:

    1. Look up code in Redis (GET link:{code}). Hit (~95%+) → respond.
    2. Miss → read from a Postgres replica, put into Redis with TTL (e.g. 24 h), respond.
    3. Not found → cache a short "negative" entry (60 s) so bots scanning random codes don't hammer the DB.
    4. Publish a click event to Kafka asynchronously (fire-and-forget from a local buffer); the redirect never waits for analytics.
    ↑ top

    6. Deep dives

    6.1 Generating unique short codes

    Problem: 40–100 creates/s across many API servers; codes must be unique, short (7 chars), and not trivially enumerable.

    Options:

    Option How Pros Cons
    Hash of URL (MD5/SHA → first 7 base62 chars) base62(md5(url))[:7] stateless, same URL → same code (dedup) collisions (must check DB and retry with salt); dedup is wrong if two users want separate stats
    Random 7 chars secrets.choice × 7 simple, not guessable collision check on every insert (rare at 6B/3.5T ≈ 0.2%, but grows)
    Single DB auto-increment + base62 nextval() → base62 no collisions, short one sequence = bottleneck/SPOF; codes are sequential = guessable
    Snowflake (64-bit: time + machine + seq) per-server generator no coordination, time-ordered 64-bit number → 11 base62 chars, too long for a short link
    Counter ranges each server leases a block (e.g. 1,000 IDs) from a coordinator (Postgres row / Redis INCRBY / ZooKeeper) no collisions, no per-request coordination lost IDs when a server dies (gaps are fine); sequential inside a block

    Choice: counter ranges. A server does UPDATE id_ranges SET next = next + 1000 RETURNING next (or Redis INCRBY ids 1000) once per 1,000 links — that is < 1 coordinator call per second. To make codes not guessable, pass the counter through a reversible bit-shuffle (e.g. a small Feistel cipher / format-preserving permutation over the ID space) before base62. Unique in, unique out — no collision check needed.

    Trade-off: we need a small coordinator and a little crypto-ish code; in return we get guaranteed uniqueness and short codes. For custom aliases we still rely on the PK unique constraint.

    6.2 301 vs 302 redirect

    301 Moved Permanently 302 Found (or 307)
    Browser caching browser caches it; next click never reaches us every click hits our server
    Load on us lower higher
    Analytics lost after the first click accurate
    Can change/expire link hard (browsers remember) easy

    Choice: 302 (or 307), because analytics and expiry are requirements. Add Cache-Control: private, max-age=0. Trade-off: more traffic to us (~4k/s), which the cache handles easily. If a customer doesn't want analytics, 301 is a valid option to save cost.

    6.3 Caching the redirect path

    • Cache-aside with Redis, key link:{code} → long_url|expires_at, TTL 24 h; LRU eviction (allkeys-lru).
    • 5 GB hot set fits one node; one replica for failover. Redis does ~100k ops/s → 12k/s peak is ~12% load.
    • Hot link (viral link, 50k/s on one key): add a tiny in-process LRU (e.g. 10k entries, TTL 60 s) in each redirect server; that removes most Redis traffic for the hottest keys.
    • Delete/expiry: on delete, DEL link:{code}; the in-process cache TTL bounds staleness to 60 s. Trade-off: a deleted link may still redirect for up to a minute — acceptable here, and we say it out loud.
    • Optional: put a CDN in front of redirects with a short TTL for the very hottest links (costs analytics accuracy; the CDN logs can feed analytics instead).

    6.4 Analytics without slowing redirects

    Problem: 4k–12k click events/s; writing each to a DB synchronously would add latency and load.

    Choice: redirect servers push events to Kafka (topic clicks, key = code). Why Kafka over RabbitMQ: high throughput, retention, and multiple consumers (analytics, fraud, billing) can read the same stream (comparison). Consumers batch-insert into ClickHouse every ~1 s or 10k rows (ClickHouse prefers big batches). A pre-aggregated table (clicks_per_code_per_day, materialized view) serves the stats API fast.

    Trade-off: stats are eventually consistent (seconds behind) and at-least-once — a consumer crash can double-count a batch. Acceptable for click stats; if exactness matters, add an event ID and deduplicate (ReplacingMergeTree).

    ↑ top

    7. Wrap-up

    • Bottlenecks: the redirect path is all reads → Redis + replicas scale it. Writes are tiny. At 100× growth: shard Postgres by hash(code) or move links to a KV store.
    • Failures:
    • Redis down → fall back to Postgres replicas (protect them with a circuit breaker + in-process cache).
    • Postgres primary down → creates fail (promote replica); redirects keep working from cache + replicas.
    • Kafka down → buffer events locally for a short time, then drop them; never block redirects.
    • ID coordinator down → servers keep using their current range; only new leases fail.
    • Abuse: rate limit creation, scan URLs against a malware/phishing list, allow takedown.
    • Monitoring: redirect p99 latency, cache hit ratio (alert < 90%), 404 rate (scanning bots), Kafka consumer lag, create error rate.
    ↑ top

    Interview checklist

    • Do the math: 7 base62 chars ≈ 3.5 trillion codes; 100:1 read:write; hot set fits in RAM.
    • Compare ID strategies (hash / random / counter / Snowflake) and explain why counter ranges + shuffle avoid both collisions and guessable codes.
    • Explain 301 vs 302 and connect it to the analytics requirement.
    • Cache-aside on the redirect path, plus negative caching for unknown codes and an in-process cache for hot links.
    • Analytics is async via Kafka → the redirect never waits; stats are eventually consistent.
    • Mention abuse: rate limiting, malicious URL checks, expiry.
    • Say clearly that one Postgres primary is enough for writes — don't shard prematurely.
