    Design Problems

    Wallet and Ledger (Crypto Exchange)

    On this page
    1. 1. Requirements
    2. 2. Estimates
    3. 3. API
    4. 4. Data model
    5. 5. High-level design
    6. 6. Deep dives
    7. 7. Wrap-up
    8. Interview checklist

    Design the wallet/ledger of a crypto exchange (like Nobitex): users hold balances in many assets (IRT, USDT, BTC, ...), deposit and withdraw on-chain, and trade. Money must never be created, lost or double-spent. Follows the 7-step framework.

    ↑ top

    1. Requirements

    Functional:

    • Per user, per asset balance: available and held (locked for open orders / pending withdrawals).
    • Deposits: detect on-chain transactions to the user's deposit address, credit after N confirmations.
    • Withdrawals: user requests → hold funds → risk checks → sign and broadcast → mark done after confirmations (or refund on failure).
    • Internal transfers: trade settlement (from the matching engine), fees, transfers between users.
    • Transaction history for the user; full audit trail for finance/regulators.

    Non-functional:

    • Correctness over everything: no negative balances, no double spend, no lost money. Strong consistency → CP, not AP.
    • Idempotent operations: every retry is safe.
    • Auditable: immutable history; any balance can be rebuilt from entries.
    • Latency: balance update p99 < 50 ms (trading depends on it).
    • Availability 99.95%; short write unavailability is better than wrong balances.

    Out of scope: KYC, fiat bank integration details, the matching engine itself (separate design), cold storage key management (mention HSM/multisig).

    ↑ top

    2. Estimates

    • 10M users, ~1M active/day. ~20 assets → up to 200M balance rows, most are zero → store only non-zero (~20M rows).
    • Ledger writes: trades are the main source. 2M trades/day → each trade touches 4 accounts (buyer base/quote, seller base/quote) + fee accounts → ~6 entries/trade → 12M entries/day + deposits/withdrawals (~500k/day) → ~13M/day ≈ 150 entries/s avg, peak ~2k/s (volatile market = 10× normal).
    • Storage: entry ≈ 200 B → 13M × 200 B ≈ 2.6 GB/day ≈ ~1 TB/year. Keep forever (audit) → partition by month.
    • Reads: balance reads ~5k/s (app, order placement checks).

    Conclusion: a single well-tuned Postgres primary handles this write rate; the hard part is correctness under concurrency, not scale.

    ↑ top

    3. API

    Internal (called by trading, deposit and withdrawal services):

    POST /v1/transfers                Header: Idempotency-Key: trade:8812:settle
  {entries: [{account, asset, amount(+/-)}...], type: "trade_settlement", ref_id}
  → 201 {transfer_id}  |  409 duplicate (returns original)  |  422 insufficient_funds

POST /v1/holds    {user_id, asset, amount, reason, ref_id}  → {hold_id}
POST /v1/holds/{id}/release
POST /v1/holds/{id}/capture  {to_account}                   (hold → real transfer)

    User-facing:

    GET  /v1/balances                        → [{asset, available, held}]
GET  /v1/transactions?asset=&cursor=     → history
POST /v1/withdrawals  Header: Idempotency-Key   {asset, amount, address, network, otp}
GET  /v1/deposits/address?asset=&network=      → deposit address (+ memo/tag)

    Amounts are integers in the smallest unit (satoshi, wei, rial) or NUMERIC(38,18) — never float.

    ↑ top

    4. Data model

    Postgres (ACID transactions, row locks, constraints — exactly what a ledger needs):

    Table Key columns Notes
    accounts id PK, owner_id (user or system), asset, type (user_available, user_held, fee, hot_wallet, deposit_suspense...) UNIQUE (owner_id, asset, type)
    balances account_id PK, amount NUMERIC, allow_negative bool CHECK (allow_negative OR amount >= 0): only system accounts may go negative
    transfers id PK, idempotency_key UNIQUE, type, ref_id, created_at one business operation
    entries id PK, transfer_id, account_id, amount (+ credit / − debit), created_at append-only; index (account_id, id); partitioned by month
    deposits (chain, tx_hash, output_index) UNIQUE, user_id, asset, amount, confirmations, status dedup of chain events
    withdrawals id PK, user_id, asset, amount, address, status, tx_hash, hold_id state machine
    outbox id PK, topic, payload, created_at, published_at see deep dive

    Double-entry rule: every transfer's entries sum to zero per asset. Money only moves between accounts; it's never created. Simple sign convention: system accounts like hot_wallet mirror the outside world and go negative when money enters. A 0.5 BTC deposit is hot_wallet −0.5 and user_available +0.5 → sum = 0. So −hot_wallet always equals what the exchange should hold on-chain, which is exactly what reconciliation checks.

    Holds are just transfers between user_available and user_held accounts — same rules, same audit trail.

    ↑ top

    5. High-level design

     matching engine ─(trades via Kafka)─┐
 user API ──► withdrawal service ────┤
                                     ▼
                       Ledger service (stateless) ──► Postgres primary (ledger, balances, outbox)
                                     │                     │ sync replica (HA)  async replicas (reads)
                                     │                     ▼
                                     │               outbox relay ──► Kafka "ledger-events"
                                     │                                   │
 blockchain nodes ──► chain watchers ──► deposit service ──┘              ├─► notification service
                                                                         ├─► user history / analytics
 signer (HSM, isolated) ◄── withdrawal service ──► broadcast              └─► reconciliation jobs

    Trade settlement: ledger consumes a trade event, builds the 4–6 entries, runs them in one DB transaction keyed by idempotency_key = trade:{trade_id}.

    Withdrawal: create hold (available → held) → risk/AML + limits + OTP check → signer signs, broadcast → watcher sees N confirmations → capture hold (user_held −X, hot_wallet +X). Failure/rejection → release hold.

    Deposit: chain watcher sees tx to a user's address → record deposits row (status pending) → after N confirmations → credit user in one transaction.

    ↑ top

    6. Deep dives

    6.1 Updating balances safely under concurrency

    Problem: a user places two orders and a withdrawal at the same time; each checks "balance ≥ amount" then subtracts. Without care, both pass → negative balance / double spend.

    Options:

    1. Pessimistic lock: SELECT ... FROM balances WHERE account_id IN (...) ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE, check, update, insert entries, commit. Lock rows in a fixed order (by id) to avoid deadlocks.
    2. Atomic conditional update: UPDATE balances SET amount = amount - :x WHERE account_id = :a AND amount >= :x → 0 rows updated = insufficient funds. No read-then-write gap; the row lock is held only for the statement + transaction.
    3. Optimistic lock: UPDATE ... SET amount = :new, version = version + 1 WHERE account_id = :a AND version = :v → retry on conflict. Bad under contention (hot accounts like fee).
    4. Single-writer per account (shard accounts to in-memory processors, like the matching engine): very fast, but much more complex; used by the biggest exchanges.

    Choice: (2) conditional updates inside one transaction, plus CHECK (amount >= 0) as a final safety net. Simple, fast, correct, and the DB does the hard work.

    Hot accounts: the fee account is credited by every trade → lock contention. Fix: split into N sub-accounts (fee_0..fee_15, pick by trade_id % 16) and sum them for reporting. Trade-off: reads must aggregate.

    Isolation: READ COMMITTED is enough with conditional updates/row locks; SERIALIZABLE also works but adds retries.

    6.2 Idempotency

    Every ledger call has an idempotency key derived from the business event (trade:{id}, deposit:{chain}:{tx_hash}:{vout}, withdrawal:{id}:capture). It's inserted into transfers in the same transaction as the entries. A retry hits the UNIQUE constraint → we return the original result. Because it's one transaction, there's no state where entries exist without the key or vice versa.

    Kafka consumers (trade settlement) are at-least-once, so this is what makes re-processing safe.

    6.3 Outbox pattern for events

    Problem: after committing a transfer we must publish balance_changed / withdrawal_completed to Kafka. If we commit then crash before publishing → event lost. If we publish then the commit fails → ghost event.

    Choice: transactional outbox. Insert the event into the outbox table in the same transaction as the entries. A relay process (polling WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id, or CDC with Debezium reading the WAL) publishes to Kafka and marks it published. Delivery is at-least-once → consumers dedup by event ID. Trade-off: a small delay (ms to ~1 s) and one more component, in exchange for no lost or ghost events (Kafka notes).

    6.4 Deposits, confirmations and reconciliation

    Confirmations: credit only after N confirmations to be safe from chain reorgs (e.g. BTC ~2–3 for small amounts, up to 6 for large; ETH waits for finality ~2 epochs ≈ 13 min, or a block depth like 12–64; Tron ~19–20). Show as "pending" before that; optionally let users trade but not withdraw a pending deposit (exchange takes the reorg risk).

    Reorg handling: watcher tracks block hashes; if a block with a credited deposit is orphaned before N confirmations, the pending deposit is cancelled. Unique (chain, tx_hash, output_index) prevents crediting the same output twice.

    Reconciliation (daily + continuous):

    • Internal: for each asset, sum of all entries = 0; balances.amount = sum of that account's entries (rebuild check).
    • External: sum of user liabilities ≤ on-chain holdings (hot + cold wallets, from node queries) — this is the base of proof of reserves.
    • Withdrawals: every completed withdrawal has a matching on-chain tx; every outgoing on-chain tx has a withdrawal record (detects stolen hot-wallet funds).
    • Mismatch → alert and pause withdrawals for that asset automatically.

    Auditability: entries are append-only (no UPDATE/DELETE; corrections are new reversing transfers), DB role for the app has no DELETE on entries, and every transfer stores who/what caused it (type, ref_id, actor).

    ↑ top

    7. Wrap-up

    • Bottlenecks: hot accounts (split them), single Postgres primary (shard by user_id later — but cross-shard transfers then need sagas; stay on one primary as long as possible).
    • Failures:
    • Primary down → failover to a synchronous replica (no data loss, RPO = 0).
    • Ledger service crash mid-request → transaction rolls back; the client retries with the same key.
    • Kafka down → outbox accumulates, nothing lost.
    • Blockchain node lagging → deposits delayed (alert on node height vs public explorers).
    • Security: signer isolated with HSM, most funds in cold storage/multisig, withdrawal limits + manual review for large amounts, address allowlists.
    • Monitoring: reconciliation diff (must be 0), negative-balance check failures, withdrawal queue age, pending deposits by confirmations, outbox lag, hot-wallet balance vs threshold.
    ↑ top

    Interview checklist

    • Double-entry: every transfer sums to zero; balances are a cache of entries and can be rebuilt.
    • Never use float; integer smallest units or NUMERIC.
    • Prevent double spend with atomic conditional UPDATE (or SELECT FOR UPDATE in fixed order) + CHECK (amount >= 0).
    • Idempotency key UNIQUE in the same transaction as the entries.
    • Outbox pattern to publish events reliably.
    • Holds as transfers available → held; withdrawals as a state machine with refund on failure.
    • Deposits after N confirmations, reorg handling, unique (tx_hash, output_index).
    • Reconciliation internal and against the blockchain; auto-pause withdrawals on mismatch.
